This section covers overhead, gantry and similar cranes [29cfr1910.179(b)(1)]. Only employer-selected, qualified ("designated") people may operate them [29cfr1910.179(a)(35)] [29cfr1910.179(b)(8)]. Rated load, the design maximum, must be marked [29cfr1910.179(a)(50)] [29cfr1910.179(b)(5)]. Exceed it only for permitted tests [29cfr1910.179(n)(1)]: test loads stay within 125 percent unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise [29cfr1910.179(k)(2)]. New cranes from August 31, 1971 follow ANSI B30.2.0-1967 design specifications [29cfr1910.179(b)(2)].

Space limits: 3 inches overhead and 2 sideways [29cfr1910.179(b)(6)(i)]; 3 around cabs [29cfr1910.179(c)(1)(ii)]; access gaps up to 12 inches (30 cm) [29cfr1910.179(c)(2)]. Footwalks need 48 inches headroom and 50 pounds per square foot strength [29cfr1910.179(d)(1)(ii)] [29cfr1910.179(d)(2)(i)]. Guards must hold a 200-pound person unless stepping there is impossible [29cfr1910.179(e)(6)(iii)].

Bumpers, with exceptions: bridge deceleration averages at most 3 ft/s/s at 20 percent rated speed, with energy capacity for at least 40 percent [29cfr1910.179(e)(2)(i)] [29cfr1910.179(e)(2)(i)(a)]; trolleys, 4.7 at one-third [29cfr1910.179(e)(3)(i)]. Hoist holding brakes need 125 percent torque with nonmechanical control braking, 100 with mechanical, or 100 each for two [29cfr1910.179(f)(2)(i)]. Hot-metal hoists with power control braking need two [29cfr1910.179(f)(2)(vi)]. Foot brakes need at most 70 pounds for rated torque [29cfr1910.179(f)(4)(i)]. Stopping feet at full speed and load equal 10 percent of feet-per-minute speed [29cfr1910.179(f)(4)(vii)].

Voltage limits: control 600; pendant buttons 150 AC, 300 DC; cab or bridge receptacles on cab cranes 300 [29cfr1910.179(g)(1)] [29cfr1910.179(g)(7)]. Rope load per part stays within 20 percent of breaking strength [29cfr1910.179(h)(2)(i)]. Keep two drum wraps [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)(viii)]. Retighten clip nuts after a new rope's first hour [29cfr1910.179(h)(2)(v)].

Each shift, try upper hoist limit switches unloaded, slowly; report faults immediately to the appointed person [29cfr1910.179(n)(4)(i)]. Balance and secure loads, avoid side pulls unless authorized, and never move with an employee on load or hook [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)]. Operators must avoid carrying loads over people and stay at controls while loads hang [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)(vi)] [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)(x)].

Inspections and maintenance help find and correct problems; unsafe conditions found by inspection must be fixed before operation resumes [29cfr1910.179(l)(3)(i)]. Frequent checks are daily to monthly, periodic ones every 1 to 12 months [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(ii)]. Hooks and chains get daily visual and monthly certified checks; hook limits include 15 percent excess opening and 10° twist [29cfr1910.179(j)(2)]. Ropes get monthly certified inspections [29cfr1910.179(m)(1)]. Idle and standby cranes have special checks, at 1 month, 6 months and semi-annually [29cfr1910.179(j)(4)].

Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.179(b)(8)]. Stay within rated load except for tests [29cfr1910.179(n)(1)]; test loads are limited to 125 percent unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise [29cfr1910.179(k)(2)]. Each shift, try every upper hoist limit under no load, inching or slowly; immediately notify the appointed person of faults. Never use it as an operating control [29cfr1910.179(n)(4)].

Check rope, lines and hook position before hoisting; secure and balance loads; avoid sudden speed changes and obstructions. Side pulls need specific authorization. No movement with employees on load or hook. Avoid carrying loads over people, test brakes near rated load, keep two full drum wraps, stay at controls, and sound warnings when required. Multi-crane lifts need one qualified responsible person in charge [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)].

Frequent inspections run daily to monthly, periodic 1 to 12 months [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(ii)]. Hooks and chains need daily visual and monthly certified checks; hook limits are over 15 percent excess throat opening or over 10° twist [29cfr1910.179(j)(2)]. Idle 1 to under 6 months requires frequent and idle-rope inspection; over 6 months, complete and idle-rope inspection; standby cranes, frequent and idle-rope inspection at least semi-annually [29cfr1910.179(j)(4)]. Running ropes need monthly certified inspection; ropes idle a month or more need appointed-person approval [29cfr1910.179(m)].

Before repair, position the crane, turn controllers off, lock the main or emergency switch open, post signs and protect against other cranes [29cfr1910.179(l)(2)(i)].

Equipment limits: ANSI B30.2.0-1967 design for new cranes from August 31, 1971 [29cfr1910.179(b)(2)]; clearances 3 inches overhead, 2 lateral, 3 around cabs; access gaps 12 inches (30 cm) maximum [29cfr1910.179(b)(6)(i)] [29cfr1910.179(c)]; footwalk headroom 48 inches, load design 50 pounds per square foot [29cfr1910.179(d)]; steppable guards support 200 pounds [29cfr1910.179(e)(6)(iii)]. Bumpers, subject to exceptions: bridge 3 ft/s/s at 20 percent rated speed, 40 percent energy capacity; trolley 4.7 at one-third [29cfr1910.179(e)]. Holding torque: 125 percent with nonmechanical control braking, 100 with mechanical, 100 each for two [29cfr1910.179(f)(2)(i)]. Foot force maximum 70 pounds; stopping feet equal 10 percent of full-load feet-per-minute speed [29cfr1910.179(f)(4)]. Voltage: control 600, pendant 150 AC/300 DC, cab-crane receptacle 300 [29cfr1910.179(g)]. Rope load per part: 20 percent breaking strength; retighten new-rope clips after one hour [29cfr1910.179(h)(2)].

Verify scope, designated operators, rated-load marking and, for new cranes constructed and installed from August 31, 1971, ANSI B30.2.0-1967 design [29cfr1910.179(b)]. Modifications and rerating require specified checks, testing and marking [29cfr1910.179(b)(3)].

Measure clearances: 3 inches overhead, 2 lateral (CMAA Specification No. 61), 3 around cabs; access gaps maximum 12 inches (30 cm) [29cfr1910.179(b)(6)(i)] [29cfr1910.179(c)]. Check footwalk headroom of 48 inches and design load of 50 pounds per square foot [29cfr1910.179(d)]. Guards support 200 pounds unless stepping is impossible [29cfr1910.179(e)(6)(iii)]. Subject to listed exceptions, bridge bumpers average at most 3 ft/s/s at 20 percent rated speed and absorb at least 40-percent-speed impacts; trolley limits are 4.7 and one-third [29cfr1910.179(e)(2)] [29cfr1910.179(e)(3)].

Holding torque minimums are 125 percent with nonmechanical control braking, 100 with mechanical, 100 each for two [29cfr1910.179(f)(2)(i)]; hot-metal units with power control braking need two brakes [29cfr1910.179(f)(2)(vi)]. Foot force maximum is 70 pounds; full-speed, full-load stopping feet equal 10 percent of feet-per-minute full-load speed [29cfr1910.179(f)(4)]. Voltage maxima: control 600; pendant 150 AC, 300 DC; cab-crane cab/bridge receptacle 300, grounded three-prong permanent [29cfr1910.179(g)]. Verify disconnects, overtravel limit and magnet switching where applicable [29cfr1910.179(g)(5)].

Rope load per part is capped at 20 percent nominal breaking strength; two wraps remain at extreme low hook; clip nuts are retightened after one hour [29cfr1910.179(h)(2)]. Lowering also preserves two full wraps [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)(viii)]. Confirm load handling and shift limit-switch trials [29cfr1910.179(n)].

Check initial inspection and operational tests [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(i)] [29cfr1910.179(k)(1)]. Test loads are capped at 125 percent unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise; reports are filed [29cfr1910.179(k)(2)]. Frequent intervals are daily to monthly; periodic, 1 to 12 months [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(ii)]. Check hook and chain certifications, daily visuals, and hook thresholds over 15 percent excess opening or 10° twist [29cfr1910.179(j)(2)].

Idle requirements cover 1 month to under 6, and "over 6 months"; standby is at least semi-annual [29cfr1910.179(j)(4)]. Check monthly running-rope records, and approval and records for ropes idle a month or more [29cfr1910.179(m)]. Verify preventive maintenance, lockout precautions, designated repairers, corrections, restoration and hook discard [29cfr1910.179(l)]. Check ladder use, cab storage and extinguisher familiarity [29cfr1910.179(o)]; carbon tetrachloride extinguishers are prohibited [29cfr1910.179(c)(3)].

This section covers crawler, locomotive, truck and wheel-mounted lifting cranes using drums and ropes, powered basically by engines or electric motors; wreck-clearance cranes are excluded [29cfr1910.180(b)(1)]. Only designated people, meaning those the employer or its representative selects as qualified, may operate them [29cfr1910.180(a)(21)] [29cfr1910.180(b)(3)]. New cranes built and used from August 31, 1971 must meet ANSI B30.5-1968 design specifications. Older ones "should be modified" by February 15, 1972, with a stated exception [29cfr1910.180(b)(2)].

Ratings help guard against tipping. Maximums, as percentages of tipping loads, are: locomotive without outriggers (support arms), 85 for booms 60 feet or less or longer, subject to a minimum 30,000 pound-feet net stabilizing moment; locomotive with them fully extended, 80; crawler without, 75; crawler fully extended, 85; truck or wheel-mounted, either way, 85 [29cfr1910.180-table-1]. Locomotive rating track is level within 1 percent grade [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(ii)(b)]. A rating chart must be visible from the operator's seat [29cfr1910.180(c)(2)]. Never exceed rated load except in permitted tests [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(i)]. Test loads stop at 110 percent [29cfr1910.180(e)(2)(ii)]. If structural strength limits the load, confirm its weight within 10 percent, plus or minus [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(ii)].

Inspect new and altered cranes before first use [29cfr1910.180(d)(1)]. Frequent checks are daily to monthly; periodic checks every 1 to 12 months or as the manufacturer recommends [29cfr1910.180(d)(2)]. Control adjustment and air or hydraulic leaks are daily checks [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)]. Hook text names cracks, over 15 percent extra throat opening, or over 10° twist, but its sentence states no action [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)(v)]. Idle cranes and ropes need checks, and ropes in use monthly ones [29cfr1910.180(d)(5)] [29cfr1910.180(g)].

Level the crane, secure and balance loads, and avoid jerks and obstructions [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)]. Keep two full rope wraps on drums [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(x)]. Nobody may ride the load or hook during movement [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(v)]. Operators stay at the controls while loads hang [29cfr1910.180(h)(4)(i)]. Never refuel with the engine running [29cfr1910.180(i)(4)(ii)].

Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.180(b)(3)]. Design: ANSI B30.5-1968 for new cranes from August 31, 1971; older cranes "should be modified" by February 15, 1972, subject to an exception [29cfr1910.180(b)(2)]. Maximum ratings (% of tipping): locomotive without outriggers, 85 (booms 60 feet or less, and over), with a 30,000 pound-feet minimum net stabilizing moment; locomotive, outriggers fully extended, 80; crawler without, 75, extended, 85; truck/wheel, without or extended, 85 [29cfr1910.180-table-1]. Locomotive rating track is within 1 percent grade [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(ii)(b)]. Account for wind, ground, tires, speeds and other stability factors [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(iv)]. Keep the chart visible from your seat [29cfr1910.180(c)(2)].

Exceed rated load only for testing [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(i)]; tests stop at 110 percent [29cfr1910.180(e)(2)(ii)]. Structurally limited loads need weight known within ±10 percent [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(ii)]. Sling loads; never wrap the hoist rope around them [29cfr1910.180(h)(2)]. Level, block, balance and control movement; no sideways dragging or riders [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)]. Test brakes by raising near-rated loads a few inches [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(viii)]. Use outriggers when load exceeds the no-outrigger rating [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(ix)]. Keep two full drum wraps [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(x)]. Multiple-crane lifts and loaded travel need a designated person [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(xii)] [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(xiv)]. Stay at controls under suspended loads [29cfr1910.180(h)(4)(i)].

Inspect new or altered cranes before use [29cfr1910.180(d)(1)]. Frequent: daily to monthly; periodic: 1 to 12 months or manufacturer's recommendation [29cfr1910.180(d)(2)]. Control maladjustment and air/hydraulic checks are daily [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)]. Hook criteria are cracks, throat over 15 percent excess, or twist over 10°; the sentence omits the action [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)(v)]. Idle one month to under 6 needs frequent and idle-rope checks; six months adds periodic; standby gets the former at least semiannually [29cfr1910.180(d)(5)]. Certify critical items and ropes monthly [29cfr1910.180(d)(6)] [29cfr1910.180(g)(1)]. Ropes idle a month or more need approval before reuse [29cfr1910.180(g)(2)(ii)]. Reinstate guards and safety devices, and remove maintenance equipment, before operating [29cfr1910.180(f)]. Never refuel running [29cfr1910.180(i)(4)(ii)].

Verify scope and designated operators [29cfr1910.180(b)(1)] [29cfr1910.180(b)(3)]; ANSI B30.5-1968 for new cranes from August 31, 1971. Earlier cranes "should be modified" by February 15, 1972, unless infeasible or uneconomic alteration and substantial compliance are shown [29cfr1910.180(b)(2)]. Rating ceilings (% tipping): locomotive without outriggers, booms 60 feet or less/over, 85, footnoted 30,000 pound-feet minimum moment; locomotive extended, 80; crawler without/extended, 75/85; truck/wheel, either, 85 [29cfr1910.180-table-1]. Locomotive stipulations include 1 percent grade, static loading and half the far-side wheels leaving rail as tipping [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(ii)]; others follow SAE J765 [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(iii)]. Check charts [29cfr1910.180(c)(2)], production tests [29cfr1910.180(e)(1)], repair/alteration reports, 110 percent test ceiling, rerating tests/reports, and manufacturer or final-assembler approval above original ratings [29cfr1910.180(e)(2)].

Check initial and interval inspections: frequent daily-monthly, periodic 1-12 months or manufacturer-recommended [29cfr1910.180(d)(1)] [29cfr1910.180(d)(2)]; daily control-maladjustment and air/hydraulic items [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)]. Hooks: cracks, over 15 percent excess throat or over 10° twist; no consequence is stated [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)(v)]. Idle at least one month, under 6: (d)(3) plus (g)(2)(ii); six months: add (d)(4). Standby: (d)(3) and (g)(2)(ii) at least semiannually [29cfr1910.180(d)(5)]. Monthly critical-item and running-rope certifications require date, signature and identifier [29cfr1910.180(d)(6)] [29cfr1910.180(g)(1)]. Idle-month ropes also need appointed or authorized inspector approval [29cfr1910.180(g)(2)(ii)].

Verify load limits, ±10 percent weight determination for structurally limited loads, attachment, handling, brake tests, outriggers/blocking, two drum wraps, designated oversight, transit and holding controls [29cfr1910.180(h)]. "Should" governs carrying over people and standing or passing under loads [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(vi)] [29cfr1910.180(h)(4)(ii)]. Check restoration after maintenance [29cfr1910.180(f)], rail clamps, counterweight (including the temporary truck-crane exception), cabs, refueling, extinguishers and adjacent-track protection [29cfr1910.180(i)]. Cross-references: approved cans, § 1910.155(c)(3) [29cfr1910.180(i)(4)(i)]; overhead lines, § 1910.333(c)(3) [29cfr1910.180(j)].

A sling connects a load to lifting equipment [29cfr1910.184(b)]. This section covers chain, wire rope, metal mesh, fiber rope and synthetic web slings used for hoisting [29cfr1910.184(a)]. A designated competent person checks slings, fastenings and attachments each day before use, and during use where conditions warrant. Damaged or defective slings come out immediately [29cfr1910.184(d)].

Never overload, kink, knot or shock load a sling. Attach it securely, protect it from sharp edges, balance basket hitches, and keep loads clear of obstructions. Employees stay clear of suspended or about-to-be-lifted loads. Keep hands from between a tightening sling and load, and never pull a sling from under a resting load. Identification must be affixed and legible [29cfr1910.184(c)]. An angle five degrees or less from vertical may count as vertical [29cfr1910.184(b)].

Chain: thorough inspections occur at least every 12 months [29cfr1910.184(e)(3)(i)]. Remove it permanently if heated above 1000 degrees F; above 600 degrees F, reduce load limits [29cfr1910.184(e)(6)]. Remove chain worn below table minimums, such as 13⁄64 inch for 1⁄4-inch chain [29cfr1910.184-table-N-184-1]. Cracked or deformed parts also require removal, as do cracked hooks, or hooks opened over 15 percent or twisted over 10 degrees [29cfr1910.184(e)(9)].

Wire rope has minimum lengths: 10, 40 or 96 times a specified diameter, by type [29cfr1910.184(f)(2)]. Temperature rules involve 200, 400 and minus 60 °F [29cfr1910.184(f)(3)]. Welded attachments need testing at twice rated capacity [29cfr1910.184(f)(4)(ii)]. Broken wires, wear, distortion, heat, corrosion or bad fittings can require removal [29cfr1910.184(f)(5)].

Mesh, fiber rope and web slings have their own marking, temperature, repair and removal rules [29cfr1910.184(g)] [29cfr1910.184(h)] [29cfr1910.184(i)]. Mesh tests use 1 1/2 times capacity [29cfr1910.184(g)(5)]. Never use repaired fiber rope slings [29cfr1910.184(h)(6)]. Repaired web slings need testing at twice capacity [29cfr1910.184(i)(8)(ii)]. Web temperature maximums are 180 °F for polyester and nylon, 200 °F for polypropylene [29cfr1910.184(i)(7)].

Inspect slings, fastenings and attachments daily before use, and during use as conditions warrant; a designated competent person does the daily check. Pull damaged or defective slings immediately [29cfr1910.184(d)]. Follow all safe practices on loading, rigging, identification and keeping clear; "Shock loading is prohibited." [29cfr1910.184(c)]. Five degrees or less from vertical may count as vertical [29cfr1910.184(b)].

Chain: thorough inspections at most 12 months apart [29cfr1910.184(e)(3)(i)]; proof test new, repaired or reconditioned slings before use [29cfr1910.184(e)(4)]. Remove permanently above 1000 degrees F; derate above 600 [29cfr1910.184(e)(6)]. Apply Table N-184-1 wear minimums (1⁄4-inch: 13⁄64) [29cfr1910.184(e)(8)] [29cfr1910.184-table-N-184-1]. Remove cracked or deformed components, and cracked hooks or hooks opened over 15 percent or twisted over 10 degrees [29cfr1910.184(e)(9)].

Wire rope: clear or circumferential minimums are 10, 40 or 96 diameters, by construction [29cfr1910.184(f)(2)]. Retire fiber-core slings exposed above 200 °F; for nonfiber core above 400 or below minus 60 °F, follow the manufacturer [29cfr1910.184(f)(3)]. Proof test welded attachments at twice capacity [29cfr1910.184(f)(4)(ii)]. Removal includes 10 random broken wires per lay or five in one strand per lay, one-third outer-wire diameter wear, and the 15-percent/10-degree hook limits, among other damage [29cfr1910.184(f)(5)].

Mesh: proof test at least 1 1/2 times capacity [29cfr1910.184(g)(5)]. Uncoated range is minus 20 to 550 °F; PVC or neoprene, zero to 200 °F [29cfr1910.184(g)(7)]. Removal limits include 25 per cent (abrasion), 15 (corrosion), 10 (slot depth or eye width) and 15 percent (handle-eye area) [29cfr1910.184(g)(9)].

Fiber rope: minus 20 to 180 °F, except wet frozen [29cfr1910.184(h)(2)]. Manila eye/short splices need three/six tucks; synthetic, four/eight. Rules also cover tails, 10-diameter clear length and 60-degree maximum eye angle [29cfr1910.184(h)(3)]. No repaired slings [29cfr1910.184(h)(6)].

Web: observe chemical restrictions [29cfr1910.184(i)(6)]; maximums are 180 °F (nylon, polyester) and 200 °F (polypropylene) [29cfr1910.184(i)(7)]. Proof test repairs to twice capacity [29cfr1910.184(i)(8)(ii)].

Verify covered scope [29cfr1910.184(a)], safe practices and legible identification [29cfr1910.184(c)], designated competent-person daily checks, warranted in-use checks and immediate removal [29cfr1910.184(d)]. Angles five degrees or less from vertical may be considered vertical [29cfr1910.184(b)].

Chain: check identification and attachment capacity [29cfr1910.184(e)(1)] [29cfr1910.184(e)(2)]; inspections at most 12 months apart and month records [29cfr1910.184(e)(3)]; proof certificate, citing A391-65 paragraph 5.2 (ANSI G61.1-1968) [29cfr1910.184(e)(4)]. Limits: removal above 1000 degrees F, derating above 600 [29cfr1910.184(e)(6)]; repairs [29cfr1910.184(e)(7)]; wear per Table N-184-1, 1⁄4 through 13⁄4 as printed [29cfr1910.184-table-N-184-1]; defective components and cracked hooks, 15 percent opening, 10 degrees twist [29cfr1910.184(e)(9)].

Wire: marking [29cfr1910.184(f)(1)]; lengths 10, 40, 96 diameters [29cfr1910.184(f)(2)]; 200 °F fiber-core retirement, nonfiber advice above 400 or below minus 60 °F [29cfr1910.184(f)(3)]; welding before assembly, except thimble covers; twice-capacity test and certificate [29cfr1910.184(f)(4)]; broken wires 10 random/lay or five/strand/lay, one-third wear, hooks 15 percent/10 degrees, other conditions [29cfr1910.184(f)(5)].

Mesh: marking, handles, joints, coatings [29cfr1910.184(g)]; 1 1/2-times minimum test, before elastomer coating [29cfr1910.184(g)(5)]; minus 20 to 550 °F uncoated, zero to 200 °F PVC/neoprene; otherwise manufacturer recommendations [29cfr1910.184(g)(7)]; repairer and records [29cfr1910.184(g)(8)]; removal includes 25/15 per cent wire loss, over 10 per cent slot/eye distortion, 15 percent area loss [29cfr1910.184(g)(9)].

Fiber: minus 20 to 180 °F; manufacturer governs outside or wet frozen [29cfr1910.184(h)(2)]. Tucks: manila three eye, six short; synthetic four, eight. Tails project six diameters under one inch, six inches otherwise; interfering tails need two added tapered tucks (approximately six diameters). Check 10-diameter length, 60-degree maximum angle [29cfr1910.184(h)(3)], marking, attachments, removal, repair ban [29cfr1910.184(h)].

Web: construction, chemicals [29cfr1910.184(i)]; maximums 180 °F polyester/nylon, 200 °F polypropylene [29cfr1910.184(i)(7)]; qualified repairer, twice-capacity test, certificate, no temporary repairs [29cfr1910.184(i)(8)]; removal conditions [29cfr1910.184(i)(9)].

This section tells you which machines the crane standard covers, so it matters for knowing whether these rules apply to your work. It covers power-operated equipment used in construction that "can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load" [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. In plain words, the machine can lift a hanging load, set it down and move it sideways. Examples include many kinds of cranes, derricks, dedicated pile drivers and variations of these. Covered equipment stays covered when used with attachments such as hooks, magnets, buckets or personnel platforms [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Some things are left out. These include excavators, backhoes and several types of loaders, even when rigging is used to lift suspended loads with them [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are left out unless set up to hoist, lower and move a suspended load sideways using a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. Other exclusions include certain converted machines, towing, digger derrick, aerial lift, maintenance, tree and drilling work or equipment, and other listed items, often with conditions [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Some material deliveries by knuckle-boom truck cranes are also excluded, but only in specific cases [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)]. For example, using the crane to hold material in place while it is attached to a structure is not excluded [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)].

All sections of this subpart apply to covered equipment unless specified otherwise [29cfr1926.1400(d)]. When the standard tells an operator, crewmember or other employee to take certain actions, your employer has a duty too. The employer must set up work rules to ensure compliance, communicate them effectively to the relevant people and enforce them [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entities also have duties, including ones in other named sections [29cfr1926.1400(e)].

Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)].

Verify scope under [29cfr1926.1400(a)]: power-operated equipment, construction use, and ability to hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load; the examples are non-exhaustive. Covered equipment used with attachments remains within the standard [29cfr1926.1400(b)]. All subpart CC sections apply unless specified otherwise [29cfr1926.1400(d)].

Test exclusion conditions under [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Conversions apply only while adapted for non-hoisting/lifting use [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Listed earthmoving machinery remains excluded when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Check use limits for wreckers [29cfr1926.1400(c)(3)], mechanic's trucks [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)] and gin poles [29cfr1926.1400(c)(12)], and the forklift configuration exception [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. For digger derricks, check qualifying pole work or other subpart V work; subpart V work must comply with all of that subpart, and telecommunication service construction with all of § 1910.268 [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)]. Other exclusions cover aerial devices and platforms, certain gantry systems, cranes, rigs and hoisting machinery, tree work, certain vessel A-frame operations, and roustabouts [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Rail welding and maintenance machines must meet the hoisting-device limitation; the defined terms require the 49 CFR 214.7 definition and exclusive railroad track use [29cfr1926.1400(c)(18)].

For knuckle-boom delivery, check ground transfer without sequencing [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)], or listed supply transfer onto structures with a boom-end fork/cradle and functioning automatic overload prevention [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion is unavailable for holding, supporting or stabilizing to facilitate construction, prefabricated components, structural steel or systems-engineered metal building components, or when "The activity is not specifically excluded" under those two paragraphs [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)].

Verify employer work rules are established, effectively communicated and enforced [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include §§ 1926.1402(c), 1926.1402(e) and 1926.1424(b) [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. For subpart V work, § 1926.959 compliance is deemed compliance with §§ 1926.1407 through 1926.1411 [29cfr1926.1400(g)]. Section 1926.1402 excludes railroad-designed cranes on FRA-regulated general-system track under 49 CFR part 213 that comply with applicable FRA requirements; see § 1926.1402(f) [29cfr1926.1400(h)].

This section is the dictionary for the subpart. It tells you what key words mean, so check a term here before assuming its everyday meaning [29cfr1926.1401]. "Equipment" means equipment the subpart covers, and "Crane/derrick" includes all of it. An operator is the person operating the equipment [29cfr1926.1401].

Some definitions describe people. A competent person can identify existing and predictable hazards and "has authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them." A qualified person has shown the ability to solve relevant problems, through a recognized degree, certificate or professional standing, or through extensive knowledge, training and experience. An A/D (assembly/disassembly) director is someone who meets the subpart's requirements for that role, whatever their job title [29cfr1926.1401].

Other words describe danger areas and events. The fall zone includes the area under the load, and more: anywhere it is reasonably foreseeable that suspended materials could fall in an accident. "Directly under the load" covers all or just part of an employee being directly beneath it. Two blocking happens when the uppermost part on the hoist line, such as a hook block, touches the boom tip or a similar part. Continued power can then make the rope or another component fail [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, encroachment means any part of the crane, load line or load, including rigging, breaches a required minimum clearance distance. A dedicated spotter must meet the signal person qualification requirements of § 1926.1428. The spotter's "sole responsibility" is watching the separation from the line and communicating with the operator so the minimum approach distance is not breached [29cfr1926.1401].

A load includes the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as slings and shackles. The term can mean the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum permitted working load under specified conditions. Also remember that "Up to" includes the stated limit, and "including" does not limit a list to the examples named [29cfr1926.1401].

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

Apply these definitions when testing coverage and compliance [29cfr1926.1401]. For multi-purpose machines, check configuration: forks/tongs are not covered; a winch pack, hook-equipped jib, or jib used with a winch is. Mobile cranes with luffing jib and/or tower attachments "are not considered tower cranes under this section." Floating cranes include manufacturer or employer designs for permanent attachment to flotation. Employer-made equipment means floating cranes/derricks an employer designed and built for its own use. Marine hoisted personnel transfer devices exclude boatswain's chairs hoisted by covered equipment. A boatswain's chair is a single-point adjustable suspension scaffold supporting one seated employee [29cfr1926.1401].

For roles, a competent person needs both hazard identification capability and authority to take prompt corrective measures. A qualified rigger meets the qualified person criteria. A certified welder meets nationally recognized certification requirements applicable to the task. A/D director status does not depend on title or management status. A non-third-party qualified evaluator is employed by the signal person's employer; a third-party evaluator is an independent, expert entity. Both require demonstrated competence in assessing signal person qualification. The controlling entity has overall construction project responsibility [29cfr1926.1401].

For power lines, verify that a dedicated spotter meets § 1926.1428 and has no other responsibility. Insulating links/devices and proximity alarms must, by definition, be listed, labeled or accepted by a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory under 29 CFR 1910.7. Electrical contact includes close proximity allowing current to pass. Encroachment includes rigging and lifting accessories [29cfr1926.1401].

A runway must be firm, level, and designed, prepared and designated as a travel path for the crane's weight and configuration when traveling with a suspended platform; existing surfaces qualify only if meeting these criteria. A travel bogie has two or more axles. Unavailable procedures are those no longer, or never, available from the manufacturer. Standard Method is the appendix A hand signal protocol. Operational aids include those listed in § 1926.1416. "Paragraph" and "Section" have stated internal-reference meanings, the former unless otherwise specified, as with the latter. "Up to" is inclusive; "including" and "such as" are non-limiting [29cfr1926.1401].

This section is about the ground under equipment. "Ground conditions" means how well the ground can support the equipment, including its slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. "Supporting materials" are items such as blocking, mats or cribbing. In marshes and wetlands, they include marsh buggies. Similar materials or devices also count [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The main rule covers both assembling and using the equipment. Neither is allowed unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and levelness. Supporting materials can be used along with the ground, if necessary, to meet them. The drainage requirement does not apply to marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)].

The controlling entity must ensure the needed ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also tell the equipment user and operator where certain hazards lie beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks or utilities. This applies to hazards identified in documents it possesses or otherwise known to it [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

If the A/D director or operator decides the ground does not meet the rule, that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity [29cfr1926.1402(e)]. Certain railroad cranes are excluded from this section [29cfr1926.1402(f)].

Do not assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. You may count supporting materials, if necessary, toward meeting them. Drainage is not required in marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in marshes or wetlands, and similar materials or devices [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also inform the equipment user and operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. The duty covers hazards identified in documents in its possession, on or off site, or hazards it otherwise knows about [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

Without a controlling entity, the preparation duty in (c)(1) falls on the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange the preparations [29cfr1926.1402(d)].

If you, as operator, or the A/D director determine that conditions fall short, that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity. The aim is to meet paragraph (b), using suitable supporting materials or devices if necessary [29cfr1926.1402(e)]. A limited exclusion applies to certain cranes on railroad tracks [29cfr1926.1402(f)].

Verify that equipment is not assembled or used unless ground firmness, drainage and grading, with supporting materials if necessary, satisfy the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. The drainage requirement alone is stated as inapplicable to marshes/wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Definitions appear at [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)] and [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the preparations needed for paragraph (b) are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must inform both the equipment user and operator of the location of under-area hazards, such as voids, tanks and utilities, if identified in documents in its possession "(whether at the site or off-site)" or otherwise known to it. Listed document examples are site drawings, as-built drawings and soil analyses [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

With no controlling entity, the (c)(1) requirement passes to the employer with site authority to make or arrange preparations. Paragraph (d) names only (c)(1) [29cfr1926.1402(d)].

Where the A/D director or operator determines paragraph (b) is not met, check that this person's employer discussed the needed preparations with the controlling entity [29cfr1926.1402(e)].

The exclusion covers cranes designed for railroad track use, when used on tracks in the general railroad system of transportation regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213, "and that comply with applicable Federal Railroad Administration requirements" [29cfr1926.1402(f)].

This section is about which procedures apply when equipment, or its attachments, is put together or taken apart. The duties it describes belong to the employer. First, during this work the employer must follow "all applicable manufacturer prohibitions" [29cfr1926.1403]. In plain words, if the manufacturer prohibits something and that prohibition applies, it stays off limits.

Second, the employer must also follow one of two sets of procedures [29cfr1926.1403]. One choice is the manufacturer's procedures that apply to assembly and disassembly [29cfr1926.1403(a)]. The other is the employer's own procedures for this work [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. The second choice has a condition. The employer may use its own procedures only if it can show that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406 [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. Choosing them does not remove the duty to follow applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1403].

There is also a special rule for synthetic slings, given in a note. When an employer uses them during assembly or disassembly rigging, the employer must follow manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. The note points to § 1926.1404(r) for more [29cfr1926.1403-note-1].

For assembly or disassembly of equipment or attachments, the employer has a fixed duty and a choice. The fixed duty is to comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1403]. The choice is which procedures to comply with. The employer must use either the manufacturer procedures or its own [29cfr1926.1403].

The first option is the "Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly" [29cfr1926.1403(a)]. The second is employer procedures for assembly and disassembly [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. That second option is conditional: employer procedures may be used "only where the employer can demonstrate" that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406 [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. In deciding between the two, keep in mind that the prohibitions duty is stated separately from the choice of procedures, so selecting employer procedures leaves applicable manufacturer prohibitions in force [29cfr1926.1403].

Synthetic slings affect this decision. According to the note, when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging, the employer must follow manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. The note refers to § 1926.1404(r) [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. This section does not set out the contents of either § 1926.1406 or § 1926.1404(r).

The scope is assembling or disassembling equipment "(or attachments)" [29cfr1926.1403]. Two conditions apply to the employer. It must comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions, and it must comply with either paragraph (a) or paragraph (b) [29cfr1926.1403]. The prohibitions requirement is joined to that choice by "and," so it applies under either option [29cfr1926.1403].

Under paragraph (a), the benchmark is the manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly [29cfr1926.1403(a)]. Under paragraph (b), the employer uses employer procedures [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. These are permitted "only where the employer can demonstrate that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406" [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. The wording places the demonstration on the employer and refers to "the procedures used" [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. This section does not state how that demonstration is to be made, or what § 1926.1406 requires.

The note addresses synthetic slings: "The employer must follow manufacturer procedures when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging." [29cfr1926.1403-note-1] Its cross-reference is § 1926.1404(r) [29cfr1926.1403-note-1], whose content is not given here. The cross-references to check against are therefore § 1926.1406 for employer procedures [29cfr1926.1403(b)] and § 1926.1404(r) for synthetic slings [29cfr1926.1403-note-1].

This section covers all assembly and disassembly of equipment. An "A/D director" directs the work. This is someone who qualifies as both a competent and a qualified person, or a competent person helped by qualified persons. Someone working alone must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)] and review them just before starting, unless they understand them and have used them on the same equipment type and setup [29cfr1926.1404(c)].

Before work starts, the director makes sure you understand your tasks, their hazards and the places to avoid. This also applies before you change tasks and when new people join [29cfr1926.1404(d)]. Before going out of the operator's view to a spot in, on or under the equipment, or near it or its load where movement could hurt you, you must tell the operator [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. An operator who knows you went there must not move anything until told, through a pre-arranged system, that you are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)].

Do not be under the boom, jib or other parts while pins are removed. The exception applies when the employer shows site limits require it. The director must then use procedures that reduce the risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacities must not be exceeded [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses hazards including ground, blocking, assist crane loads, lifting points, balance, support when pins come out, snagged ropes, counterweights, brakes, backward tipping and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Limits on unsupported cantilevered boom must be followed [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Component weights must be readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Parts and setup follow set rules, with inspection after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)].

Remove reusable shipping pins and similar items, and store them so they cannot become falling hazards [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. Pile-driving equipment must have no jib attached while driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)]. Outriggers and stabilizers (supports extended from the equipment) have setup and blocking rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. A qualified rigger does assembly and disassembly rigging, and synthetic slings must be protected and used as their maker directs [29cfr1926.1404(r)].

Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)].

Verify the A/D director meets [29cfr1926.1404(a)], including both qualifications if working alone; understands procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)]; and reviewed them immediately beforehand unless the understanding-and-prior-application exception applies [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Check crew understanding, including task changes and new personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)]; out-of-view notification and the operator's movement hold [29cfr1926.1404(e)]; and, for anyone under components during pin removal, the employer's site-constraint demonstration and director's procedures [29cfr1926.1404(f)(2)]. Check rated capacities in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)].

Under [29cfr1926.1404(h)], check each hazard, including ground (see § 1926.1402), blocking, pick points, pin-removal stability, snagging, counterweights, backward stability, wind and weather. Assist crane loads for each phase require advance verification under § 1926.1417(o)(3) [29cfr1926.1404(h)(4)]. Check center-of-gravity identification where the stability method requires it, and protective measures where information is insufficient [29cfr1926.1404(h)(6)]. Confirm brake testing before each reliance and alternative protection if insufficient [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Check cantilever limits, including the written registered professional engineer determination if manufacturer limits are unavailable [29cfr1926.1404(j)], and component weights [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Verify configuration against manufacturer requirements, written engineer approval where unavailable, or approved modifications under § 1926.1434; check post-assembly inspection (§ 1926.1412(c)) [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Check shipping hardware removal and storage [29cfr1926.1404(o)] and no jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

For required or used outriggers/stabilizers, check full extension or manufacturer-permitted load-chart deployment, attached floats where used, visibility to operator or signal person, and blocking location and adequacy. Wheel unloading excludes stabilizers and locomotive cranes. For locomotive cranes, check manufacturer procedures for outrigger or stabilizer use, and for truck wedges or screws when lifting without them [29cfr1926.1404(q)].

For rigging, check qualified-rigger work, synthetic sling protection from edges and capacity-reducing configurations, and compliance with sling manufacturer requirements and recommendations. 29 CFR 1926.251 and other rigging requirements also apply [29cfr1926.1404(r)]; the note points to 1926.251(c)(9) for wire rope slings [29cfr1926.1404-note-1].

This section is about taking apart booms and jibs. That includes taking them apart to change their length [29cfr1926.1405]. It applies whether the work follows the manufacturer's procedures or the employer's procedures [29cfr1926.1405]. It has four rules about when pins must stay in. In all four, removing a pin even "partly or completely" counts.

First, when the pendants are in tension, do not remove any of the pins in the pendants [29cfr1926.1405(a)].

Second, while the pendants are in tension, also leave in the top and bottom pins on boom sections between the pendant attachment points and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(b)].

Third, the boom may be held up by its uppermost section resting on the ground or another support. Then no top or bottom pins may be removed on sections between that uppermost section and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(c)].

Fourth, part of the boom being removed may be cantilevered. The text describes this as "the portion being removed ahead of the pendant attachment points". Do not remove any top pins on boom sections there until the cantilevered section to be removed is "fully supported" [29cfr1926.1405(d)].

These additional disassembly requirements cover dismantling booms and jibs, including dismantling to change their length. They apply under both manufacturer procedures and employer procedures [29cfr1926.1405]. Each restriction covers removing a pin "partly or completely", so before moving any pin, the questions are where it is and how the boom is held.

With the pendants in tension, no pins in the pendants may be removed [29cfr1926.1405(a)]. In that same condition, no top or bottom pins may be removed on boom sections located between the pendant attachment points and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(b)].

When the boom is supported by its uppermost section resting on the ground or other support, the restriction covers top and bottom pins on sections between that uppermost section and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(c)].

For the cantilevered portion of the boom being removed, meaning the portion ahead of the pendant attachment points, no top pins on its boom sections may be removed "until the cantilevered section to be removed is fully supported" [29cfr1926.1405(d)]. This paragraph names top pins only, while (b) and (c) name both top and bottom pins.

Scope: dismantling of booms and jibs, "including dismantling for changing the length of" them, under both manufacturer and employer procedures [29cfr1926.1405]. Each prohibition reaches partial as well as complete pin removal. The section states no numeric limits and no exceptions.

To verify compliance, match each pin's location with the support condition at the time of removal. Under (a), the condition is pendants in tension, and the prohibition covers pins in the pendants [29cfr1926.1405(a)]. Under (b), the condition is again pendants in tension, and the covered pins are top or bottom pins on boom sections between the pendant attachment points and the crane/derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(b)].

Under (c), the trigger is the boom "being supported by the uppermost boom section resting on the ground (or other support)". Covered pins are top or bottom pins on sections between the uppermost section and the crane/derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(c)].

Under (d), check top pins on boom sections on the cantilevered portion being removed, defined as the portion being removed ahead of the pendant attachment points. None may be removed until the cantilevered section to be removed is "fully supported" [29cfr1926.1405(d)]. Paragraph (d) does not mention bottom pins. The text cites no other paragraphs or consensus standards.

This section is about assembly and disassembly of equipment, meaning putting it together and taking it apart. It applies when the employer's own procedures are used instead of the manufacturer's procedures. In that case, the employer has to make sure those procedures do certain things [29cfr1926.1406(a)].

First, they must stop any part of the equipment from moving in a dangerous way that nobody intended, and stop any part from collapsing. The text says to "Prevent unintended dangerous movement, and prevent collapse, of any part of the equipment." [29cfr1926.1406(a)(1)]

Second, they must give all parts of the equipment enough support and keep them stable [29cfr1926.1406(a)(2)].

Third, they must deal with where people are. Employees involved in the assembly or disassembly work must be positioned so that their exposure is minimized if part or all of the equipment moves unexpectedly or collapses [29cfr1926.1406(a)(3)]. This matters to you if you are one of those employees, because this requirement concerns where you are placed during the work.

The section also says who creates these procedures. They must be developed by a "qualified person" [29cfr1926.1406(b)]. This section does not explain what that term means.

When assembly or disassembly is done under employer procedures instead of manufacturer procedures, the employer has a duty to ensure those procedures meet the conditions in this section [29cfr1926.1406(a)].

The procedures must prevent two things for any part of the equipment: unintended dangerous movement and collapse [29cfr1926.1406(a)(1)]. They must also "Provide adequate support and stability of all parts of the equipment." [29cfr1926.1406(a)(2)] Note the scope of the wording: the first condition reaches "any part of the equipment" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(1)], and the support and stability condition reaches all parts [29cfr1926.1406(a)(2)].

The procedures must also address employee position. Employees involved in the assembly/disassembly operation must be positioned so that their exposure to unintended movement or collapse is minimized. This covers movement or collapse of "part or all of the equipment" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(3)]. The wording for this condition is that exposure is "minimized" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(3)].

Development of the procedures is assigned to a particular role: "Employer procedures must be developed by a qualified person." [29cfr1926.1406(b)] The text of this section gives no definition of a qualified person. It also states no numeric limits for support, stability, or employee position.

The trigger for paragraph (a) is the use of employer procedures instead of manufacturer procedures for assembly/disassembly. The quoted condition is "When using employer procedures instead of manufacturer procedures" [29cfr1926.1406(a)]. Where it is met, the employer "must ensure" that the procedures satisfy the listed items [29cfr1926.1406(a)].

Check the procedures against each item. For movement and collapse, they must prevent unintended dangerous movement, and prevent collapse, of "any part of the equipment" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(1)]. For support, they must provide "adequate support and stability" of all parts of the equipment [29cfr1926.1406(a)(2)]. For employee exposure, they must position employees involved in the assembly/disassembly operation so that "their exposure to unintended movement or collapse of part or all of the equipment is minimized." [29cfr1926.1406(a)(3)] Item (a)(1) refers to unintended "dangerous" movement [29cfr1926.1406(a)(1)], while the wording of (a)(3) is "unintended movement or collapse" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(3)].

Also verify authorship: employer procedures must be developed by a qualified person [29cfr1926.1406(b)].

The provided text states no exceptions, numeric criteria, documentation requirements, or cross-references to other sections or consensus standards. It also does not define "adequate," "minimized," or "qualified person."

This section covers power line safety, up to 350 kV, while equipment is assembled or disassembled [29cfr1926.1407]. First, your employer must determine whether the equipment, load line or load, including rigging, could get closer than 20 feet to a line [29cfr1926.1407(a)]. If so, there are three choices: confirm with the utility that the line is deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite [29cfr1926.1407(a)(1)], keep everything at least 20 feet away [29cfr1926.1407(a)(2)], or use the voltage-based Table A distance [29cfr1926.1407(a)(3)].

Precautions against getting too close include a planning meeting [29cfr1926.1407(b)(1)], nonconductive tag lines if tag lines are used [29cfr1926.1407(b)(2)], and at least one effective extra measure [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)]. This can be a dedicated spotter, a warning or movement-limiting device, or a visible warning line, barricade or signs [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)]. They apply under the 20-foot choice, or under Table A as that option requires [29cfr1926.1407(b)] [29cfr1926.1407(a)(3)(ii)].

Unless the employer confirms the utility has deenergized the line and visibly grounded it at the worksite, no crane or derrick part, load line or load may be below it [29cfr1926.1407(c)] or inside the Table A distance [29cfr1926.1407(d)]. Lines are presumed energized unless the utility confirms otherwise, as the rule describes [29cfr1926.1407(f)]. Electrocution warnings must be posted on the equipment [29cfr1926.1407(g)].

Before assembly or disassembly, the employer determines whether equipment, load line or load, including rigging and lifting accessories, could get within 20 feet of a line in that direction or area [29cfr1926.1407(a)]. If so, it uses deenergizing with visible grounding [29cfr1926.1407(a)(1)], 20-foot clearance [29cfr1926.1407(a)(2)], or Table A clearance based on line voltage [29cfr1926.1407(a)(3)(i)]. The utility must provide requested voltage information within two working days [29cfr1926.1407(e)].

Required encroachment precautions include a planning meeting with the A/D director, operator, crew and others in the area [29cfr1926.1407(b)(1)], nonconductive tag lines if used [29cfr1926.1407(b)(2)], and at least one effective measure [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)]: a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with you [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(i)], a proximity alarm [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(ii)], an automatic stop-warning device [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(iii)], an automatic range limiter [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(iv)], or a high-visibility marked warning line, barricade or sign line in your view [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(v)]. The spotter must give timely information so clearance can be maintained [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(i)(D)].

Nothing from a crane or derrick, partially or fully assembled, including load line and load, may be below a line [29cfr1926.1407(c)] or inside Table A's minimum approach distance [29cfr1926.1407(d)] without confirmed deenergizing and worksite grounding. Assume lines are energized absent the confirmation in [29cfr1926.1407(f)]. At least one electrocution warning goes in your view in the cab, plus two outside, except on overhead gantry and tower cranes for the outside ones [29cfr1926.1407(g)].

Check the pre-task determination for the 20-foot trigger in the direction or area of assembly/disassembly [29cfr1926.1407(a)]. Verify the option: utility confirmation of deenergizing and visible worksite grounding [29cfr1926.1407(a)(1)]; 20-foot clearance using paragraph (b) [29cfr1926.1407(a)(2)]; or voltage and Table A (§ 1926.1408) determinations, with (b) required if encroachment could occur [29cfr1926.1407(a)(3)]. Utilities must supply requested voltage information within two working days [29cfr1926.1407(e)].

Where (b) applies, verify all requirements: the specified planning meeting, nonconductive tag lines if used, and at least one effective measure [29cfr1926.1407(b)]. For spotters, check continuous operator contact [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(i)], a distance-identifying visual aid [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(i)(A)], effective positioning [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(i)(B)], direct-communication equipment where necessary [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(i)(C)], and timely information [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(i)(D)]. Alternatives are proximity alarms and automatic warning devices giving sufficient warning [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(ii)] [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(iii)], range limiters set to prevent encroachment [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(iv)], or operator-visible, high-visibility marked lines, barricades or signs [29cfr1926.1407(b)(3)(v)].

For crane/derrick parts, load lines or loads below lines [29cfr1926.1407(c)] or inside Table A minimum approach distance [29cfr1926.1407(d)], require employer confirmation of utility deenergizing and worksite visible grounding. Presumed-energized status requires utility confirmation the line "has been and continues to be" deenergized and visibly grounded [29cfr1926.1407(f)]. Check one or more conspicuous cab warnings in operator view, and at least two exterior, excepting overhead gantry and tower cranes from the exterior requirement [29cfr1926.1407(g)].

This section is about keeping equipment, such as a crane, from causing electrocution near power lines. Before operations begin, your employer must mark a work zone and keep the operator inside it, or treat it as the full circle around the equipment out to its maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. If the equipment, load line or load, including rigging and lifting accessories, could get closer than 20 feet to a line, the employer has three choices: have the utility confirm the line is deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite, keep a 20-foot clearance, or use the Table A distance for the line's voltage [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. In kilovolts (kV), Table A requires 10 feet up to 50; 15 over 50 to 200; 20 over 200 to 350; 25 over 350 to 500; 35 over 500 to 750; and 45 over 750 to 1,000. Above 1,000, the utility or a qualified registered professional engineer sets it. Each "to" value is included [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. The utility must provide requested voltage information within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

The two clearance choices can require a planning meeting, a visible warning line, barricade or signs, non-conductive tag lines if used, and at least one more safeguard, such as an alarm or spotter. Subpart V work is excepted from that last requirement [29cfr1926.1408(b)]. Going below a line is generally barred unless it is confirmed deenergized and visibly grounded; exceptions exist [29cfr1926.1408(d)].

Assume every line is energized unless the utility confirms it has been, and still is, deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite [29cfr1926.1408(e)]. Operators and assigned crew must be trained, including on what to do after electrical contact and on staying clear of equipment and loads [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)].

Before operating, the employer must identify the work zone: demarcated boundaries you are prohibited from passing, or 360 degrees out to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. If equipment, load line or load (with rigging and accessories) could get within 20 feet of a line at that radius, one option applies: utility-confirmed deenergizing with visible worksite grounding, 20-foot clearance, or Table A clearance [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. Table A (AC, nominal kV): up to 50, 10 feet; over 50 to 200, 15; over 200 to 350, 20; over 350 to 500, 25; over 500 to 750, 35; over 750 to 1,000, 45; over 1,000, set by the utility or a qualified registered professional engineer. Upper values are inclusive [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. Requested voltage information is due from the utility within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

Where encroachment precautions are required, there must be a planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines if used, and a flagged or high-visibility warning line, barricade or sign line in your view at the applicable distance [29cfr1926.1408(b)]. At least one measure is also required: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, automatic warning device, automatic range limiter, or insulating link/device; subpart V work is excepted from this [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1408(b)(5)]. If you cannot see the warning line, a dedicated spotter is required plus one of the other four [29cfr1926.1408(b)(3)]. Spotters need continuous contact, a visual aid, effective positioning, direct communication equipment where necessary, and must give timely information [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)].

Operating below lines requires confirmed deenergizing and worksite grounding unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1408(d)]. Presume lines energized [29cfr1926.1408(e)]. Near transmitter towers where charge could be induced, deenergize the transmitter, or ground the equipment and use only non-conductive tag lines if any [29cfr1926.1408(f)]. Training covers contact procedures, line presumptions, device limitations and grounding [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)]. Safety devices, aids and contact-prevention means used for compliance must meet manufacturer procedures and conditions [29cfr1926.1408(h)].

Check pre-operation work-zone identification: boundaries with an operator prohibition, or 360 degrees to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. Verify the 20-foot determination includes equipment, load line, load, rigging and accessories. If triggered, confirm Option (1) utility confirmation of deenergizing and visible worksite grounding, Option (2) 20-foot clearance, or Option (3) voltage and Table A determinations; under Option (3), paragraph (b) applies if the minimum could be breached [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. Table A (kV/feet): up to 50/10; over 50–200/15; over 200–350/20; over 350–500/25; over 500–750/35; over 750–1,000/45; over 1,000, utility or qualified registered professional engineer determines. Upper values are inclusive [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. Utilities must supply requested voltage within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

For required encroachment precautions, check the planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines, and visible, marked warning line, barricade or signs at 20 feet or the Table A distance. An operator unable to see it needs a spotter plus measure (i), (iii), (iv) or (v) [29cfr1926.1408(b)(3)]. Otherwise at least one listed measure applies [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)]; check spotter conditions, alarm or warning settings, limiter settings, or insulating-link placement and § 1926.1401 definition. Paragraph (b)(4) excludes subpart V work [29cfr1926.1408(b)(5)].

Below-line exceptions require employer demonstration: subpart V; boom clearance, with the uppermost part more than 20 feet or the Table A distance below the line's plane at true vertical (extensible or articulating booms fully extended); or infeasibility plus § 1926.1410 compliance [29cfr1926.1408(d)(2)].

Verify the energized presumption [29cfr1926.1408(e)], transmitter precautions [29cfr1926.1408(f)], operator/crew training, including the uninsulated presumption [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)], spotter training [29cfr1926.1408(g)(2)], administration under § 1926.1430(g) [29cfr1926.1408(g)(3)], and manufacturer conditions for covered devices (see § 1926.1415) [29cfr1926.1408(h)].

This section is about safety around power lines rated over 350 kV. It does not start from scratch. It says the requirements in two other sections, §§ 1926.1407 and 1926.1408, apply to these lines, but with two exceptions [29cfr1926.1409]. So you need to read those two sections together with this one. Their contents are not repeated here.

The first exception covers lines over 350 kV that are at or below 1000 kV. Wherever those requirements specify "20 feet", you must use "50 feet" instead [29cfr1926.1409(a)]. In other words, the larger distance replaces the smaller one every place it is specified.

The second exception covers lines over 1000 kV. This section does not give a number of feet for them. Instead, someone has to establish the minimum clearance distance. It must be established by "the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution" [29cfr1926.1409(b)]. A line's voltage therefore determines which of these two exceptions applies to it.

For power lines over 350 kV, you work under the requirements of §§ 1926.1407 and 1926.1408, subject to two exceptions set out here [29cfr1926.1409]. This section does not restate those requirements, so they have to be read from those sections.

Which exception applies depends on the line's voltage. For lines in this group that are at or below 1000 kV, the distance "50 feet" must be substituted wherever "20 feet" is specified [29cfr1926.1409(a)]. The wording is "wherever", so the substitution is not limited to a particular provision within the requirements that apply. A line at exactly 1000 kV falls under this exception.

For lines over 1000 kV, the section states no fixed distance. The "minimum clearance distance must be established" by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1409(b)]. The section names who must establish that distance. It does not describe a method for doing so, or state what form the result must take.

Scope: §§ 1926.1407 and 1926.1408 apply to power lines over 350 kV, except as paragraphs (a) and (b) provide [29cfr1926.1409]. The text of those two sections is the cross-reference for the underlying requirements; this section does not reproduce them.

Paragraph (a) applies to lines in this scope that are "at or below 1000 kV", including a line at exactly 1000 kV. The condition to verify is substitution: wherever the distance "20 feet" is specified, "the distance “50 feet” must be substituted" [29cfr1926.1409(a)]. The paragraph's substitution concerns that specified distance. It states no other change.

Paragraph (b) applies to lines "over 1000 kV". Here the minimum clearance distance must be established, and the section supplies no figure [29cfr1926.1409(b)]. The points of compliance are that such a distance has been established and who established it. The text names "the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution" [29cfr1926.1409(b)]. The section does not specify a calculation method or documentation format, and it does not define "qualified person" within this text.

Working with equipment closer to an energized power line than the Table A distance in § 1926.1408 is "prohibited" unless the employer shows that every requirement here is met [29cfr1926.1410]. This covers any part of the equipment, load line, load or rigging. The aim is to prevent electrical contact and electrocution [29cfr1926.1410(d)].

First, the employer must find that the work is infeasible without going closer [29cfr1926.1410(a)]. After consulting the utility, the employer must also find it infeasible to deenergize and ground the line, or move it [29cfr1926.1410(b)]. A qualified party then sets a minimum clearance for site conditions [29cfr1926.1410(c)(1)]. Subpart V work uses different distances [29cfr1926.1410(c)(2)].

A planning meeting sets safety procedures [29cfr1926.1410(d)]. These include disabling automatic power restoration, if its design permits [29cfr1926.1410(d)(1)]. A dedicated spotter stays in continuous contact with the operator [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)], using a visual aid to judge clearance [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)(i)] and giving timely information [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)(iv)]. Other protections include a warning line or barricade [29cfr1926.1410(d)(3)] and an insulating link between load line and load [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(i)], with subpart V exceptions to both. Temporary substitutes for the link ran only until November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(iv)] or November 8, 2013 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)]. Perimeter barricades are at least 10 feet from the equipment, or as far as feasible where obstacles prevent that [29cfr1926.1410(d)(8)]. Only essential personnel may be near the crane and load [29cfr1926.1410(d)(10)]. The procedures also cover rigging, tag lines, range limiters, touching, remote operation, grounding and line covers [29cfr1926.1410(d)].

Procedures must be written down and on-site [29cfr1926.1410(e)], reviewed with the operator and nearby workers [29cfr1926.1410(f)], and carried out [29cfr1926.1410(g)]. One identified person directs them and can stop work [29cfr1926.1410(h)]. If they fail or prove inadequate, work stops safely [29cfr1926.1410(j)]. Operators and assigned crew must be trained [29cfr1926.1410(m)].

Operating inside the § 1926.1408 Table A distance is prohibited unless the employer demonstrates that all conditions are met [29cfr1926.1410]. The employer must determine that breaching it is unavoidable for feasibility reasons [29cfr1926.1410(a)] and, after consulting the utility, that deenergizing and grounding or relocating the line is infeasible [29cfr1926.1410(b)]. The line owner/operator or a qualified registered professional engineer sets the minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1410(c)(1)]; subpart V work uses employer-established § 1926.960(c)(1)(i) distances [29cfr1926.1410(c)(2)].

Planned procedures [29cfr1926.1410(d)] include disabling automatic reclosing before work, if design permits [29cfr1926.1410(d)(1)]; a continuously connected, well-positioned spotter with a visual aid, giving timely information, with direct communication equipment where necessary [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)]; and a flagged or similarly marked elevated warning line or barricade, unattached to the crane and visible to you directly or by video [29cfr1926.1410(d)(3)]. An insulating link goes between the load line end (or below) and load [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(i)]. Subpart V is excepted from both. Link substitutes ran only until November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(iv)] and November 8, 2013 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)].

Rigging that may enter the Table A distance, and any tag line, must be nonconductive [29cfr1926.1410(d)(5)] [29cfr1926.1410(d)(7)]. Any range limiter must be used and set to protect the established clearance [29cfr1926.1410(d)(6)]. Perimeter barricades are at least 10 feet out, or as far as feasible where obstructed [29cfr1926.1410(d)(8)]. Others may not touch the crane or the load line above the link; remote ground operators need isolating wireless controls or insulating mats [29cfr1926.1410(d)(9)]. Only essential personnel stay near [29cfr1926.1410(d)(10)]. Ground the equipment [29cfr1926.1410(d)(11)]. The utility installs line hose or cover-up unless unavailable for the voltage [29cfr1926.1410(d)(12)].

Procedures are documented, reviewed and implemented [29cfr1926.1410(e)] [29cfr1926.1410(f)] [29cfr1926.1410(g)]. One director has stop-work authority [29cfr1926.1410(h)]. Problems or inadequacy require safely stopping; before resuming, develop new procedures or have the utility deenergize and visibly ground, or relocate, the line [29cfr1926.1410(j)]. Safety devices and aids follow manufacturer conditions [29cfr1926.1410(k)]. Training follows § 1926.1408(g) [29cfr1926.1410(m)].

Verify that the employer demonstrates every condition for operating inside the § 1926.1408 Table A distance [29cfr1926.1410]: both infeasibility determinations, including utility consultation [29cfr1926.1410(a)] [29cfr1926.1410(b)]; and clearance set by the line owner/operator or qualified engineer, considering the listed non-exhaustive site factors, such as stopping time, wind and line sway [29cfr1926.1410(c)(1)]. For subpart V, § 1926.960(c)(1)(i) distances apply instead [29cfr1926.1410(c)(2)].

Check the planning meeting [29cfr1926.1410(d)] and minimum procedures: reclosing disabled if design permits [29cfr1926.1410(d)(1)]; spotter contact, visual aid, positioning, necessary communication equipment and timely information [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)]; visible, marked warning line or barricade not attached to the crane, except subpart V [29cfr1926.1410(d)(3)]; and insulating link [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(i)], except subpart V [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(ii)]. Until November 8, 2011, insulating or guarding exposed employees (not operators on the equipment) could substitute [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(iv)]. Until November 8, 2013, a qualifying unapproved link manufactured on or before November 8, 2011 could substitute, with additional protection [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)(A)] [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)(B)].

Also check nonconductive rigging and tag lines, and range limiters [29cfr1926.1410(d)]; barricades at least 10 feet away, or as far as feasible where obstacles prevent this [29cfr1926.1410(d)(8)]; touching and remote-operation controls [29cfr1926.1410(d)(9)]; essential personnel only [29cfr1926.1410(d)(10)]; grounding [29cfr1926.1410(d)(11)]; and utility-installed line covers, unless unavailable for the voltage [29cfr1926.1410(d)(12)].
