Confirm on-site documentation, worker review and implementation [29cfr1926.1410(e)] [29cfr1926.1410(f)] [29cfr1926.1410(g)]; one identified director with stop-work authority [29cfr1926.1410(h)]; required stoppage and correction after problems or inadequacy [29cfr1926.1410(j)]; manufacturer compliance for covered devices, referencing § 1926.1415 [29cfr1926.1410(k)]; and operator and crew training under § 1926.1408(g) [29cfr1926.1410(m)].

This section is about power line safety when equipment travels under or near a power line on a construction site with no load [29cfr1926.1411(a)]. If the equipment is carrying a load, other rules apply [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

Your employer must make sure the boom or mast and its support system are lowered enough to meet these rules [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)]. Required clearances, meaning distances from the line, must be kept [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)]. Speed and ground conditions must be considered so that equipment movement, including boom or mast movement, does not break the minimum distance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

The minimum depends on the line's nominal alternating current voltage in kV: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the utility owner/operator or a qualifying registered professional engineer sets it [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

If any part will get closer than 20 feet while traveling, a "dedicated spotter" must stay in "continuous contact with the driver/operator" [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. At night or in poor visibility, there are extra rules: identify where the lines are, by lighting or another way, and identify and use a safe path [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)].

These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

The employer must ensure the boom/mast and its support system are lowered sufficiently [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], Table T clearances are maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and speed and terrain effects, including boom/mast movement, are considered so they do not cause a breach of minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T minimums, by nominal AC voltage in kV, are: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the distance is established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

If any part of traveling equipment will get closer than 20 feet to the line, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with you is required [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. The spotter must be positioned to gauge clearance effectively, use direct communication equipment where necessary, and give you "timely information" so clearance can be maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)].

At night or in poor visibility, lines must also be illuminated or otherwise located, and a safe travel path identified and used [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)].

Scope: equipment traveling under or near a power line on a construction site with no load. For loaded travel, the cross-references are § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, as appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

Verify that the employer ensures sufficient lowering of the boom/mast and support system [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], maintenance of Table T clearances [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and consideration of speed and terrain effects on movement, including the boom/mast, so minimum distances are not breached [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T (nominal kV, AC): up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6; over 50 to 345, 10; over 345 to 750, 16; over 750 to 1,000, 20. Over 1,000, distance is set by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer who is a qualified person regarding electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

Spotter trigger: any equipment part that, while traveling, will get "closer than 20 feet to the power line" [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. Check continuous contact with the driver/operator [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)], effective positioning [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)(i)], direct-communication equipment "Where necessary" [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)(ii)], and timely information supporting required clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)(iii)].

For night or poor-visibility travel, (b)(1) through (4) measures remain, plus line illumination or another means of identifying line location [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)(i)], and an identified, used safe path [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)(ii)].

This section says when equipment must be inspected. Many checks look for problems that affect safe operation. Before each shift in which the equipment will be used, a competent person must start a visual check for "apparent deficiencies". It must be finished before or during that shift [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)]. It covers items such as controls, pressurized lines, hooks, wire rope, electrical parts, tires in use, ground support, cab windows and safety devices. Level is checked before each shift and after each move and setup [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xi)]. Some rail ground and track checks have an exception for certain federally regulated railroad track [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(x)] [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xiii)].

For most problems, the competent person must decide immediately whether there is a safety hazard. If there is, the equipment comes out of service until corrected [29cfr1926.1412(d)(2)]. Safety device and operational aid problems require action under other sections before use [29cfr1926.1412(d)(3)].

A qualified person inspects after changes affecting safe operation or capacity [29cfr1926.1412(a)(1)], after safety-related repairs or adjustments [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)], and after assembly [29cfr1926.1412(c)(1)]. Each has conditions that must be shown to be met before use.

Each month in service, equipment gets the shift-type inspection [29cfr1926.1412(e)(1)]. Records are kept at least three months [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(ii)]. At least every 12 months, a qualified person performs annual inspections [29cfr1926.1412(f)(1)], including a detailed one [29cfr1926.1412(f)(2)]. Annual records are kept at least 12 months [29cfr1926.1412(f)(7)].

If severe use makes damage or excessive wear reasonably probable, the employer must stop using the equipment, and a qualified person must inspect it [29cfr1926.1412(g)]. Equipment idle for 3 months or more needs a qualified person's monthly-type inspection before use [29cfr1926.1412(h)]. Certain stricter manufacturer inspection procedures must also be followed [29cfr1926.1412(j)].

Each shift, a competent person begins a visual inspection beforehand and completes it before or during the shift. It covers at least the listed controls, drives, lines, hydraulic fluid, hooks, rope and reeving, electrical apparatus, tires, ground, level, windows, rail components and safety devices/aids. Disassembly or booming down is needed only if visual inspection or trial operation shows it. Determinations are reassessed during operation [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)]. Level is checked against manufacturer tolerances before each shift and after each move and setup [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xi)]. Ground and rail items have exceptions for certain FRA-regulated track [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(x)] [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xiii)]. Hazardous deficiencies under items (i)-(xiii), or additional type-specific items, take equipment out of service until corrected [29cfr1926.1412(d)(2)]. Safety device/aid deficiencies require §§ 1926.1415 and 1926.1416 action before use [29cfr1926.1412(d)(3)].

Monthly, while in service, the shift inspection applies. Use waits until it shows no corrective action is required [29cfr1926.1412(e)(2)]. The inspecting employer documents it [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(i)] and retains it at least three months [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(ii)].

Qualified persons inspect safety- or capacity-affecting modifications [29cfr1926.1412(a)(1)], safety-related repairs/adjustments [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)] and completed assemblies [29cfr1926.1412(c)(1)]. Required criteria must be shown met before use [29cfr1926.1412(a)(2)] [29cfr1926.1412(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1412(c)(3)].

At least every 12 months, qualified persons conduct the shift-based [29cfr1926.1412(f)(1)] and comprehensive inspections, disassembling as necessary [29cfr1926.1412(f)(2)], with functional testing [29cfr1926.1412(f)(3)]. Hazards remove equipment from service until corrected, subject to specified temporary alternative measures [29cfr1926.1412(f)(5)]. Deficiencies needing monitoring must be checked monthly [29cfr1926.1412(f)(6)]. Records are retained at least 12 months [29cfr1926.1412(f)(7)].

Severe service requires stopping use and inspection [29cfr1926.1412(g)]. Equipment idle 3 months or more needs a qualified person's monthly inspection before use [29cfr1926.1412(h)]. Specified stricter manufacturer procedures apply [29cfr1926.1412(j)].

For safety- or capacity-affecting modifications, verify qualified-person inspection before initial use, conformity with § 1926.1434 approval, and functional testing [29cfr1926.1412(a)(1)]. For safety-related repairs/adjustments, also before initial use, verify qualified-person inspection [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)], applicable, available manufacturer criteria or developed criteria [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)(ii)], and testing of repaired and potentially affected components [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)(iii)]. Post-assembly configuration follows manufacturer criteria [29cfr1926.1412(c)(1)]; if unavailable, developed criteria [29cfr1926.1412(c)(2)]. The qualified person determines RPE need (for assembly, one familiar with the equipment type); the employer ensures the RPE or, if unneeded, qualified person develops criteria [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)(ii)(A)] [29cfr1926.1412(c)(2)(i)]. Check use restrictions [29cfr1926.1412(a)(2)] [29cfr1926.1412(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1412(c)(3)].

Check competent-person shift inspections against minimum items [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)], including level after each move/setup [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xi)]; note FRA/49 CFR part 213 exceptions [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(x)] [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xiii)]. Verify immediate hazard determinations and removal [29cfr1926.1412(d)(2)] (see § 1926.1417), and §§ 1926.1415/1926.1416 action [29cfr1926.1412(d)(3)]. Monthly: check use restriction [29cfr1926.1412(e)(2)], items, results, name, signature, date [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(i)], retained minimum three months [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(ii)].

At least every 12 months, verify both qualified-person inspections [29cfr1926.1412(f)(1)] [29cfr1926.1412(f)(2)]: comprehensive scope spans structure, mechanical, power, travel, pressure, electrical and operator-access/safety items. Check functional testing [29cfr1926.1412(f)(3)], hazard/monitoring determinations [29cfr1926.1412(f)(4)], removal and §§ 1926.1416(d)/1926.1435(e) exception [29cfr1926.1412(f)(5)], monthly follow-up [29cfr1926.1412(f)(6)], and records retained minimum 12 months [29cfr1926.1412(f)(7)].

Severe service: check cessation, structural inspection, relevant (f) items and (f)(4)-(6) actions [29cfr1926.1412(g)]. Idle 3 months or more: qualified-person monthly inspection before use [29cfr1926.1412(h)]. Check safety-related manufacturer procedures that are more comprehensive or frequent [29cfr1926.1412(j)], and document availability to section inspectors during retention [29cfr1926.1412(k)].

Wire ropes are checked each shift, monthly and at least yearly. A competent person must start a visual check before each shift the equipment is used and finish it before or during that shift. It covers moving (running) and fixed (standing) ropes likely to be used. Opening the rope or lowering the boom is not required. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(1)] Extra attention goes to certain places and uses, such as rotation resistant rope, boom hoists, spots on drums and rope ends. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(3)]

Problems fall into three groups. Category I includes significant crushing, kinking or corrosion, heat damage, and bad end connections. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(i)] The competent person must immediately decide whether it is a safety hazard. If so, work using that rope stops until it is fixed. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(i)]

Category II covers broken wires. A rope lay is the length in which one strand wraps once around the rope. The limits are six scattered breaks in one lay, or three in one strand in one lay, for running rope [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(1)]; two in six rope diameters or four in 30 for rotation resistant rope [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(2)]; and, for pendants or standing rope, more than two per lay away from end connections and/or more than one in a lay at one [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(3)]. Diameter shrinking more than 5% from nominal also counts. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(B)] Use stops until the rope is replaced, a localized problem is cut out, or the manufacturer-based removal rule is met. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(ii)]

Category III includes a broken strand, past power line contact, or signs of core failure in rotation resistant rope. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(iii)] Use stops until replacement or an allowed cut. Cutting cannot cure power line contact. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iii)]

After any cut, splicing lengths together is banned, and the drum must keep "two wraps" at the lowest load and/or boom position. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(i)(B)] Removed rope means tagging out the equipment or hoist. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iv)] Monthly and yearly checks must be documented. [29cfr1926.1413(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1413(c)(4)] Lubricants that hinder inspection are banned. [29cfr1926.1413(d)]

Each shift the equipment is used, a competent person begins a visual inspection beforehand, completing it before or during the shift, of running and standing ropes likely to be used. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(1)] Critical review items include rotation resistant, boom and luffing hoist ropes, drum wear points, terminal ends, and limited-travel sheaves or saddles. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(3)]

Category I (significant distortion or corrosion, certain arc or heat damage, defective end connections) requires an immediate hazard determination by the competent person. A hazard bars use until replacement or severing out a localized defect. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(i)]

Category II triggers: running rope, six random broken wires in one lay or three in one strand in one lay [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(1)]; rotation resistant, two random breaks in six diameters or four in 30 [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(2)]; pendants or standing rope, more than two per lay beyond end connections and/or more than one per lay at an end connection [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(3)]; or diameter reduction over 5% from nominal [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(B)]. Use is barred until replacement, localized severing, or compliance with the manufacturer's removal criterion or one it approved in writing for that rope. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(ii)]

Category III (rotation resistant core failure indications, prior power line contact, broken strand) bars use until replacement or localized severing; severing is unavailable for power line contact. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iii)] After severing, the undamaged portion may be used, splicing lengths is prohibited, and the drum must retain two wraps with load and/or boom lowest. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(ii)(C)] Tag out the equipment or hoist until repair or replacement. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iv)]

Monthly inspections follow shift procedures, include items flagged for monitoring, and are documented. Ropes stay unused until inspection shows no corrective action is required. [29cfr1926.1413(b)]

At least every 12 months, a qualified person performs the shift-type inspection [29cfr1926.1413(c)(1)] and a thorough full-length surface inspection [29cfr1926.1413(c)(2)(ii)]. Findings need immediate hazard decisions; hazards require replacement or localized severing. [29cfr1926.1413(c)(3)] Document it. [29cfr1926.1413(c)(4)] Inspection-hindering lubricants are prohibited. [29cfr1926.1413(d)]

Verify competent-person shift inspections, including timing and apparent deficiencies; untwisting and booming down are not required. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(1)] Check attention to all critical review items, including reverse bends on boom and luffing hoists, drum points, terminal ends and limited-travel sheaves. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(3)]

Category I requires an immediate hazard determination; prohibition applies if hazardous. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(i)] Its arc damage is "from a source other than power lines". [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(i)(C)] Category II limits: running, six random breaks per lay or three in one strand per lay; rotation resistant, two in six diameters or four in 30; pendants/standing, more than two per lay beyond end connections and/or more than one per lay at one [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)]; diameter loss more than 5% from nominal [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(B)]. Its alternative to replacement or localized severing is compliance with the manufacturer's criterion, or a different one approved in writing for that rope. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(ii)(A)] For Category III, localized severing excludes power line contact, and repairing rope that contacted an energized line is prohibited. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iii)(B)] Check no splice-joining, two drum wraps after shortening [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(i)(B)], and equipment or hoist tag-out under § 1926.1417(f)(1) [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iv)].

Check monthly inspections, monitored items, pre-use clearance of (a)(4) corrective action, and documentation under § 1926.1412(e)(3). [29cfr1926.1413(b)]

At least every 12 months, verify both qualified-person inspections: shift-type [29cfr1926.1413(c)(1)] and complete, full-length surface coverage for listed deficiency types, emphasizing critical items, normally hidden sections, reverse bends and sheaves [29cfr1926.1413(c)(2)]. The infeasibility exception, for setup/configuration or site conditions, addresses (c)(2): perform when feasible, within an additional 6 months for running ropes; for standing ropes, at disassembly. [29cfr1926.1413(c)(2)(iii)] Verify immediate hazard determinations, prohibition pending replacement or localized severing, and monthly follow-up of monitored nonhazards [29cfr1926.1413(c)(3)], plus § 1926.1412(f)(7) documentation [29cfr1926.1413(c)(4)]. Confirm no inspection-hindering lubricants [29cfr1926.1413(d)] and document access for all inspectors during applicable retention periods [29cfr1926.1413(e)].

This section covers how wire rope is chosen and installed, for both original and replacement rope [29cfr1926.1414(a)]. Replacement rope is selected following the recommendations of the rope manufacturer, the equipment manufacturer, or a qualified person [29cfr1926.1414(a)]. All rope must be "compatible with the safe functioning of the equipment" [29cfr1926.1414(c)].

Rope that is not rotation resistant must meet one of two design options. One uses section 5-1.7.1 of ASME B30.5-2004, without its paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1414(b)(1)]. The other requires enough breaking strength and design factor for the required inspections to work in "preventing sudden rope failure" [29cfr1926.1414(b)(2)].

Rotation resistant rope has three types. Type I has at least 15 outer strands in at least three layers [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)(i)]. Type II has at least 10 in two or more layers [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)(ii)]. Type III has no more than nine in two layers [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)(iii)]. All need an operating design factor of at least 3.5 [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. The usual minimum is 5. Type I may go below 5 with written approval from both manufacturers [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. Types II and III may if special per-lift rules are met [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iv)], but never for duty cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(i)]. Those rules cover inspection, careful operation, and records [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)].

The boom hoist has limits. Fiber core rope is banned there, except on derricks [29cfr1926.1414(d)(1)]. Rotation resistant rope is allowed only when load hoists serve as boom hoists for certain attachments and every listed condition is met, including 18-times-rope-diameter sizing and a design factor of at least five [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)].

Clips used with wedge sockets go only on the unloaded dead end; devices made for dead-ending are allowed [29cfr1926.1414(f)]. Socketing follows the rope or fitting maker's method [29cfr1926.1414(g)]. Before cutting rope, place seizings on both sides of the cut, with length and number set by the rope maker's instructions [29cfr1926.1414(h)].

Original and replacement rope must be selected and installed under this section. Replacement selection follows the rope manufacturer's, equipment manufacturer's, or a qualified person's recommendations [29cfr1926.1414(a)]. Rope must be compatible with safe equipment functioning [29cfr1926.1414(c)]. Non-rotation-resistant rope must meet ASME B30.5-2004 section 5-1.7.1, excluding paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1414(b)(1)], or the performance option tied to rated capacity and § 1926.1413 inspections [29cfr1926.1414(b)(2)].

Rotation resistant types are Type I (at least 15 outer strands, at least three layers), Type II (at least 10, two or more layers) and Type III (no more than nine, two layers) [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)]. The operating design factor floor for all is 3.5 [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. Type I needs at least 5 unless both the rope and equipment manufacturers approve the factor in writing [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. Types II and III below 5 are barred from duty cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(i)]. For other lifts below 5, each operation requires a qualified person's inspection under § 1926.1413(a), with use only if no hazardous deficiencies are found; more than one broken wire in any one rope lay is a hazard [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(i)]. Operating manner and speed must minimize dynamic effects [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(ii)]. Record each such lift in the monthly and annual inspection documents; the qualified person considers prior uses before reuse [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(iii)].

For boom hoists, fiber core rope is allowed only on derricks [29cfr1926.1414(d)(1)]. Rotation resistant rope is allowed only where load hoists act as boom hoists for attachments such as luffing or boom and mast systems. Drum first-layer and all sheave pitch diameters must be at least 18 times nominal rope diameter, the system design factor at least five, and the other listed conditions met, including any power-controlled lowering system's capability [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)].

Wedge socket clips attach only to the unloaded dead end, though purpose-designed dead-ending devices are permitted [29cfr1926.1414(f)]. Socket as the rope or fitting manufacturer specifies [29cfr1926.1414(g)]. Before cutting, seize both sides, following the rope manufacturer's length and number instructions [29cfr1926.1414(h)].

Verify selection and installation of original and replacement rope; replacement selection must follow the rope manufacturer, equipment manufacturer, or a qualified person [29cfr1926.1414(a)], and rope must be compatible with safe equipment functioning [29cfr1926.1414(c)]. Non-rotation-resistant rope: ASME B30.5-2004 section 5-1.7.1 except paragraph (c), or the § 1926.1413-linked performance option [29cfr1926.1414(b)]. No fiber core boom hoist reeving except derricks [29cfr1926.1414(d)(1)].

Classify by construction; each type's outer lay opposes the underlying layer. Type I: at least 15 outer strands, at least three layers, two operations; II: at least 10, two or more layers, two or three operations; III: no more than nine, two layers, two operations [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)]. All require at least 3.5 operating design factor [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. Type I requires 5 unless both manufacturers approve in writing [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. II/III below 5: no duty cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(i)]; for each operation, check qualified-person inspection under § 1926.1413(a) and no hazardous deficiencies (more than one broken wire per rope lay is hazardous), minimized dynamic effects, lift entries in monthly and annual inspection documents, and consideration of prior uses [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)].

Rotation resistant boom hoist reeving requires load hoists used as boom hoists for attachments [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)]. Check drum first-layer pitch diameter at least 18 times nominal rope diameter [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)(A)]; § 1926.1426(a), regardless of manufacture date, and (b) [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)(B)]; ASME B30.5-2004 5-1.3.2(a), (a)(2)-(a)(4), (b), (d), substituting 18 for 16 in multiple rope reeving [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)(C)]; all sheaves at least 18 times [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)(D)]; factor at least five [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)(E)], calculated as total minimum breaking force of all rope parts divided by load from static structure and load weights within rated capacity [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)(F)]; and any power-controlled lowering system handling manufacturer-specified rated capacities and speeds [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)(G)].

Check wedge socket clips on the unloaded dead end only, excepting purpose-designed devices [29cfr1926.1414(f)]; manufacturer-specified socketing [29cfr1926.1414(g)]; and pre-cut seizings on both sides per rope manufacturer instructions [29cfr1926.1414(h)].

This section lists safety devices that equipment covered by this subpart must have, "unless otherwise specified" [29cfr1926.1415(a)]. One is a crane level indicator, either built in or available on the equipment [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(i)]. Some equipment, including derricks and portal cranes, is excluded from this indicator requirement [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(iii)]. There must also be a horn. It is either built in, or on the equipment and "immediately available to the operator" [29cfr1926.1415(a)(7)(i)].

The other items are boom stops [29cfr1926.1415(a)(2)], jib stops when a jib is attached [29cfr1926.1415(a)(3)], locks on equipment with foot pedal brakes [29cfr1926.1415(a)(4)], holding devices or check valves built into hydraulic outrigger and stabilizer jacks [29cfr1926.1415(a)(5)], and rail clamps and rail stops for equipment on rails [29cfr1926.1415(a)(6)]. Some of these have exceptions.

Why it matters: work must not start unless all listed devices work properly. If one stops working during work, the operator must safely stop operations. If any listed device is not working properly, the equipment must be taken out of service, and work cannot restart until that device works again. No substitute measures are allowed [29cfr1926.1415(b)].

Unless otherwise specified, all equipment covered by this subpart requires these devices [29cfr1926.1415(a)]. A crane level indicator must be built in or available on the equipment [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(i)], with exclusions for certain cranes and derricks, including portal and floating types [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(iii)]. A horn must be built in, or on the equipment and immediately available to you [29cfr1926.1415(a)(7)(i)]. For either device, a faulty built-in unit must be tagged out or removed, while a faulty removable one must be removed [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(ii)] [29cfr1926.1415(a)(7)(ii)].

Also required are boom stops, except on derricks and hydraulic booms [29cfr1926.1415(a)(2)]; jib stops if a jib is attached, except on derricks [29cfr1926.1415(a)(3)]; locks where there are foot pedal brakes [29cfr1926.1415(a)(4)]; an integral holding device/check valve on hydraulic outrigger and stabilizer jacks [29cfr1926.1415(a)(5)]; and rail clamps and rail stops on rail-mounted equipment, except portal cranes [29cfr1926.1415(a)(6)].

Operations must not begin unless all listed devices work properly. If one fails during operations, you must safely stop. With any listed device not working properly, the equipment must be taken out of service until that device works again. "Alternative measures are not permitted to be used." The text refers to § 1926.1417 (Operation) [29cfr1926.1415(b)].

Scope is all equipment covered by this subpart, "unless otherwise specified" [29cfr1926.1415(a)]. Verify:

A level indicator built in or available on the equipment [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(i)]. This requirement excludes portal cranes, derricks, floating cranes/derricks, and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other flotation [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(iii)]. Boom stops, except for derricks and hydraulic booms [29cfr1926.1415(a)(2)]. Jib stops where a jib is attached, except for derricks [29cfr1926.1415(a)(3)]. Locks on equipment with foot pedal brakes [29cfr1926.1415(a)(4)]. An integral holding device/check valve on hydraulic outrigger and stabilizer jacks [29cfr1926.1415(a)(5)]. Rail clamps and rail stops on equipment on rails, except portal cranes [29cfr1926.1415(a)(6)]. A horn built in, or on the equipment and immediately available to the operator [29cfr1926.1415(a)(7)(i)].

For malfunctioning level indicators and horns, check that built-in units are tagged-out or removed and removable units are removed [29cfr1926.1415(a)(1)(ii)] [29cfr1926.1415(a)(7)(ii)].

Check that operations did not begin unless all listed devices were in proper working order, and that the operator safely stopped if one failed during operations. If any listed device is not working properly, the equipment must be out of service, without resumption until it works again. Alternative measures are prohibited. Cross-reference: § 1926.1417 (Operation) [29cfr1926.1415(b)].

Operational aids are listed devices that equipment covered by this subpart must have unless the section says otherwise [29cfr1926.1416(a)]. Work must not start unless they work properly. The exception is an aid under repair while the employer uses the specified temporary substitute method. Any more protective method from the crane or derrick maker must be followed [29cfr1926.1416(b)]. If an aid fails during work, the operator must safely stop until that method is in place or the device works again [29cfr1926.1416(c)].

Category I covers devices that limit boom hoist or luffing jib movement, and anti two-blocking devices. Two-blocking protection concerns contact between parts such as the load block and boom tip. Repair is due within 7 calendar days. If the employer documents ordering parts within those 7 days, repair is due within 7 days of receiving them [29cfr1926.1416(d)]. Boom limiters are required on equipment made after December 16, 1969 [29cfr1926.1416(d)(1)(i)]. Substitutes include angle indicators or cable marks; older equipment without a limiter must use at least one [29cfr1926.1416(d)(1)(ii)]. Luffing jibs also need limiters [29cfr1926.1416(d)(2)]. Anti two-blocking rules depend on crane type and date: February 28, 1992 for telescopic and lattice booms, November 8, 2011 for stricter lattice boom and derrick rules, and December 31, 1999 for articulating cranes with load hoists [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)]. Substitutes use cable marks and, in some cases, spotters.

Category II has a 30-day repair limit, with a parts-delay exception [29cfr1926.1416(e)]. It includes boom angle or radius, jib angle and boom length indicators, each where applicable. Certain equipment rated over 6,000 pounds and made after March 29, 2003 needs a load-related device [29cfr1926.1416(e)(4)(i)]. So do articulating cranes made after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1416(e)(4)(ii)]. Equipment made after that date also needs outrigger or stabilizer position and hidden hoist drum rotation devices, where applicable [29cfr1926.1416(e)(5)]. Some rules have equipment exceptions [29cfr1926.1416(a)].

Listed aids must work before operations begin, unless one is under repair and the specified temporary measures are used; follow any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1416(b)]. On failure during operations, you must safely stop until those measures are in place or the device works. If a replacement part is no longer available, a same-function substitute is permitted [29cfr1926.1416(c)]. Articulating cranes are excluded from (e)(1)-(3); (d)(3), (e)(1) and (e)(4) apply only to digger derricks made after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1416(a)].

Category I repair: 7 calendar days, or, with documented parts ordering within 7 days, 7 days after receipt [29cfr1926.1416(d)]. Boom hoist limiters are required after December 16, 1969. Use at least one fallback: angle indicator, or cable mark visible to you or a spotter, allowing time to stop within minimum allowable radius. Add mirrors or video if you need them to see your mark. Older unequipped machines need one of these [29cfr1926.1416(d)(1)]. Luffing jib limiters use corresponding fallbacks [29cfr1926.1416(d)(2)].

Anti two-blocking: telescopic cranes after February 28, 1992 need automatic prevention; fallback is cable mark plus spotter when extending [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(i)]. Lattice cranes after Feb 28, 1992 need prevention or timely warning; lattice cranes and derricks after November 8, 2011 need automatic prevention. Specified uses, such as dragline or pile driving, are excepted. Fallback is cable mark or spotter [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(ii)]. Articulating cranes with load hoists after December 31, 1999 need automatic prevention. Use mark or spotter if only hoist movement can cause two-blocking; otherwise, if it can occur without that movement, mark and use a spotter when extending [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(iii)].

Category II repair: 30 days, with a parts exception. It covers angle/radius, jib and boom length indicators; fallbacks involve measurement, and for length, marks or calculation also work [29cfr1926.1416(e)]. Load devices apply to specified equipment over 6,000 pounds after March 29, 2003, and articulating cranes after November 8, 2011; fallback load weights must reach you before lifting [29cfr1926.1416(e)(4)]. Post-November 8, 2011 equipment has outrigger/stabilizer and drum rotation aids where applicable [29cfr1926.1416(e)(5)].

Scope: listed aids apply to all covered equipment unless otherwise specified; (e)(1)-(3) exclude articulating cranes, and (d)(3), (e)(1), (e)(4) reach only digger derricks manufactured after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1416(a)]. Check pre-operation function or, during repair, specified alternatives and any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1416(b)]. Mid-operation failure requires a safe stop until alternatives are implemented or function returns. Unavailable parts permit same-function substitutes, not modifications under § 1926.1434 [29cfr1926.1416(c)].

Category I: repair within 7 calendar days of deficiency; if parts ordering within 7 days is documented, within 7 days of receipt [29cfr1926.1416(d)]. Category II: 30 days; extension requires documented ordering within 7 days and receipt too late for 30-day completion, then repair within 7 days of receipt [29cfr1926.1416(e)]. Both cross-reference § 1926.1417(j).

Verify boom limiters after December 16, 1969; for failed ones, or older unequipped machines, at least one of indicator, operator-visible mark (mirrors/video if necessary) or spotter-visible mark [29cfr1926.1416(d)(1)]. Luffing jibs require limiters and analogous alternatives [29cfr1926.1416(d)(2)].

Anti two-blocking covers all possible points: telescopic after February 28, 1992 [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(i)]; lattice cranes after Feb 28, 1992 (prevention or warning), lattice cranes/derricks after November 8, 2011 (automatic), subject to listed-use exceptions; marine exception is for operations "that do not involve hoisting personnel" [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(ii)(C)]; articulating cranes with load hoists after December 31, 1999 [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(iii)]. Alternatives differ by paragraph: mark, spotter, or both.

Check angle/radius readability from the operator's station, luffing jib indicators, and telescopic boom length indicators (unless capacity is length-independent), with specified alternatives [29cfr1926.1416(e)]. Load devices: non-derrick, non-articulating equipment after March 29, 2003, over 6,000 pounds; articulating cranes after November 8, 2011, which may also use automatic overload prevention. Recognized-source or calculated weights go to operators before lifting [29cfr1926.1416(e)(4)]. After November 8, 2011, check outrigger/stabilizer monitoring (alternative: pre-operation position verification per manufacturer procedures) and nonvisible-drum indicators (alternative: marking, mirrors/video if necessary) [29cfr1926.1416(e)(5)].

This section covers how equipment is operated. Your employer must follow the manufacturer's operating procedures, including those for attachments [29cfr1926.1417(a)]. If these are unavailable, the employer must develop safe ones and ensure they are followed. A qualified person develops control procedures. A registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment develops and signs capacity procedures [29cfr1926.1417(b)]. Operating information, including load charts, must be "readily available in the cab at all times". If electronic-only load charts become inaccessible, the operator must immediately stop or follow safe shut-down procedures until they are available [29cfr1926.1417(c)].

While operating, the operator must avoid distractions, such as phone use other than for signals [29cfr1926.1417(d)]. Leaving the controls with a suspended load is prohibited unless strict conditions are all met. A limited exception covers lightweight working gear [29cfr1926.1417(e)]. Out-of-service equipment or functions need tags, and warning signs restrict starting or activation [29cfr1926.1417(f)]. Before starting the engine, the operator checks control positions and that people are clear [29cfr1926.1417(g)]. Needed repairs must be reported and communicated [29cfr1926.1417(j)].

Never exceed rated capacity, and the operator must not be required to do so. The operator verifies the load is within it, using reliable weight information or a hoisting test with a 75 percent trigger [29cfr1926.1417(o)]. Brake tests apply at 90% or more of maximum line pull [29cfr1926.1417(s)]. Neither load nor boom may go so low that less than two full wraps of rope remain on their drums [29cfr1926.1417(t)].

Other rules address storms, slack rope and weather [29cfr1926.1417(h)] [29cfr1926.1417(m)] [29cfr1926.1417(n)]. They also cover obstructions, side pulls, lifting over the front, traveling, swinging and brake adjustment [29cfr1926.1417(p)] [29cfr1926.1417(q)] [29cfr1926.1417(r)] [29cfr1926.1417(u)] [29cfr1926.1417(v)] [29cfr1926.1417(w)] [29cfr1926.1417(x)] [29cfr1926.1417(z)]. Safety devices never replace the operator's professional judgment [29cfr1926.1417(k)]. The operator must obey any stop signal, "irrespective of who gives it" [29cfr1926.1417(y)]. Counterweight rules also apply [29cfr1926.1417(aa)].

Follow applicable manufacturer procedures; where unavailable, the employer's substitutes apply [29cfr1926.1417(a)] [29cfr1926.1417(b)(1)]. Keep procedures and load charts in the cab; if electronic-only capacities become inaccessible, cease operations or follow safe shut-down until available [29cfr1926.1417(c)]. Avoid diverting activities while operating [29cfr1926.1417(d)].

Leaving controls under a suspended load requires all of these: you stay adjacent without other duties; the hold exceeds normal lifting time; the competent person finds it safe and restrains specified functions; and barricades or caution lines, plus notices, keep all employees out of the fall zone [29cfr1926.1417(e)(1)]. Negligible-weight working gear not over an entrance or exit is excepted [29cfr1926.1417(e)(2)].

With warning signs, don't start or activate the affected control until an authorized person removes the sign, or you verify nobody is servicing, working on or dangerously positioned on the machine, and it is repaired and working properly [29cfr1926.1417(f)(2)]. Before engine start, verify control positions and clear personnel [29cfr1926.1417(g)]. Promptly report needed repairs in writing to the designated person and any next-shift operator [29cfr1926.1417(j)(1)].

Stay within rated capacity [29cfr1926.1417(o)(1)]. Verify load weight through recognized or equally reliable information, provided before the lift on request. Alternatively, begin hoisting with a listed device to check whether it exceeds 75 percent of maximum rated capacity at the longest radius to be used; if so, don't proceed until weight is verified by the first method [29cfr1926.1417(o)(3)].

At 90% or more of maximum line pull, lift a few inches and apply brakes each time; in duty-cycle or repetitive lifts all at that level, test only the first [29cfr1926.1417(s)]. Keep at least two full wraps on drums [29cfr1926.1417(t)].

No obstruction contact, side dragging or pulling, or front-area lifts on wheeled equipment unless the manufacturer permits [29cfr1926.1417(p)] [29cfr1926.1417(q)] [29cfr1926.1417(r)]. Control swing and load rotation, adjust brakes properly, and obey anyone's stop signal [29cfr1926.1417(v)] [29cfr1926.1417(w)] [29cfr1926.1417(x)] [29cfr1926.1417(y)]. Travel, slack-rope, wind/ice/snow, locomotive-crane and counterweight conditions also apply [29cfr1926.1417(u)] [29cfr1926.1417(m)] [29cfr1926.1417(n)] [29cfr1926.1417(z)] [29cfr1926.1417(aa)]. Safety devices and aids don't replace judgment [29cfr1926.1417(k)].

Check manufacturer compliance, or substitute procedures: qualified person for operational controls; familiar registered professional engineer, signing, for capacity [29cfr1926.1417(a)] [29cfr1926.1417(b)]. Check in-cab availability, electronic-failure shutdown and operator distraction [29cfr1926.1417(c)] [29cfr1926.1417(d)].

Unattended suspended loads require every condition: adjacent operator without other duties, longer-than-normal hold, competent-person safety determination and restraints, and barriers or caution lines with notices. No employees may enter the fall zone, including those listed in §§ 1926.1425(b)(1)-(3), (d) or (e) [29cfr1926.1417(e)(1)]. The working-gear exception requires negligible weight relative to capacity as positioned and suspension away from entrances and exits [29cfr1926.1417(e)(2)].

Check out-of-service tags and sign response, including authorized removal or both verifications [29cfr1926.1417(f)]; pre-start checks [29cfr1926.1417(g)]; storm-warning determinations on manufacturer securing recommendations [29cfr1926.1417(h)]; and written repair reporting plus each-shift employee notification, including alternative measures [29cfr1926.1417(j)]. Devices cannot substitute for judgment [29cfr1926.1417(k)]. Slack-rope re-spooling and weather adjustments involve the competent person [29cfr1926.1417(m)] [29cfr1926.1417(n)].

Verify rated-capacity compliance, no required violation, and at least one load-weight method. The hoisting method's threshold is exceeding 75 percent of maximum rated capacity at the longest planned radius, triggering weight verification before proceeding [29cfr1926.1417(o)]. Brake testing applies at 90% or more of maximum line pull, with the first-lift-only rule for qualifying duty-cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1417(s)]. At least two full wraps must remain [29cfr1926.1417(t)].

Check obstruction, side-pull and front-lift restrictions [29cfr1926.1417(p)] [29cfr1926.1417(q)] [29cfr1926.1417(r)]. For load travel, check manufacturer prohibition, competent-person supervision and implemented determinations, and specified tire pressure [29cfr1926.1417(u)]. Check swing speed, restraint lines, brake adjustment and stop-signal obedience [29cfr1926.1417(v)] [29cfr1926.1417(w)] [29cfr1926.1417(x)] [29cfr1926.1417(y)]. Locomotive swings toward possible railcar strikes require determining adjacent-track cars aren't moving and establishing flag protection [29cfr1926.1417(z)]. Except tower cranes, require specified counterweight or ballast without exceeding the specified maximum; tower requirements are in § 1926.1435(b)(8) [29cfr1926.1417(aa)].

This section is about what an operator must be allowed to do when safety is in question. Its heading is "Authority to stop operation." [29cfr1926.1418] The rule applies "Whenever there is a concern as to safety" [29cfr1926.1418]. When that happens, the operator must have the power to stop. The operator must also have the power to refuse to handle loads. In plain words, the operator has to be able to say no to handling a load while a safety concern is still open.

This matters because the authority is tied directly to safety. It lasts "until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured." [29cfr1926.1418] So the end point is a specific decision: a qualified person has to determine that safety has been assured. The text names a qualified person as the one who makes that determination. This short section does not define that term. It also gives no numeric limits, such as a time period or a load value.

In daily work, this section concerns your authority when safety is in doubt. The trigger is broad as written: "Whenever there is a concern as to safety" [29cfr1926.1418]. The wording speaks of a concern. It does not list particular kinds of hazards, and it states no numeric threshold that must be reached first.

When there is such a concern, you as operator must have two forms of authority: to stop, and to refuse to handle loads. The exact words are that the operator "must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads" [29cfr1926.1418].

The section also sets the point that this authority runs to: "until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured." [29cfr1926.1418] The decision point is therefore a determination by a qualified person, and what that person must determine is that safety has been assured. The section does not define "qualified person," describe how the determination is made or recorded, or set a time limit for making it. It also does not say who must be told about a stop or how a concern must be raised.

The requirement is a single sentence. Its condition is "Whenever there is a concern as to safety" [29cfr1926.1418]. Under that condition, "the operator must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads" [29cfr1926.1418]. The duration is bounded by the clause "until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured." [29cfr1926.1418]

Read against that wording, the points of compliance are these: whether the operator has the authority; whether it covers both stopping and refusing to handle loads; and whether it holds until the stated determination has been made. That determination has two elements in the text: it is made by a qualified person, and its substance is that safety has been assured.

The section states no exceptions and no numeric limits. It contains no cross-references and names no consensus standards. Within this text, "qualified person" is not defined. The section also specifies no form, documentation, notification step or deadline for the determination. It does not limit the trigger to listed hazards, and it does not say who must hold the concern.

A signal person is required when the operator cannot fully see the load's travel or the area at or near where it is placed; when the equipment is traveling and the view that way is blocked; or when the operator or load handler decides site safety concerns call for one [29cfr1926.1419(a)].

Signals may be hand, voice, audible or new signals [29cfr1926.1419(b)]. Hand signals normally follow the Standard Method, with limited exceptions [29cfr1926.1419(c)(1)]. If non-standard ones are used, the people involved must agree on them beforehand [29cfr1926.1419(c)(2)]. New signals have conditions [29cfr1926.1419(d)]. Signals and the way they are sent must suit the site [29cfr1926.1419(e)].

If signal contact is interrupted, the operator must safely stop work that needs signals until contact returns and a proper signal is given and understood [29cfr1926.1419(f)]. An operator who notices a safety problem and needs to tell the signal person must also stop safely [29cfr1926.1419(g)].

Normally only one person signals a crane or derrick at a time [29cfr1926.1419(h)]. However, anyone who notices a safety problem must give the operator or signal person a stop or emergency stop signal [29cfr1926.1419(j)]. Directions use the operator's point of view [29cfr1926.1419(k)]. With multiple cranes or derricks, each signal's intended machine must be identified [29cfr1926.1419(m)].

Provide a signal person if the point of operation is not in your full view, the view in the travel direction is obstructed, or you or the load handler find one necessary for site-specific safety concerns [29cfr1926.1419(a)]. Signals must be hand, voice, audible or new [29cfr1926.1419(b)], and they and their means of transmission must suit site conditions [29cfr1926.1419(e)]. New signals require an employer demonstration [29cfr1926.1419(d)].

Use Standard Method hand signals unless that is infeasible or it does not cover the operation or attachment use [29cfr1926.1419(c)(1)]. Before using non-standard signals, the signal person, operator and any lift director must make contact and agree on them [29cfr1926.1419(c)(2)].

Safely stop operations requiring signals if transmission is interrupted. Wait until it is restored and a proper signal is given and understood [29cfr1926.1419(f)]. If you need to communicate a safety problem to the signal person, stop safely; resume only after you both agree it is resolved [29cfr1926.1419(g)].

Only one person signals at a time, subject to the paragraph (j) exception [29cfr1926.1419(h)]: anyone aware of a safety problem must alert you or the signal person with a stop or emergency stop signal [29cfr1926.1419(j)]. The section notes that § 1926.1417(y) requires you to obey it. Signal-person directions use your direction perspective [29cfr1926.1419(k)]. Across multiple cranes or derricks, identify the intended one before each function or direction, or use an equally effective method [29cfr1926.1419(m)].

Check signal-person triggers: point of operation not in the operator's full view, obstructed view in the travel direction, or necessity determined by operator or load handler from site-specific safety concerns [29cfr1926.1419(a)]. Verify permitted signal types [29cfr1926.1419(b)] and suitability of signals and transmission means [29cfr1926.1419(e)].

Standard Method (appendix A) applies to hand signals. Non-standard signals are excepted where it is infeasible or does not cover the operation or attachment use [29cfr1926.1419(c)(1)], with prior contact and agreement among signal person, operator and any lift director [29cfr1926.1419(c)(2)]. For new signals, the employer must demonstrate that they, or a national consensus standard they comply with, provide communication "at least equally effective" as voice, audible or Standard Method hand signals [29cfr1926.1419(d)].

Confirm transmission is maintained; interruption requires a safe stop until restoration plus a proper, understood signal [29cfr1926.1419(f)]. Operator-identified safety problems needing communication require a safe stop and mutual agreement on resolution before resuming [29cfr1926.1419(g)].

Check one signaler at a time [29cfr1926.1419(h)], except under paragraph (j): anyone aware of a safety problem must give stop or emergency stop to alert operator or signal person; see § 1926.1417(y) [29cfr1926.1419(j)]. Directions must use the operator's direction perspective [29cfr1926.1419(k)]. For multiple cranes/derricks, verify pre-signal identification each time or an equally effective method [29cfr1926.1419(m)].

This section covers signals sent by radio, telephone or other electronic means [29cfr1926.1420]. The people involved in a lift may depend on these messages, so the equipment and the way signals travel both matter. First, before operations begin, the devices that send signals must be tested at the site [29cfr1926.1420(a)]. The test is to make sure that signal transmission is "effective, clear, and reliable." [29cfr1926.1420(a)]

Second, signals must travel on a "dedicated channel" [29cfr1926.1420(b)]. There are two exceptions. In one, several cranes or derricks and one or more signal persons may share a dedicated channel to coordinate operations [29cfr1926.1420(b)(1)]. Notice that the shared channel in this case is still a dedicated one. The other exception involves a crane working on or next to railroad tracks. It applies where the crane operator's actions need to be coordinated with the movement of trains or other equipment on those tracks or on neighboring ones [29cfr1926.1420(b)(2)].

Third, the operator must receive signals through a "hands-free system." [29cfr1926.1420(c)]

When signals go by radio, telephone or another electronic method, three requirements apply [29cfr1926.1420].

Testing comes first. The devices used to transmit signals must be tested on site before operations begin. The purpose is to ensure that transmission is "effective, clear, and reliable" [29cfr1926.1420(a)]. The text places this test both at the site and ahead of the start of operations.

Next is the channel. Signal transmission must use a dedicated channel unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1420(b)]. Under the first, multiple cranes or derricks and one or more signal persons "may share a dedicated channel for the purpose of coordinating operations" [29cfr1926.1420(b)(1)]. This permits sharing for that purpose, and the channel being shared is still described as dedicated.

The second exception concerns a crane operating on or adjacent to railroad tracks, where the crane operator's actions need to be coordinated with the movement of other equipment or trains on the same or adjacent tracks [29cfr1926.1420(b)(2)]. Both the location and the need for coordination are part of its wording.

Finally, the way you receive signals as operator is specified: reception "must be by a hands-free system" [29cfr1926.1420(c)].

Verify three requirements for signals transmitted by radio, telephone or other electronic means [29cfr1926.1420].

Testing: the transmitting device or devices must be tested "on site before beginning operations" [29cfr1926.1420(a)]. Check both location and timing against the stated aim of ensuring that signal transmission is "effective, clear, and reliable" [29cfr1926.1420(a)]. This section states no test method or recordkeeping requirement.

Channel: transmission must be through a dedicated channel, subject to two exceptions [29cfr1926.1420(b)]. The first allows multiple cranes/derricks and one or more signal persons to share a dedicated channel "for the purpose of coordinating operations" [29cfr1926.1420(b)(1)]. Check that purpose, and note that the wording still refers to a dedicated channel.

The second applies where a crane is operated "on or adjacent to railroad tracks" [29cfr1926.1420(b)(2)] and the crane operator's actions need to be coordinated with the movement of other equipment or trains on the same or adjacent tracks [29cfr1926.1420(b)(2)]. The two conditions are joined by "and," so check for both. Proximity to track alone does not satisfy the wording.

Reception: confirm that the operator receives signals by a "hands-free system" [29cfr1926.1420(c)]. The exceptions are set out under the dedicated-channel requirement in paragraph (b) [29cfr1926.1420(b)].

This section covers voice signals. Before operations begin, the operator, the signal person and the lift director (if there is one) must contact each other. They must agree on which voice signals they will use [29cfr1926.1421(a)].

After they agree, they do not have to meet again about voice signals unless something specific happens. That means another worker is added or substituted, there is confusion about the signals, or a signal is going to be changed [29cfr1926.1421(a)].

Every voice signal has three parts, and they must be given in order [29cfr1926.1421(b)]. The section writes them as "function (such as hoist, boom, etc.), direction; distance and/or speed; function, stop command." Read by its semicolons, the first part is the function and direction. The function is something such as hoist or boom. The second part is distance, speed, or both. The third part is the function and the stop command [29cfr1926.1421(b)].

Language also matters. The operator, signal person and any lift director must all be able to "effectively communicate in the language used" [29cfr1926.1421(c)].

Before operations begin, you, the signal person and the lift director (if there is one) must contact each other and agree on the voice signals to be used [29cfr1926.1421(a)]. Once you have agreed, another meeting about voice signals is not needed unless one of these occurs: another worker is added or substituted, there is confusion about the voice signals, or a voice signal is to be changed [29cfr1926.1421(a)].

Each voice signal must contain three elements in a set order [29cfr1926.1421(b)]. The text lists them as "function (such as hoist, boom, etc.), direction; distance and/or speed; function, stop command." Following the semicolon grouping, a signal starts with the function and its direction. It then gives the distance and/or speed. It finishes with the function and the stop command [29cfr1926.1421(b)]. Hoist and boom appear as examples of functions, and the "etc." shows that the examples are not a complete list.

The operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one) must also be able to communicate effectively in whatever language is used for this work [29cfr1926.1421(c)].

Check three requirements. First, timing, participants and agreement: "Prior to beginning operations," the operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one) must contact each other and agree on the voice signals to be used [29cfr1926.1421(a)]. After agreement, these workers need not meet again to discuss voice signals, subject to these exceptions: another worker is added or substituted, there is confusion about the voice signals, or a voice signal is to be changed [29cfr1926.1421(a)]. When reviewing whether the original agreement still suffices, check for each of these conditions.

Second, content and sequence: each voice signal must contain "the following three elements, given in the following order" [29cfr1926.1421(b)]. The text reads "function (such as hoist, boom, etc.), direction; distance and/or speed; function, stop command." The semicolons separate function and direction; distance and/or speed; and function and stop command. Verify both that all three elements are present and that their order matches. Hoist and boom are given as examples of functions [29cfr1926.1421(b)].

Third, language: the operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one) must be able to communicate effectively in the language used [29cfr1926.1421(c)]. This paragraph states the standard as effective communication and names no particular language. The text of this section cites no other provisions or consensus standards.

This section covers protection against falls on and around equipment in this subpart. Some parts apply to all of it, some exclude tower cranes, and some cover only tower cranes [29cfr1926.1423(a)].

For equipment other than tower cranes, if it was made after November 8, 2011 and has a lattice boom measuring 6 or more feet top to bottom (between cord centerlines), the boom needs walkways [29cfr1926.1423(b)(1)] at least 12 inches wide [29cfr1926.1423(b)(2)(i)]. Guardrails there are not required, are banned in some cases, and where allowed can be no higher than 45 inches [29cfr1926.1423(b)(2)(ii)].

Your employer must keep originally equipped steps, handholds, ladders and rails in good condition [29cfr1926.1423(c)(2)]. Newer equipment (made after that date) must provide safe ways to get on and off, with slip-resistant walking surfaces and devices meeting named standards unless infeasible [29cfr1926.1423(c)(3)] [29cfr1926.1423(c)(4)].

Away from tower cranes, your employer must provide fall protection and ensure you use it at unprotected edges in listed situations. For work other than assembly or disassembly, the height is more than 6 feet, with specific rules for moving between points and for work stations [29cfr1926.1423(e)]. For assembly or disassembly, it is more than 15 feet [29cfr1926.1423(f)]. Tower cranes use more than 6 feet, or more than 15 feet for erecting, climbing and dismantling [29cfr1926.1423(h)]. Some exceptions cover being in the cab, on the deck, or near running draw-works.

Body belts or harnesses must be used in fall arrest and fall restraint systems [29cfr1926.1423(d)]. Rules control what you can anchor to [29cfr1926.1423(g)]. Anchoring a fall arrest system to the hook or load line is allowed only if every listed condition is met, including having no load hanging from the line [29cfr1926.1423(j)].

If you may face fall hazards while on, or hoisted by, this equipment, your employer must train you [29cfr1926.1423(k)].

Except on tower cranes, lattice booms on equipment manufactured after November 8, 2011 need walkways where the vertical profile, cord centerline to cord centerline, is 6 or more feet [29cfr1926.1423(b)(1)]. Walkways must be at least 12 inches wide. Guardrails and permanent attachments are not required. They are prohibited if removable, or on pendant-supported booms where ropes or bars could snag them. Otherwise, guardrails or railings may be no more than 45 inches high [29cfr1926.1423(b)(2)].

The employer must maintain originally equipped access hardware [29cfr1926.1423(c)(2)]. Post-date equipment needs safe access and egress, slip-resistant surfaces, and devices meeting specified SAE or ISO standards except where infeasible [29cfr1926.1423(c)(3)] [29cfr1926.1423(c)(4)].

Outside tower cranes, the employer must provide and ensure fall protection at unprotected sides or edges. In non-assembly/disassembly work, the trigger is more than 6 feet. When moving point-to-point, it covers non-lattice booms, non-horizontal lattice booms, and horizontal lattice booms with a fall distance of 15 feet or more. It also covers work stations anywhere on the equipment, except in the cab, on the deck, or at or near running draw-works [29cfr1926.1423(e)]. Assembly/disassembly uses more than 15 feet, with those same three exceptions [29cfr1926.1423(f)].

Tower cranes use more than 6 feet, with those exceptions, except for erecting, climbing and dismantling, where the trigger is more than 15 feet [29cfr1926.1423(h)].

Fall arrest and restraint systems use fall arrest components and either body belts or harnesses [29cfr1926.1423(d)]. Arrest and positioning systems go to any apparently substantial part unless a competent person would visually conclude, without engineering analysis, that the referenced criteria would not be met. Attachable anchors must meet those criteria. Restraint anchorages must withstand twice the maximum load an employee may impose in reasonably anticipated use [29cfr1926.1423(g)].

Hook or load-line anchoring for fall arrest requires a qualified person's capacity determination, an operator on site and informed, and no suspended load [29cfr1926.1423(j)].

Training covers this subpart's fall protection requirements and applicable parts of §§ 1926.500 and 1926.502 [29cfr1926.1423(k)].

Check scope first. (b), (c)(3), (e) and (f) exclude tower cranes; (c)(1)-(2), (d), (g), (j) and (k) cover all subpart equipment; (c)(4) and (h) cover only tower cranes [29cfr1926.1423(a)]. § 1926.502(b) does not apply [29cfr1926.1423(c)(1)]; originally equipped access hardware must be in good condition [29cfr1926.1423(c)(2)].

After November 8, 2011 manufacture: lattice booms with a 6 or more feet cord-centerline profile need walkways [29cfr1926.1423(b)(1)], at least 12 inches wide. Guardrails, railings and permanent attachments are optional, but prohibited if removable-type, or snaggable on pendant-supported booms; permitted guardrails or railings cannot exceed 45 inches [29cfr1926.1423(b)(2)]. Access devices must meet SAE J185 (May 2003) or ISO 11660-2:1994(E) [29cfr1926.1423(c)(3)(i)]; tower cranes, ISO 11660-1:2008(E) and ISO 11660-3:2008(E) or SAE J185 (May 2003) [29cfr1926.1423(c)(4)(i)]; each "except where infeasible." Surfaces need slip resistance; crawler treads are excepted under (c)(3) [29cfr1926.1423(c)(3)(ii)] [29cfr1926.1423(c)(4)(ii)].

Verify provision and use at unprotected sides/edges: non-assembly/disassembly, more than 6 feet, for specified point-to-point travel (horizontal lattice booms: fall distance 15 feet or more) and work stations, the latter excepting cab, deck, and at or near running draw-works [29cfr1926.1423(e)]. Assembly/disassembly: more than 15 feet, same exceptions [29cfr1926.1423(f)]. Tower cranes: more than 6 feet with those exceptions; erecting, climbing, dismantling: more than 15 feet, with none stated [29cfr1926.1423(h)].

Components must meet § 1926.502(d), excluding (d)(15); body belts or harnesses are used [29cfr1926.1423(d)]. §§ 1926.502(d)(15) and (e)(2) apply only as (g)(2) delineates [29cfr1926.1423(g)(1)]. Check arrest/positioning anchorages under the competent-person visual test; attachable anchors must meet the applicable criteria [29cfr1926.1423(g)(2)]. Restraint anchorages need twice the maximum anticipated employee load [29cfr1926.1423(g)(3)].

Load-line arrest anchoring requires qualified-person determination that set-up and rated capacity meet § 1926.502(d)(15), an informed operator on site, and no suspended load [29cfr1926.1423(j)]. Check training of exposed employees, including those hoisted, on subpart fall protection and applicable §§ 1926.500 and 1926.502 requirements [29cfr1926.1423(k)].

Part of some equipment rotates. This part is called the rotating superstructure, and it may be mounted permanently or temporarily. The swing radius rules for keeping employees out apply where there are accessible areas in which it poses a "reasonably foreseeable risk" of striking and injuring an employee, or of pinching or crushing an employee against another object or another part of the equipment [29cfr1926.1424(a)(1)].

If you are assigned to work on or near the equipment, your employer must train you to recognize these struck-by and pinch/crush areas [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(i)]. The employer must also put up and maintain barriers, such as warning lines or railings, to mark the area boundaries. If the employer can show that barriers are not feasible either on the ground or on the equipment, warning signs combined with high visibility markings must clearly mark the areas. You must then be trained to understand what the markings mean [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(ii)].

Before you go to a spot in a hazard area where the operator cannot see you, you, or someone you instruct, must make sure the operator is told you are going there [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(i)].

Separately, when cranes or derricks can reach into each other's working radius, a system to coordinate their operations must be set up [29cfr1926.1424(b)].

Swing radius requirements in (a)(2) apply to accessible areas where the rotating superstructure, permanent or temporary, poses a reasonably foreseeable risk of striking and injuring an employee, or pinching or crushing one against the equipment or another object [29cfr1926.1424(a)(1)].

To keep employees out, the employer must train "authorized personnel", meaning each employee assigned to work on or near the equipment, to recognize these hazard areas [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(i)]. The employer must also erect and maintain control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers at the boundaries. An exception applies when the employer can demonstrate that barriers are feasible neither on the ground nor on the equipment. Warning signs plus high visibility equipment markings must then clearly mark the areas, and employees must be trained on what these markings signify [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(ii)].

An employee heading to a hazard area location out of your view must ensure, personally or through someone they instruct, that you are informed beforehand [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(i)]. When you know an employee went to a location covered by (a)(1), you must not rotate the superstructure until informed, through a pre-arranged communication system, that the employee is "in a safe position" [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(ii)].

Where any part of a crane or derrick is within another's working radius, operations must be coordinated through an instituted system [29cfr1926.1424(b)].

Check applicability: accessible areas where the rotating superstructure, "whether permanently or temporarily mounted", poses a reasonably foreseeable risk of striking and injuring, or pinching/crushing, an employee against equipment parts or objects [29cfr1926.1424(a)(1)].

Verify each employee assigned to work on or near the equipment is trained to recognize both hazard types [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(i)]. Verify boundary barriers (control lines, warning lines, railings or similar) are erected and maintained. For the exception, the employer must demonstrate that barriers are "neither feasible to erect" on the ground "nor on the equipment". Then check for the combination of warning signs and high visibility equipment markings clearly identifying the areas, plus training on their meaning [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(ii)].

For hazard area locations out of the operator's view, confirm the employee, or someone the employee instructed, ensures the operator is informed beforehand [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(i)]. Where the operator knows an employee went to an (a)(1) location, confirm no rotation occurs until a safe-position notice arrives under a pre-arranged communication system [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(ii)].

Where any part of a crane/derrick is within another's working radius, verify the controlling entity instituted a coordination system. Without a controlling entity, this falls to the sole employer operating the multiple pieces of equipment, "or employers" [29cfr1926.1424(b)].

This section is about "Keeping clear of the load." Where routes are available that reduce how much workers are exposed to hoisted loads, they must be used, as far as this is consistent with public safety [29cfr1926.1425(a)].

While the operator is not moving a hanging load, you must stay out of the fall zone unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1425(b)]. The exceptions cover workers hooking, unhooking or guiding a load [29cfr1926.1425(b)(1)], first attaching it to a component or structure [29cfr1926.1425(b)(2)], or operating a concrete hopper or bucket [29cfr1926.1425(b)(3)].

If you are in the fall zone to hook, unhook, guide or make that first connection, all of these conditions apply [29cfr1926.1425(c)]. Materials must be rigged so they cannot shift unintentionally [29cfr1926.1425(c)(1)], and a qualified rigger must rig them [29cfr1926.1425(c)(3)]. Hooks need self-closing latches or something equivalent, although "J" hooks may be used to set wooden trusses [29cfr1926.1425(c)(2)].

When a load is landing, only workers needed to receive it may be in the fall zone [29cfr1926.1425(d)]. During tilt-up or tilt-down work, nobody may be directly under the load [29cfr1926.1425(e)(1)], and only essential workers may be in the fall zone [29cfr1926.1425(e)(2)].

Hoisting routes that minimize employee exposure to hoisted loads must be used where available, "to the extent consistent with public safety" [29cfr1926.1425(a)]. While you are not moving a suspended load, employees must be out of the fall zone unless they are hooking, unhooking or guiding it, making its initial attachment to a component or structure, or operating a concrete hopper or bucket [29cfr1926.1425(b)].

For those hooking, unhooking, guiding or initially connecting within the fall zone, all criteria apply [29cfr1926.1425(c)]: rigging that prevents unintentional displacement [29cfr1926.1425(c)(1)]; hooks with self-closing latches or their equivalent, except that "J" hooks are permitted for setting wooden trusses [29cfr1926.1425(c)(2)]; and rigging by a qualified rigger [29cfr1926.1425(c)(3)].

During landing, only employees needed to receive the load may be in the fall zone [29cfr1926.1425(d)]. In tilt-up or tilt-down operations, no one may be directly under the load [29cfr1926.1425(e)(1)]. Only essential employees may be in the fall zone, and not directly under the load. Essential means physically guiding it, closely monitoring and instructing on its movement, or detaching or initially attaching it, where the employer can demonstrate that doing the task from outside the zone is infeasible [29cfr1926.1425(e)(2)].

Boom free fall is prohibited with an employee in the boom's or load's fall zone. Load line free fall is prohibited with an employee directly under the load. The note refers to § 1926.1426 [29cfr1926.1425-note-1].

Check route use: where available, exposure-minimizing hoisting routes are required "to the extent consistent with public safety" [29cfr1926.1425(a)]. While the operator is not moving a suspended load, fall-zone presence is limited to the exceptions [29cfr1926.1425(b)]: hooking, unhooking or guiding [29cfr1926.1425(b)(1)]; initial attachment to a component or structure [29cfr1926.1425(b)(2)]; or operating a concrete hopper or bucket [29cfr1926.1425(b)(3)].

For employees in the fall zone while hooking, unhooking, guiding or initially connecting, verify all criteria [29cfr1926.1425(c)]: rigging against unintentional displacement [29cfr1926.1425(c)(1)]; self-closing latches or equivalent, with "J" hooks permitted for setting wooden trusses [29cfr1926.1425(c)(2)]; and a qualified rigger [29cfr1926.1425(c)(3)].

At landing, confirm each employee in the fall zone is needed to receive the load [29cfr1926.1425(d)]. For tilt-up or tilt-down, no employee may be directly under the load [29cfr1926.1425(e)(1)]. Anyone in the fall zone must be essential: conducting physical guiding, close monitoring with movement instructions, or detachment or initial attachment (for example, initial connection or bracing installation). The employer must also be able to demonstrate that performing that operation from outside the zone is infeasible [29cfr1926.1425(e)(2)].

Cross-reference § 1926.1426: boom free fall is prohibited with an employee in the boom or load fall zone; load line free fall, with an employee directly under the load [29cfr1926.1425-note-1].

This section covers when a boom or load may drop freely. A boom designed to free fall is called a "live boom". You may not use that equipment if an employee is in the fall zone of the boom or load, or is being hoisted [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)]. It is also banned for certain exposures involving power lines, including nearby clearance areas [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(iii)]. Other bans cover a load over a shaft, unless no employees are in it [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(iv)], or over a cofferdam, unless no employees are in the fall zone [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(v)]. It is banned during lifting in a refinery or tank farm [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(vi)].

Even with none of these present, live boom equipment is allowed only if it was made before October 31, 1984, or is a floating crane/derrick or a land crane/derrick on a vessel or flotation device [29cfr1926.1426(a)(2)]. Where it is banned, the boom hoist needs a backup to stop the boom falling if the primary system fails [29cfr1926.1426(b)]. Hydraulic telescoping booms need a built-in holding device against retraction if hydraulics fail [29cfr1926.1426(c)].

For the load line, you must lower in a controlled way, without free fall, if someone is directly under the load or being hoisted, in listed power line situations, or if the load is over a shaft. This also applies over a cofferdam unless no employees are in the load's fall zone [29cfr1926.1426(d)].

Live boom use is prohibited with an employee in the boom or load fall zone or being hoisted, and during refinery or tank farm lifting [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)]. It is also prohibited with the load or boom directly over a power line or its Table A (§ 1926.1408) clearance area on each side, or with any part of that area within the boom's or load's radius of vertical travel [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(iii)]. Shaft and cofferdam bans have exceptions: no employees in the shaft, or none in the boom or load fall zone at the cofferdam [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(iv)] [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(v)]. Otherwise, use also requires manufacture before October 31, 1984, or a floating or vessel/flotation-mounted crane or derrick [29cfr1926.1426(a)(2)].

Where prohibited, the boom hoist needs secondary fall protection [29cfr1926.1426(b)]. Friction drums need a friction clutch plus braking device, and a secondary braking or locking device [29cfr1926.1426(b)(1)]. Hydraulic drums need an integral holding device or internal static brake [29cfr1926.1426(b)(2)]; hydraulic boom cylinders need an integral holding device [29cfr1926.1426(b)(4)]. Clutches and hydraulic motors do not count as brakes or locks [29cfr1926.1426(b)(3)]. Telescoping hydraulic booms need an integral anti-retraction holding device [29cfr1926.1426(c)].

Controlled load lowering is required with an employee directly under the load or being hoisted, in listed power line exposures, over a shaft, or over a cofferdam unless its load fall zone has no employees [29cfr1926.1426(d)].

For live booms, check each (a)(1) trigger: employee in boom or load fall zone; employee hoisted; power line exposure; shaft, excepting no employees in it; cofferdam, excepting none in boom or load fall zone; refinery or tank farm lifting [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)]. Power line exposure includes load or boom over the line or its Table A (§ 1926.1408) clearance area on each side, or any part of that area within boom or load vertical-travel radius [29cfr1926.1426(a)(1)(iii)]. Permission requires no trigger, plus manufacture "prior to October 31, 1984" or a floating, or vessel/flotation-mounted land, crane/derrick [29cfr1926.1426(a)(2)].

Where prohibited, verify a secondary mechanism or device against primary-system failure [29cfr1926.1426(b)]. Friction drums: clutch and braking device for controlled lowering [29cfr1926.1426(b)(1)(i)], plus manually or automatically engaged secondary braking or locking backup while held [29cfr1926.1426(b)(1)(ii)]. Hydraulic drums: integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake [29cfr1926.1426(b)(2)]. Clutches and hydraulic motors do not qualify as brakes or locks [29cfr1926.1426(b)(3)]. Boom cylinders: integrally mounted holding device [29cfr1926.1426(b)(4)]. Check hydraulic telescoping booms for integral retraction protection [29cfr1926.1426(c)].

Load line free fall is prohibited for employees directly under the load or hoisted [29cfr1926.1426(d)]; the corresponding load-only power line conditions [29cfr1926.1426(d)(3)]; any load over a shaft [29cfr1926.1426(d)(4)]; and cofferdams unless the load fall zone has no employees [29cfr1926.1426(d)(5)]. Unlike (a)(1)(iv), (d)(4) states no empty-shaft exception.

Before running covered equipment, you must be trained, certified or licensed, and evaluated [29cfr1926.1427(a)]. Until certified or licensed and evaluated, you may operate only as a supervised operator-in-training [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sideboom cranes, and equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less are excluded, though their own training rules still apply [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Qualified U.S. military employees have a separate route [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Your employer must give formal and practical instruction so you can work safely and "recognize and avert risk" [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Your trainer must be qualified to direct you, work for your employer or as its agent, and avoid distracting tasks [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Except on tower cranes, you need direct sight of each other and voice or hand-signal communication. Tower cranes require direct communication [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)(iii)].
