Trainer breaks last at most 15 minutes, once per hour at most. Beforehand, the trainer must tell you your tasks and limits, and tasks must be within your abilities [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)(iv)].

Until certified, you cannot operate where equipment, load line or load, at maximum working radius, could come within 20 feet of lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet of higher-voltage lines. Personnel hoisting, multiple-equipment lifts, and work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms are also barred. So are multiple-lift rigging operations, unless your trainer finds your skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Certification or licensing costs you nothing when required [29cfr1926.1427(c)(3)]. It involves written and practical tests [29cfr1926.1427(j)]. Qualifying government licenses last up to 5 years [29cfr1926.1427(c)(1)(v)]. Accredited-organization and employer-program certifications last 5 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)(4)] [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Accreditation is reviewed at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)(1)(v)]. Employer programs are audited within 3 months of starting, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. A significant deficiency brings a repeat audit within 180 days after confirmed correction, an OSHA report within 15 days of the finding, and 3-year audit record retention [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

A certificate alone cannot qualify you under the employer's evaluation; you must demonstrate your abilities [29cfr1926.1427(f)]. Earlier assessments may count if you were employed before December 10, 2018 [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section took effect then, except evaluation and documentation, effective February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)].

Covered equipment requires training, certification or licensing, and evaluation; otherwise, you operate only as a supervised trainee [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sidebooms and equipment rated 2,000 pounds or less are excepted, but their training rules remain [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualifications are employer-specific and last as the issuer stipulates [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Trainees need formal and practical instruction, assigned tasks within their ability, and continuous on-site monitoring by a qualified employer employee or agent doing nothing distracting [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Non-tower cranes require line of sight plus verbal or hand signals; tower cranes require direct communication. Breaks are limited to 15 minutes, one per hour, after a task-and-limits briefing, with tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Uncertified trainees cannot work where equipment, line or load at maximum radius could reach within 20 feet of power lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet above that voltage. They also cannot hoist personnel, make multiple-equipment lifts, or work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging is barred unless the trainer finds their skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Qualifying state or local licensing governs within its jurisdiction (maximum validity 5 years); otherwise certification is required, with no employee cost [29cfr1926.1427(c)]. Accredited certification is type-based or type-and-capacity-based, portable among employers required to use that option, and valid 5 years; accreditation review occurs at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)]. Audited-employer certification lasts 5 years and is not portable [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Audits occur within 3 months of program start, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. Significant deficiencies halt qualification until confirmed correction, require re-audit within 180 days afterward and an auditor's OSHA report within 15 days of determination; auditors keep audit records 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

Evaluation covers safe operation, equipment-specific features and assigned hoisting [29cfr1926.1427(f)(1)]. Other equipment is allowed if the employer can demonstrate no substantially different abilities are needed [29cfr1926.1427(f)(5)]. Performance or knowledge evaluation indicating a need triggers retraining and subject re-evaluation [29cfr1926.1427(b)(5)] [29cfr1926.1427(f)(7)]. Pre-December 10, 2018 employees may be covered by prior assessments [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section's effective date is December 10, 2018; evaluation and documentation, February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)].

Verify training, certification/licensing and evaluation; uncertified or unevaluated employees operate only as supervised trainees [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Exceptions: derricks, sidebooms, capacity 2,000 pounds or less, with other training rules continuing [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualification covers federal employees, not contractors' employees; it is nonportable, with issuer-set validity [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Check instruction, ability-limited assignments, retraining, trainer eligibility, undistracted monitoring and communication [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Breaks: maximum 15 minutes, one hourly, prior task/limit briefing, tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)(iv)]. Without certification, trainees are barred if maximum-radius operation could bring equipment, load line or load within 20 feet of lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet over 350 kV; from personnel or multiple-equipment lifts; and over shafts/cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging has a trainer-determined skill exception [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Check licensing criteria and 5-year maximum [29cfr1926.1427(c)(1)], free required credentials [29cfr1926.1427(c)(3)], and combined testing/training criteria [29cfr1926.1427(c)(4)]. Accredited option: tests, retesting, recertification, type basis, limited portability, 5-year validity, accreditation review at least every 3 years; similar-type certification applies when no accredited exam exists, with certified type stated [29cfr1926.1427(d)].

Audited option: check test development/approval, administration, auditor qualifications and independence, requalification, and audit within 3 months, then at least every 3 years. Significant deficiencies require suspended qualification pending confirmed correction, re-audit within 180 days afterward, auditor reporting to OSHA's Regional Office within 15 days of determination, and auditor retention/availability of audit records for 3 years. Certification: nonportable, 5 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)].

Check evaluator competence, evaluation content and worksite documentation: names, evaluator signature, date, equipment make/model/configuration. Prior assessments for pre-December 10, 2018 employees have specific documentation [29cfr1926.1427(f)]. Check language/literacy conditions [29cfr1926.1427(h)] and written/practical criteria [29cfr1926.1427(j)], including shift-inspection items (§ 1926.1412(d)) [29cfr1926.1427(j)(2)(i)]. Effective December 10, 2018; evaluation/documentation February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)].

This section is about who may give signals as a signal person. The employer of the signal person must make sure you meet the Qualification Requirements "prior to giving any signals" [29cfr1926.1428(a)]. There are two ways to show this. In the first, you have documentation from a third party qualified evaluator [29cfr1926.1428(a)(1)]. In the second, your employer's qualified evaluator assesses you, decides you meet the requirements and documents that decision. Other employers are not permitted to use this second kind of assessment [29cfr1926.1428(a)(2)].

You must know and understand the type of signals used. For hand signals, this includes the Standard Method [29cfr1926.1428(c)(1)]. You must be competent in using those signals [29cfr1926.1428(c)(2)]. You also need a basic understanding of how the equipment works and its limits. This includes how cranes behave when swinging and stopping loads, and how the boom bends from hoisting loads [29cfr1926.1428(c)(3)]. You must know the relevant requirements of §§ 1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and 1926.1428 [29cfr1926.1428(c)(4)]. You show all of this through an oral or written test, and also a practical test [29cfr1926.1428(c)(5)].

If your later actions indicate you do not meet the requirements, your employer must stop you from continuing as a signal person until you are retrained and a new assessment confirms you qualify [29cfr1926.1428(b)].

The signal person's employer must ensure each signal person meets the Qualification Requirements before giving any signals, using Option (1) or Option (2) [29cfr1926.1428(a)]. Option (1) relies on documentation from a third party qualified evaluator showing the person meets them [29cfr1926.1428(a)(1)]. Under Option (2), the employer's qualified evaluator assesses the person, determines that the requirements are met and documents that determination. This assessment "is not portable": other employers may not use it to meet this section [29cfr1926.1428(a)(2)].

Under either option, the documentation must be available at the site while the employer employs the signal person. It must specify each type of signaling, such as hand or radio signals, for which the person qualifies [29cfr1926.1428(a)(3)].

Qualification covers knowing the signals used, including the Standard Method if hand signals are used [29cfr1926.1428(c)(1)]; competence in applying them [29cfr1926.1428(c)(2)]; a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including swing and stopping dynamics and boom deflection [29cfr1926.1428(c)(3)]; and the relevant requirements of §§ 1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and 1926.1428 [29cfr1926.1428(c)(4)]. These are demonstrated through an oral or written test and a practical test [29cfr1926.1428(c)(5)].

If later actions indicate a signal person does not qualify, the employer must not allow continued signaling work until retraining and a confirming re-assessment under paragraph (a) [29cfr1926.1428(b)].

Verify that the signal person's employer ensured qualification under paragraph (c) "prior to giving any signals", using Option (1) or Option (2) [29cfr1926.1428(a)]. For Option (1), check for documentation from a third party qualified evaluator, a term defined in § 1926.1401, showing the requirements are met [29cfr1926.1428(a)(1)]. For Option (2), check that the employer's qualified evaluator (not a third party; see § 1926.1401) assessed the individual, determined qualification and documented it. Another employer may not use that assessment to meet this section [29cfr1926.1428(a)(2)].

Confirm the documentation is available at the site during employment and specifies "each type of signaling" for which the person qualifies [29cfr1926.1428(a)(3)].

The qualification elements are knowledge and understanding of the signals used, including the Standard Method where hand signals are used [29cfr1926.1428(c)(1)]; competence in applying them [29cfr1926.1428(c)(2)]; basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including swinging and stopping dynamics and boom deflection [29cfr1926.1428(c)(3)]; and the relevant requirements of §§ 1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and 1926.1428 [29cfr1926.1428(c)(4)]. Demonstration of (c)(1) through (4) requires "an oral or written test, and through a practical test" [29cfr1926.1428(c)(5)].

Where subsequent actions indicate nonqualification, check that the individual was not allowed to continue as signal person until both re-training and a re-assessment under paragraph (a), confirming qualification, occurred [29cfr1926.1428(b)].

This section is about when people doing maintenance, inspection or repair work may operate the equipment. They may do so only if all the requirements in paragraph (a) are met [29cfr1926.1429(a)].

First, what you do with the equipment is limited. The operation covers only the functions needed to "perform maintenance, inspect the equipment, or verify its performance" [29cfr1926.1429(a)(1)].

Second, you must meet one of two conditions [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)]. One choice is to operate under the "direct supervision" of an operator. That operator must meet the requirements of § 1926.1427, which is titled Operator qualification and certification [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)(i)]. The other choice is to be familiar with how that type of equipment operates, along with its limitations, characteristics and hazards [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)(ii)].

There is also a rule about qualifications. Maintenance and repair personnel must meet the definition of a "qualified person" for both the equipment and the maintenance or repair tasks they perform [29cfr1926.1429(b)]. The text of this section does not spell out that definition.

Why it matters: these conditions set the limits on when this work allows you to operate the equipment.

Maintenance, inspection and repair personnel are permitted to operate the equipment only where all the requirements of paragraph (a) are met [29cfr1926.1429(a)].

The scope limit is that operation is restricted to the functions necessary to perform maintenance, inspect the equipment, or verify its performance [29cfr1926.1429(a)(1)].

The personnel must also satisfy one of two alternatives [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)]. Under the first, they operate under the direct supervision of an operator who meets the requirements of § 1926.1427 (Operator qualification and certification) [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)(i)]. Under the second, they are "familiar with the operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards" associated with the type of equipment [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)(ii)]. Because the two are joined by "either" and "or", the text offers them as alternatives [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)] [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)(i)].

Separately, maintenance and repair personnel must meet the definition of a qualified person "with respect to the equipment and maintenance/repair tasks performed" [29cfr1926.1429(b)]. In practice, that qualification is tied to both the particular equipment and the work being done. This section does not state the definition itself.

Check that every requirement in paragraph (a) is met where maintenance, inspection or repair personnel operate the equipment. Their permission applies "only where all of the following requirements are met" [29cfr1926.1429(a)].

Verify the functional limit: operation is confined to functions necessary to perform maintenance, inspect the equipment, or verify its performance [29cfr1926.1429(a)(1)].

Then verify at least one alternative under [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)]. One is operation under "the direct supervision of an operator" who meets the requirements of § 1926.1427 (Operator qualification and certification) [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)(i)]. The other is that the personnel are familiar with the operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards associated with the type of equipment [29cfr1926.1429(a)(2)(ii)]. The wording of the second alternative refers to the equipment type.

Also check that maintenance and repair personnel meet the definition of a qualified person with respect to both the equipment and the maintenance/repair tasks performed [29cfr1926.1429(b)]. Note the difference in wording: paragraph (a) names "Maintenance, inspection and repair personnel" [29cfr1926.1429(a)], while paragraph (b) names "Maintenance and repair personnel" [29cfr1926.1429(b)].

The cross-reference named for the supervising operator is § 1926.1427. This section does not state the qualified person definition, the content of § 1926.1427, or what direct supervision consists of.

This section says what training your employer must give. Some of it depends on your job. Certain employees, identified in two other sections, must be trained in the powerline topics listed in § 1926.1408(g) [29cfr1926.1430(a)]. If you will be a signal person and don't meet the requirements of § 1926.1428(c), you get training in the areas it addresses [29cfr1926.1430(b)]. Operators are trained on safe operation of the equipment they will use [29cfr1926.1430(c)]. They also learn certain practices. One is a boom brake check when moving a boom off a support [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(i)]. Another is the manufacturer's emergency steps for stopping unintended movement, "Where available" [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(ii)]. Competent and qualified persons learn the rules that apply to their roles [29cfr1926.1430(d)].

If you work with the equipment, you must be trained to "keep clear of holes, and crush/pinch points" and the hazards in § 1926.1424 [29cfr1926.1430(e)]. Operators, and others allowed to start or energize equipment or work its controls, learn tag-out and start-up procedures [29cfr1926.1430(f)].

Your employer must check that you understand required training [29cfr1926.1430(g)(1)]. You get refresher training on relevant topics when your conduct or a knowledge evaluation indicates it is needed [29cfr1926.1430(g)(2)]. Training required under subpart CC comes "at no cost to the employee" [29cfr1926.1430(g)(3)].

Your employer must train you on safe operation of the equipment you will use, in accordance with § 1926.1427(a) and (b) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(1)]. Operators covered under the exception in § 1926.1427(a)(2) must also be trained on safe operation of their equipment [29cfr1926.1430(c)(2)].

Operators of equipment covered by this subpart are trained in specific practices [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)]. On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, you "first raise the boom a short distance", enough to take the boom's load, to determine whether the boom hoist brake needs adjustment. The practice also applies to other equipment with a boom. There, typically the brake can't be adjusted, so if it doesn't hold, "a repair is necessary". See also § 1926.1417(f) and (j) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(i)]. Where available, training covers the manufacturer's emergency procedures for halting unintended equipment movement [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(ii)].

You also receive training in the tag-out and start-up procedures in § 1926.1417(f) and (g), as do other employees authorized to start or energize equipment or operate controls [29cfr1926.1430(f)]. Employees working with the equipment are trained on holes, crush/pinch points and § 1926.1424 hazards [29cfr1926.1430(e)].

Employers must evaluate required trainees to confirm understanding [29cfr1926.1430(g)(1)], give refresher training when conduct or a knowledge evaluation indicates retraining is necessary [29cfr1926.1430(g)(2)], and provide subpart CC training free to employees [29cfr1926.1430(g)(3)]. Other paragraphs address powerlines, signal persons, and competent and qualified persons [29cfr1926.1430(a)] [29cfr1926.1430(b)] [29cfr1926.1430(d)].

Verify employer training by role. Powerlines: employees specified in §§ 1926.1408(g) and 1926.1410(m), on the § 1926.1408(g) topics [29cfr1926.1430(a)]. Signal persons: each employee to be assigned who does not meet § 1926.1428(c), in its areas [29cfr1926.1430(b)]. Operators: safe operation of the equipment to be used, per § 1926.1427(a) and (b) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(1)], including those under the § 1926.1427(a)(2) exception [29cfr1926.1430(c)(2)].

For operators of covered equipment, check the boom-off-support practice: on friction equipment, a short raise sufficient to take the boom's load, testing whether the boom hoist brake needs adjustment. It applies to other boom equipment, where typically adjustment isn't possible and a brake that doesn't hold needs repair; see § 1926.1417(f) and (j) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(i)]. Also check manufacturer emergency procedures for unintended movement, where available [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(ii)].

Check competent and qualified persons' role-specific training [29cfr1926.1430(d)]; hole, crush/pinch point and § 1926.1424 hazard training for employees working with equipment [29cfr1926.1430(e)]; and § 1926.1417(f) and (g) tag-out and start-up training for operators and others authorized to start/energize equipment or operate controls, such as maintenance and repair employees [29cfr1926.1430(f)].

Confirm evaluation of understanding [29cfr1926.1430(g)(1)], refresher training in relevant topics when conduct or knowledge evaluation indicates need [29cfr1926.1430(g)(2)], and no employee cost for subpart CC training [29cfr1926.1430(g)(3)].

Using equipment such as a crane to lift people is generally prohibited. The employer must show that usual ways of reaching the work, such as ladders or scaffolds, would be more hazardous or are impossible because of structural design or worksite conditions. Steel erection and routine underground shaft access are excluded from this ban [29cfr1926.1431(a)]. You normally ride in a personnel platform [29cfr1926.1431(b)(1)]. Exceptions cover drill shafts up to 8 feet across, pile driving, marine transfer, and storage-tank, shaft and chimney work, each with its own rules [29cfr1926.1431(b)(2)].

Equipment must be within one percent of level on footing a qualified person approves, with any outriggers or stabilizers equally extended and locked [29cfr1926.1431(c)]. Loads stay at or below 50 percent of rated capacity, except in proof tests [29cfr1926.1431(d)]. Required safety devices must work, or operations stop [29cfr1926.1431(d)(5)(vii)].

Platforms stay within 10 degrees of level [29cfr1926.1431(e)(2)] and support their own weight plus five times the maximum intended load [29cfr1926.1431(e)(4)]. Mesh sides have openings of 1/2 inch (1.27 cm) at most [29cfr1926.1431(e)(6)]; see-through overhead mesh may have up to 1/2 inch openings [29cfr1926.1431(e)(10)]. Rigging hardware and hooks need five times strength; slings used with rotation resistant rope need ten [29cfr1926.1431(g)(3)].

Trial lifts and checks come before people ride [29cfr1926.1431(h)]. Proof tests use 125 percent of rated capacity [29cfr1926.1431(j)(1)], held at least five minutes [29cfr1926.1431(j)(2)]. Attend the pre-lift meeting [29cfr1926.1431(m)].

Keep your body inside while moving, subject to positioning and signaling exceptions, and don't climb on rails [29cfr1926.1431(k)(2)]. Use fall arrest, though water work has different rules [29cfr1926.1431(k)(10)]. Above 20 mph wind, a qualified person judges safety [29cfr1926.1431(k)(8)(i)]. A platform-mounted factory winch has a 500 pounds limit and must also respect winch and platform ratings [29cfr1926.1431(k)(11)(ii)]. Power-line exclusion distances are 20 feet up to 350 kV and 50 feet above it, except subpart V work [29cfr1926.1431(n)]. A boatswain's chair, where allowed, carries one person: drill shafts [29cfr1926.1431(o)(3)(vii)], piles [29cfr1926.1431(p)(4)(vi)], tanks and chimneys [29cfr1926.1431(s)(3)(vi)].

Personnel hoisting requires the employer's demonstration that conventional access is more hazardous or not possible; subpart R work and routine underground shaft access fall outside that paragraph [29cfr1926.1431(a)]. Platforms are required except in specified drill-shaft (up to 8 feet diameter), pile, marine-transfer and tank/shaft/chimney cases [29cfr1926.1431(b)].

Set up within one percent of level on footing a qualified person approves; extend any outriggers or stabilizers equally and lock them, following manufacturer procedures and charts [29cfr1926.1431(c)]. The 50 percent capacity limit applies except during proof testing [29cfr1926.1431(d)]. Engage brakes and locking features while the occupied platform is stationary [29cfr1926.1431(d)(4)]. If a required device fails, safely stop until it works; "Alternative measures are not permitted." [29cfr1926.1431(d)(5)(vii)] Controlled lowering is required [29cfr1926.1431(d)(5)(vi)]; free fall is prohibited [29cfr1926.1431-note-1].

Platform limits include 10 degrees from level [29cfr1926.1431(e)(2)], five-times strength [29cfr1926.1431(e)(4)], 1/2 inch (1.27 cm) side-mesh openings [29cfr1926.1431(e)(6)] and, for see-through overhead protection, an example of up to 1/2 inch openings [29cfr1926.1431(e)(10)]. Observe rated and occupancy limits [29cfr1926.1431(f)]. Rigging hardware and hooks need five times; slings with rotation resistant rope need ten [29cfr1926.1431(g)(3)].

Complete trial lifts and competent-person checks, including raising the loaded platform a few inches before each lift [29cfr1926.1431(h)]. Proof test to 125 percent [29cfr1926.1431(j)(1)], suspended at least five minutes, and pass before hoisting people [29cfr1926.1431(j)(2)-(4)]. Hold the pre-lift meeting [29cfr1926.1431(m)].

Move slowly; remain at the controls for platforms without controls [29cfr1926.1431(k)]. Above 20 mph sustained or gusts, a qualified person decides whether lifting is unsafe [29cfr1926.1431(k)(8)(i)]. Other load lines are barred except in pile driving [29cfr1926.1431(k)(11)(i)]; original factory winches on boom-mounted platforms are limited to 500 pounds and winch/platform ratings [29cfr1926.1431(k)(11)(ii)]. Traveling is restricted; derricks cannot travel [29cfr1926.1431(k)(12)-(13)]. Except for subpart V work, stay beyond 20 feet of lines up to 350 kV and 50 feet over 350 kV [29cfr1926.1431(n)]. Special methods have separate conditions [29cfr1926.1431(o)] [29cfr1926.1431(p)] [29cfr1926.1431(r)] [29cfr1926.1431(s)], including one rider per boatswain's chair.

Verify the access demonstration and paragraph (a) exclusions [29cfr1926.1431(a)], and platform exceptions, including drill shafts up to 8 feet [29cfr1926.1431(b)]. Check footing, level within one percent, outriggers/stabilizers [29cfr1926.1431(c)], 50 percent capacity except proof testing, brakes, devices and controlled lowering [29cfr1926.1431(d)]. Anti two-block excepts pile driving [29cfr1926.1431(d)(5)(v)]. Luffing-jib platform attachment is barred [29cfr1926.1431(d)(6)].

Check design, welding, guarding, gates and markings [29cfr1926.1431(e)]: 10 degrees; five-times platform strength, excluding guardrails and anchorages; 1/2 inch (1.27 cm) side openings; overhead mesh example, up to 1/2 inch. Check loading [29cfr1926.1431(f)] and rigging [29cfr1926.1431(g)], including five times for hardware/hooks and ten for slings with rotation resistant rope [29cfr1926.1431(g)(3)].

Verify trial timing, repeats, inspections, corrections and the few inches test hoist [29cfr1926.1431(h)]; 125 percent proof testing, five-minute minimum suspension and competent-person pass [29cfr1926.1431(j)]. Check work practices [29cfr1926.1431(k)]: 20 mph wind evaluation; fall arrest and water provisions (§§ 1926.502, 1926.106); factory-winch 500 pounds and ratings; travel conditions. Confirm meeting [29cfr1926.1431(m)] and, except subpart V, prohibition within 20 feet up to 350 kV or 50 feet over 350 kV [29cfr1926.1431(n)].

For platforms, apply (a)-(n) in drill-shaft [29cfr1926.1431(o)(2)], marine [29cfr1926.1431(r)(2)] and tank/shaft/chimney work [29cfr1926.1431(s)(2)]; pile driving specifies (b)-(n) [29cfr1926.1431(p)(3)]. Pile cable marking applies to lattice booms with the spotter as an alternative; telescopic booms require both [29cfr1926.1431(p)(2)].

For chairs, use each incorporated-paragraph list; pile driving includes (j), unlike drill-shaft and tank lists [29cfr1926.1431(o)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1431(p)(4)(i)] [29cfr1926.1431(s)(3)(i)]. Check controlled travel, harness attachment, § 1926.502 compliance, five-times chair strength and one rider [29cfr1926.1431(o)(3)] [29cfr1926.1431(p)(4)] [29cfr1926.1431(s)(3)]. Tank/shaft/chimney chairs require demonstrated platform infeasibility [29cfr1926.1431(s)(1)]. Drill shafts require an opening signal person [29cfr1926.1431(o)(3)(ii)]. Marine devices have their own incorporated list, transfer-only use, design occupancy and required U.S. Coast Guard flotation devices [29cfr1926.1431(r)(3)].

This section covers lifts where "more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load." Such an operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)]. So planning comes first, and the work comes after.

Not just anyone can write the plan. A qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. The plan must be designed to make sure the requirements of this subpart, the larger group of rules this section belongs to, are met [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. The qualified person may decide that the planning needs engineering expertise. If so, the employer must make sure it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

Someone must also direct the lift. This role is called the lift director. It can be filled in either of two ways. One is a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The other is a competent person who has help from one or more qualified persons [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)].

The lift director must go over the plan in a meeting with "all workers who will be involved with the operation" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. If you will be involved in the operation, this review includes you.

These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)].

Applicability turns on whether more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. For such an operation, planning is required "Before beginning" it [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

Plan development checks follow three conditions. First, whether a qualified person developed the plan [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. Second, whether the plan is designed to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]; the reference is to the subpart as a whole, and this section's text does not itemize those requirements. Third, the conditional engineering duty: "Where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided." [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)]. As written, the trigger is the qualified person's determination, and the duty to ensure provision falls on the employer.

For implementation, verify who directed the lift. The lift director must be either a person meeting the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)].

Also verify that the lift director reviewed the plan "in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. The elements to compare are who conducted the review, that it occurred in a meeting, and that all involved workers were included.

This section covers how certain equipment must be designed, built and tested. Its opening line applies it to equipment the manufacturer rates to lift "more than 2,000 pounds" [29cfr1926.1433].

The manufacture date matters. Crawler, truck and locomotive cranes made before November 8, 2010 have a choice of named design, construction and testing requirements [29cfr1926.1433(a)]. Mobile and locomotive cranes made on or after that date must meet listed parts of ASME B30.5-2004, as applicable [29cfr1926.1433(b)]. Those newer cranes, and newer tower cranes, also have rules for testing a prototype [29cfr1926.1433(c)].

All equipment covered by this subpart has further requirements [29cfr1926.1433(d)]. Information in the cab must include, among other things, the full range of rated capacities, charts, rope details, warnings and operating instructions [29cfr1926.1433(d)(1)]. Areas where no load is to be handled must be clearly shown [29cfr1926.1433(d)(1)(iii)].

Hooks, ball assemblies and load blocks must be heavy enough to "overhaul the line" under stated conditions [29cfr1926.1433(d)(2)]. Hook and ball assemblies and load blocks must show rated capacity and weight [29cfr1926.1433(d)(3)]. Hooks need latches unless the exception is met [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(i)]. It lists a qualified person's safety decision [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(ii)(A)] and advance route planning that limits who must work in the fall zone [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(ii)(B)].

Required warnings must stay readable [29cfr1926.1433(d)(5)], and an accessible fire extinguisher must be on board [29cfr1926.1433(d)(6)]. Cabs have rules for air, visibility, doors, windows and exit paths [29cfr1926.1433(d)(7)]. Roof areas used as workstations must support 250 pounds without permanent distortion [29cfr1926.1433(d)(7)(v)]. The section also covers guarding, hot parts, fluid and air lines, exhaust, brakes, clutches and hydraulic hoists [29cfr1926.1433(d)].

The opening line applies these requirements to equipment with a manufacturer-rated capacity of more than 2,000 pounds [29cfr1926.1433]. Design standards depend on manufacture date: before November 8, 2010, crawler, truck and locomotive cranes follow paragraph (a)'s options [29cfr1926.1433(a)]. On or after it, mobile and locomotive cranes meet listed ASME B30.5-2004 portions as applicable [29cfr1926.1433(b)]. Prototype testing rules also apply by crane type and date [29cfr1926.1433(c)].

Cab information on rated capacity must cover, at minimum, full capacity ratings, work area and no-load areas, reeving and wire rope, applicable tire pressure and gantry or boom suspension details, warnings including the least stable direction, boom erection and telescoping instructions, hoist holding control and free fall, and hydraulic relief valve settings [29cfr1926.1433(d)(1)].

Hooks, ball assemblies and load blocks need enough weight to overhaul the line from the highest hook position for the boom or boom and jib lengths and parts of line in use [29cfr1926.1433(d)(2)]. Hook and ball assemblies and load blocks must be marked with capacity and weight [29cfr1926.1433(d)(3)]. Unlatched or disabled-latch hooks are barred unless the stated exception applies [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(ii)]: a qualified person determines going without is safer [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(ii)(A)], and routes are pre-planned so only employees needed for hooking or unhooking must work in the fall zone [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(ii)(B)]. Latches must close the throat and be designed to retain slings or other devices when rigging is slack [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(iii)].

Keep in mind that required and original manufacturer warnings must be maintained legible [29cfr1926.1433(d)(5)], with an accessible fire extinguisher on the equipment [29cfr1926.1433(d)(6)]. Remaining provisions address cabs, including a 250-pound roof workstation limit without permanent distortion, guarding, exhaust, lines, friction mechanisms and hydraulic drums [29cfr1926.1433(d)].

Check capacity (opening line: more than 2,000 pounds) [29cfr1926.1433]; paragraph (d) refers to "All equipment covered by this subpart" [29cfr1926.1433(d)]. Before November 8, 2010, crawler, truck and locomotive cranes must meet applicable requirements in ANSI B30.5-1968, PCSA Std. No. 2 (1968), paragraph (b), or applicable DIN standards in effect at manufacture [29cfr1926.1433(a)]; prototype testing follows (a) [29cfr1926.1433-note-1]. From that date, mobile and locomotive cranes meet listed ASME B30.5-2004 portions [29cfr1926.1433(b)], with exclusions and limits; for rotation resistant rope in the boom hoist item, § 1926.1414(c)(4)(ii)(A) applies [29cfr1926.1433(b)(4)]. Their prototypes use Option A or B; tower cranes made then or later use BS EN 14439:2006 [29cfr1926.1433(c)]. A requires SAE J1063 (cantilevered) or J987 (pendant supported lattice) tests and margins [29cfr1926.1433(c)(1)]. B requires BS EN 13000:2004 plus modeling of SAE load cases and margins; SAE physical testing applies unless modeling reliability has documented strain-gauge verification, alone or with other physical testing [29cfr1926.1433(c)(2)].

Verify minimum cab information (see § 1926.1417(c)) [29cfr1926.1433(d)(1)], hook/block weight and markings [29cfr1926.1433(d)(2)] [29cfr1926.1433(d)(3)], warnings and extinguisher [29cfr1926.1433(d)(5)] [29cfr1926.1433(d)(6)]. For latchless use, check both listed items, which (d)(4)(i) calls "requirements" [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(i)] [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(ii)]; check latch design [29cfr1926.1433(d)(4)(iii)].

Check cab ventilation, doors, windows, passageway and 250-pound roof capacity without permanent distortion [29cfr1926.1433(d)(7)]; guarding, and insulation or guarding of hot components, subject to maintenance/repair-employee exceptions [29cfr1926.1433(d)(8)] [29cfr1926.1433(d)(9)]; lines and exhaust [29cfr1926.1433(d)(10)] [29cfr1926.1433(d)(11)]; friction capacity and adjustment [29cfr1926.1433(d)(12)]; and drum holding device or brake [29cfr1926.1433(d)(13)].

Employer obligations under (a)-(c) and (d)(7)-(13) are met where equipment is unchanged, except under § 1926.1434, and manufacturer documentation shows compliant design, construction and testing; (d)(1)-(6) are outside this provision [29cfr1926.1433(e)].

This section is about changing equipment or adding something to it. If a change affects "the capacity or safe operation of the equipment," it is prohibited unless the requirements of one of five routes are met [29cfr1926.1434(a)].

In the first route, the manufacturer approves the change in writing. Load charts, procedures, manuals and instruction plates, tags and decals are updated as needed to match. The equipment's original safety factor must not be reduced [29cfr1926.1434(a)(1)].

The other routes rely on a registered professional engineer who is also a qualified person for that equipment. This engineer approves the change, states which equipment setups the approval covers, and updates those documents and labels as needed. Again, the original safety factor must not be reduced [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)]. These routes cover a manufacturer that has been asked but declines to review, or does not acknowledge or start within 30 days [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)]; one that is unavailable [29cfr1926.1434(a)(3)]; one that agrees to review but does not finish within 120 days [29cfr1926.1434(a)(4)]; and certain marine equipment with parts from several manufacturers [29cfr1926.1434(a)(5)].

If the manufacturer reviews the technical safety merits, rejects the proposal and explains why in writing, the change is prohibited [29cfr1926.1434(b)]. Paragraphs (a) and (b) do not apply to changes made or approved by the U.S. military [29cfr1926.1434(c)].

Modifications or additions affecting capacity or safe operation are prohibited unless the requirements of (a)(1), (2), (3), (4) or (5) are met [29cfr1926.1434(a)]. Manufacturer approval must be written, affected load charts, procedures, manuals and plates/tags/decals must be modified as necessary, and the original safety factor must not be reduced [29cfr1926.1434(a)(1)].

The refusal route requires giving the manufacturer a detailed description and asking for approval. It applies if the manufacturer declines to review the technical merits, or fails within 30 days to acknowledge the request or initiate review [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)]. A registered professional engineer, qualified for the equipment, must approve the change, specify the configurations covered, and modify those materials as necessary [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)(i)]. The original safety factor must not be reduced [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)(ii)].

Those engineer and safety-factor requirements also apply when the manufacturer is unavailable [29cfr1926.1434(a)(3)]; when it agrees to review but does not complete review within 120 days of receiving the detailed description [29cfr1926.1434(a)(4)]; or when equipment designed for marine work sites has major structural components from more than one manufacturer [29cfr1926.1434(a)(5)].

A rejection after technical safety review, explained in a written response, means the change is prohibited. Without written reasons, the employer may treat rejection as refusal to review under (a)(2) [29cfr1926.1434(b)]. U.S. military-made or military-approved modifications are outside paragraphs (a) and (b) [29cfr1926.1434(c)].

First determine whether the modification or addition affects capacity or safe operation; if so, it is prohibited unless a listed exception's requirements are met [29cfr1926.1434(a)]. Check whether it was made or approved by the U.S. military, in which case paragraphs (a) and (b) do not apply [29cfr1926.1434(c)].

For (a)(1), check written manufacturer approval, necessary changes to load charts, procedures, instruction manuals and plates/tags/decals, and an unreduced original safety factor [29cfr1926.1434(a)(1)].

For (a)(2), check that the manufacturer received a detailed description and approval request, then declined technical review or failed, within 30 days, to acknowledge or initiate it [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)]. Verify the engineer is registered and a qualified person for the equipment, approved the change, specified applicable configurations, and modified materials as necessary [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)(i)]; verify the safety factor [29cfr1926.1434(a)(2)(ii)].

Both (a)(2)(i) and (ii) also apply to an unavailable manufacturer [29cfr1926.1434(a)(3)] and marine-design equipment with multiple manufacturers' major structural components [29cfr1926.1434(a)(5)]. Under (a)(4), they apply where the manufacturer received the description and request, agreed to review, but missed completion within 120 days of receiving the description [29cfr1926.1434(a)(4)].

Check any rejection: following technical safety review, one with written reasons means prohibition. Without written reasons, the employer may treat it as refusal under (a)(2) [29cfr1926.1434(b)].

These are extra rules for tower cranes. The rest of the subpart also applies unless specified otherwise [29cfr1926.1435(a)]. Listed assembly and disassembly rules cover erecting, climbing and dismantling, except as otherwise specified [29cfr1926.1435(b)(1)]. On self-erecting cranes, stay out from in or under the tower, jib or rotating part during this work until it is locked and the competent person says entry is safe. The exception is when manufacturer instructions direct otherwise and only necessary personnel are there [29cfr1926.1435(b)(2)].

The manufacturer or a registered professional engineer (RPE) designs foundations and supports [29cfr1926.1435(b)(3)]. The A/D director checks their installation and addresses other listed hazards, including backward stability and wind limits [29cfr1926.1435(b)(4)]. A qualified person verifies the tower is plumb. Without a manufacturer tolerance, it needs at least 1:500 (about 1 inch in 40 feet) [29cfr1926.1435(b)(5)]. Fixed jib cranes may pass over each other but must be unable to contact another crane's structure [29cfr1926.1435(b)(6)]. Climbing requires following manufacturer prohibitions and RPE verification of host-structure strength [29cfr1926.1435(b)(7)]. Counterweight and ballast rules [29cfr1926.1435(b)(8)] and sign rules [29cfr1926.1435(c)] also apply.

Required safety devices include stops, brakes and controls. Work cannot start unless they work. If one fails, the operator safely stops, and no substitute measures are allowed [29cfr1926.1435(d)(3)]. Operational aids, such as limiting devices and indicators, can have specified temporary measures [29cfr1926.1435(e)(3)]. These include marked cables, or spotters within 10 feet of trolley or rail end stops [29cfr1926.1435(e)(5)]. Category I repairs are due within 7 calendar days [29cfr1926.1435(e)(5)], and Category II within 30 [29cfr1926.1435(e)(6)], with parts-order exceptions. Some device requirements cover cranes made after November 8, 2011, including one keeping the last 2 hoist-cable wraps on the drum [29cfr1926.1435(e)(5)(iv)].

A qualified person inspects each component before erection [29cfr1926.1435(f)(2)]. Every erection is followed by a load test [29cfr1926.1435(f)(3)(i)]. Monthly and annual checks add items such as bolts [29cfr1926.1435(f)].

Subpart rules apply unless specified otherwise [29cfr1926.1435(a)], including §§1926.1403–.1406 for erecting, climbing and dismantling, except as otherwise specified [29cfr1926.1435(b)(1)]. Self-erecting cranes have an entry restriction until locked and cleared, with a manufacturer-instruction exception [29cfr1926.1435(b)(2)]. Foundations need manufacturer or registered professional engineer (RPE) design [29cfr1926.1435(b)(3)]. The A/D director addresses §1926.1404(h)(1)–(9), installation per design, backward stability and wind [29cfr1926.1435(b)(4)]. Plumb defaults to at least 1:500 (approximately 1 inch in 40 feet) absent a manufacturer tolerance; a qualified person verifies it [29cfr1926.1435(b)(5)]. Multiple hammerheads may overfly but not be able to contact another's structure [29cfr1926.1435(b)(6)]. Climbing [29cfr1926.1435(b)(7)], counterweight/ballast [29cfr1926.1435(b)(8)] and signs [29cfr1926.1435(c)] have manufacturer or RPE controls.

Safety devices cover stops, rail clamps, hydraulic protections, automatic-setting brakes, control levers and an emergency stop [29cfr1926.1435(d)(2)]. All must work before starting. On failure, stop safely; the crane leaves service until repair, without alternative measures [29cfr1926.1435(d)(3)]. For a failed operational aid, stop until temporary measures are in place or it works [29cfr1926.1435(e)(4)]. Follow any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1435(e)(3)].

Category I covers travel, boom, two-block, drum, moment and line-pull limits plus boom-drum locking. Repair within 7 calendar days; if parts are documented as ordered within 7, repair within 7 of receipt [29cfr1926.1435(e)(5)]. Alternatives include marks, spotters, radius and load determination, capacity checks or manual setting. Trolley Option B and rail travel require communicating spotters within 10 feet of end stops. Post-November 8, 2011 cranes need protection for the last 2 drum wraps.

Category II covers angle/radius, deceleration, wind and load indicators. The limit is 30 days; with parts documented as ordered within 7 but arriving too late, 7 from receipt [29cfr1926.1435(e)(6)]. The post-November 8, 2011 condition applies to hammerhead radius and load indicators. Alternatives include measurements, cab notices, wind information or estimates, and load-weight determination.

Inspections include pre-erection, post-erection load testing, monthly and annual items [29cfr1926.1435(f)].

Check other subpart requirements [29cfr1926.1435(a)], §§1926.1403–.1406 with substituted terms [29cfr1926.1435(b)(1)], and self-erector entry controls beyond §1926.1404(e) [29cfr1926.1435(b)(2)]. Verify manufacturer or registered professional engineer (RPE) foundation design [29cfr1926.1435(b)(3)]; A/D director coverage of §1926.1404(h)(1)–(9), installation, stability and wind [29cfr1926.1435(b)(4)]; qualified-person plumb verification, defaulting to 1:500 (approximately 1 inch in 40 feet) minimum tolerance [29cfr1926.1435(b)(5)]; hammerhead separation [29cfr1926.1435(b)(6)]; climbing prohibitions and RPE host verification [29cfr1926.1435(b)(7)]; counterweight/ballast [29cfr1926.1435(b)(8)]; and signs, including written RPE approval when specifications are unavailable [29cfr1926.1435(c)].

§§1926.1415 and .1416 do not apply [29cfr1926.1435(d)(1)] [29cfr1926.1435(e)(1)]. Check required stops, clamps, hydraulics, automatic brakes, controls and emergency stop [29cfr1926.1435(d)(2)], including shutdown without alternatives [29cfr1926.1435(d)(3)]; see §1926.1417(f). For aids, check temporary and more protective manufacturer measures, with §1926.1417(j) [29cfr1926.1435(e)(3)]. Unavailable replacements permit same-function substitutes, not considered §1926.1434 modifications [29cfr1926.1435(e)(4)].

Category I: repair within 7 calendar days, or, with documented ordering within 7 of occurrence, within 7 of receipt. Verify limiter and locking functions and their specific alternatives, including 10 feet spotter thresholds (trolley Option B; rail) and last 2 wraps protection for cranes manufactured after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1435(e)(5)].

Category II: 30 days; documented ordering within 7 plus receipt too late for timely repair allows 7 from receipt. Check indicators, deceleration, wind-device mounting and alternatives. Hammerhead radius and load-display requirements specify manufacture after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1435(e)(6)].

Apply §1926.1412, substituting "erection" for "assembly," and §1926.1413 [29cfr1926.1435(f)(1)]. Check pre-erection component findings, rejection or repair/reinspection, and monitoring documentation [29cfr1926.1435(f)(2)]; certified or certified-scale-weighed test loads and procedures, beyond §1926.1412(c) [29cfr1926.1435(f)(3)]; monthly structural bolts and support attachments [29cfr1926.1435(f)(4)]; and annual turntable/tower bolt condition and torque, beyond §1926.1412(f) [29cfr1926.1435(f)(5)].

A derrick is powered lifting equipment with a mast, or a similar part, held by guys or braces, plus a hoisting mechanism. It may have a boom. Types include guy, stiffleg and gin pole, though not gin poles for erecting communication towers. These rules add to the rest of the subpart, which applies unless specified otherwise [29cfr1926.1436(a)]. Your employer must train you, as an operator, to safely operate your equipment [29cfr1926.1436(q)]. A competent person must supervise derrick work [29cfr1926.1436(o)], and the A/D director supervises jumping the derrick [29cfr1926.1436(n)].

Load charts show rated capacity and other setup details [29cfr1926.1436(b)(2)]. Guy derricks need at least 6 equally spaced guys unless a qualified person or the manufacturer approves variations and adjusts rated capacity [29cfr1926.1436(c)(2)(i)]. Stiffleg masts need at least two stifflegs [29cfr1926.1436(c)(3)(i)]. Construction and anchoring rules also apply [29cfr1926.1436(c)] [29cfr1926.1436(d)].

New hoists are load tested at 110% to 125% of rated capacity unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise [29cfr1926.1436(e)(2)(ii)]. Before first use, new or reinstalled derricks need anchorage approval, a no-load function test and a load test [29cfr1926.1436(g)]. Test loads are generally 100% to 110% of rated capacity, never below the maximum expected load; the manufacturer or a qualified person may recommend otherwise than that range [29cfr1926.1436(g)(3)(i)].

Without a working boom angle indicator, marked cable or a warning or automatic stopping device is required [29cfr1926.1436(f)(2)]. Certain newer derricks rated over 6,000 pounds need a load-related aid [29cfr1926.1436(f)(3)(i)]. Faulty load weight or capacity devices generally must be repaired within 30 days [29cfr1926.1436(f)(3)(ii)].

If power fails, safely stop, set brakes or locks, and turn clutch and power controls off [29cfr1926.1436(j)]. When holding the boom still, engage its positive holding mechanisms [29cfr1926.1436(m)(1)]. For 30 days or more out of service, secure it by a listed method [29cfr1926.1436(m)(2)]. Check guy tension daily [29cfr1926.1436(p)(1)].

Section 1926.1417 applies except paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1436(b)(1)]. Charts cover capacities by boom angle or radius, component lengths and reeving; rope size and construction go there or in the operating manual [29cfr1926.1436(b)(2)]. Post charts visibly on permanent fixed-length installations; keep them readily available on site for non-permanent ones [29cfr1926.1436(b)(3)]. A competent person supervises operations [29cfr1926.1436(o)], the A/D director supervises jumping [29cfr1926.1436(n)], and employers train operators [29cfr1926.1436(q)].

Guy derricks need at least 6 equally spaced guys unless a qualified person or the manufacturer approves variations and revises capacity [29cfr1926.1436(c)(2)(i)]. Required guy data must be held, with more for those made after December 18, 1970 [29cfr1926.1436(c)(2)]. Stifflegs number at least two [29cfr1926.1436(c)(3)(i)]. Gin poles must not be used in unstable positions [29cfr1926.1436(c)(4)(i)].

Without a working boom angle indicator, use visible caution and stop cable marks or a limit-warning or preventing device [29cfr1926.1436(f)(2)]. Derricks made more than one year after November 8, 2010, rated over 6,000 pounds, need a load weighing device, load moment indicator, or rated capacity indicator or limiter. Under "Temporary alternative measures", the operator gets the load weight, reliably determined, before lifting [29cfr1926.1436(f)(3)(i)]. Repair faulty load weight/capacity devices within 30 days; if parts are documented as ordered within 7 days but arrive too late, finish within 7 days of receipt [29cfr1926.1436(f)(3)(ii)].

New or reinstalled derricks need anchorage approval, functional and load testing, and documentation [29cfr1926.1436(g)]. Repairs or changes affecting capacity or safe operation require qualified-person evaluation for load testing [29cfr1926.1436(h)].

On power failure, safely stop, set brakes or locks, and move clutch and power controls off [29cfr1926.1436(j)]. Winch-head rope handling requires your knowledge; during use, stay within reach of the power control lever [29cfr1926.1436(k)]. Engage positive holding mechanisms for a fixed boom. Out 30 days or more, lay it down or sling-secure it to a stationary member; guy and stiffleg derricks have additional options [29cfr1926.1436(m)]. Inspect guy tension daily [29cfr1926.1436(p)(1)].

Verify scope; communication-tower erection gin poles are excluded from the definition [29cfr1926.1436(a)]. Check chart content and location [29cfr1926.1436(b)]; 1926.1417(c) is excepted [29cfr1926.1436(b)(1)]. Check design stresses and welding to ANSI/AWS D14.3-94 or AWS D1.1/D1.1M:2002 [29cfr1926.1436(c)(1)]. Guy derricks: at least 6 equally spaced guys, absent qualified-person or manufacturer-approved variation with revised capacity; guy data, including post-December 18, 1970 items; mast base and cap [29cfr1926.1436(c)(2)]. Check stiffleg (at least two), gin pole and Chicago boom criteria [29cfr1926.1436(c)(3)] [29cfr1926.1436(c)(4)] [29cfr1926.1436(c)(5)], anchoring data and design [29cfr1926.1436(d)], and swinger, boom and hoist suitability and anchorage [29cfr1926.1436(e)(1)].

Base-mounted drum hoists: specified ASME B30.7-2001 provisions, with exceptions [29cfr1926.1436(e)(2)(i)]. New hoists: test 110% to 125% unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise; manufacturer testing satisfies this [29cfr1926.1436(e)(2)(ii)]. Check repaired-hoist evaluation, test procedure and competent-person pass determination [29cfr1926.1436(e)(2)(iii)] [29cfr1926.1436(e)(2)(iv)].

Check 1926.1416 exceptions and boom-angle alternatives [29cfr1926.1436(f)]. Over 6,000 pounds, manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010: verify a listed load device; see temporary measures and 1926.1417(j) [29cfr1926.1436(f)(3)(i)]. Repair: 30 days; exception requires documented parts ordering within 7 days, late receipt, and completion within 7 days after receipt [29cfr1926.1436(f)(3)(ii)].

New/reinstalled: anchorage approval, any needed rock/hairpin testing, competent-person functional and load tests [29cfr1926.1436(g)]. Load: 100% to 110% unless manufacturer or qualified person recommends otherwise, never below maximum anticipated [29cfr1926.1436(g)(3)(i)]. Records need date, results, tester; retain until retest or dismantling, whichever first, available to 1926.1412 inspectors [29cfr1926.1436(g)(4)]. Check modified-derrick evaluations and required testing/documentation [29cfr1926.1436(h)].

Check power-failure, winch and boom-securing duties, including 30 days or more out of service [29cfr1926.1436(j)] [29cfr1926.1436(k)] [29cfr1926.1436(m)]; supervision [29cfr1926.1436(n)] [29cfr1926.1436(o)]; daily guy tension and annual gudgeon pin and foundation items [29cfr1926.1436(p)]; operator training. Section 1926.1427 does not apply [29cfr1926.1436(q)].

These are extra rules for floating cranes and derricks, including land models on barges or other flotation. Other subpart rules apply unless stated otherwise. This section doesn't cover jacked barges fully supported by jacks deployed to the bed [29cfr1926.1437(a)].

Hazard areas need barriers, or warning signs plus high-visibility equipment markings, with training on the markings [29cfr1926.1437(c)(2)]. The usual keeping-clear-of-the-load section doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Added devices include a list and trim device, a house lock and, when a competent person finds wind matters, a wind indicator [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block devices are required only for hoisting people or over occupied cofferdams or shafts [29cfr1926.1437(f)(1)].

The vessel gets shift and monthly checks [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)], annual external inspections [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)], and internal surveys every four years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. A hazardous deficiency takes it out of service until fixed. Four-year inspection records are kept at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

With divers, a crane moving them does nothing else until all are aboard. The operator stays at the controls, and crane securing allows no shifting [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. The operator and diver's tender need clear sight or electronic signals [29cfr1926.1437(j)(3)]. Vessel load limits must be respected [29cfr1926.1437(k)(2)].

Permanently attached marine equipment follows water load charts, which consider at least 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. Maximum list and trim (two kinds of tilt) are each 5 degrees at 25 tons or less, 7 above that, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. It must be stable at 60 mph with 2 feet of freeboard (deck height above water) at rated capacity or high boom without load, and 1 foot at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]. Backward stability uses 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3].

Land cranes need reduced capacity ratings [29cfr1926.1437(n)(1)]. Vessel tilt is capped at the lowest applicable limit, never above 5 degrees [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)]. Decks stay above water and the whole bottom submerged [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Cranes are secured against shifting, with a limited exception for some mobile auxiliary cranes [29cfr1926.1437(n)].

This supplements the subpart for floating and barge-mounted cranes and derricks, excluding jacked barges fully supported by deployed jacks [29cfr1926.1437(a)]. Work area control applies except § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii); use barriers, or signs plus equipment markings and employee training [29cfr1926.1437(c)]. § 1926.1425 doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Add list/trim and house-lock devices, plus a wind indicator when a competent person finds wind relevant [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block applies only to personnel hoisting or hoisting over occupied cofferdams or shafts; listed work has load-weighing relief [29cfr1926.1437(f)]. Cab or no-cab information-access rules apply [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Competent persons inspect the flotation each shift and monthly [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)]. Annual external and four-year internal inspections require specified expertise; hazards remove the vessel from service, and flagged nonhazards are monitored [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. Document monthly, annual and four-year inspections; keep four-year records at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

Diver work requires dedicated crane use until all divers return, continuous control attendance, tender sightline or electronic signals, and no-shift securing [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. Don't exceed vessel environmental, operating or transit limits [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

For permanent marine equipment, follow water charts and their parameters; charts consider minimum 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim maximums, in degrees, are 5 each at 25 tons or less, 7 over 25, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. Stability: 60 mph with 2 ft freeboard at rated capacity or high boom/no load; 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; backward stability, high boom/no load/full back list, 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Employer-made equipment needs engineer-signed proof [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)].

Land equipment needs expert derating [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed the least of 5 degrees or the manufacturer's limit (qualified person's if unspecified), and must preserve above-water decks and a fully submerged bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Crane list/trim limits also apply [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(ii)]. Secure by attachment, corral, rails or centerline cable, except qualifying mobile auxiliaries under a plan [29cfr1926.1437(n)]. Both equipment categories have hull requirements [29cfr1926.1437(m)(5)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(7)].

Check scope and jacked-barge exclusion [29cfr1926.1437(a)]; (c)-(k) cover both categories [29cfr1926.1437(b)]. Verify area control, excluding §1926.1424(a)(2)(ii) [29cfr1926.1437(c)]; §1926.1425 is inapplicable [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Check devices, conditional wind indicator, anti two-block and load-weighing exceptions, and information access [29cfr1926.1437(e)] [29cfr1926.1437(f)] [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Beyond §1926.1412, verify shift/monthly competent-person, annual external and four-year internal vessel inspections, specified contents, expertise, hazard removal and monitoring [29cfr1926.1437(h)]. Records follow §1926.1412(e)(3) monthly and (f)(7) annual/four-year; four-year retention is minimum 4 years; inspectors under §1926.1412 get access during retention [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)]. Check diver controls [29cfr1926.1437(j)] and vessel load capability and limits, using qualified-person limits if manufacturer's are unavailable [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

Permanent marine equipment: water charts, all applicable parameters, minimum 40 mph [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim: 5/5 degrees at 25 tons or less, 7/7 over, excluding derricks; derricks 10/10 [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. At 60 mph, freeboard minimum is 2 ft at rated capacity and high boom/no load, 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; full-back-list, high-boom/no-load backward stability: 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Check employer-made engineer-signed documentation and hull strength, subdivision and void access [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(m)(5)].

Land equipment: verify location-specific, condition-based derating and qualified performer [29cfr1926.1437(n)(1)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed what preserves (n)(4), or the least of 5 degrees, manufacturer amount, or qualified-person amount if unspecified [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)]. Check separate crane limits [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(ii)], above-water decks and submerged entire bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Verify securing option requirements and qualified design [29cfr1926.1437(n)(5)]. Mobile auxiliaries on floating-crane decks need demonstrated implementation of signed, compliant plans and procedures, marked areas and conditions; exceedance requires Option (1), (2) or (4), omitting rails [29cfr1926.1437(n)(6)]. Check hull requirements, including anticipated deck loads [29cfr1926.1437(n)(7)].

This section tells you which rules apply to overhead and gantry cranes used in construction. The first question it raises is whether the crane is permanently installed in a facility.

If it is, the requirements of § 1910.179 apply, except § 1910.179(b)(1). The requirements of this subpart, called subpart CC, do not apply. This covers overhead and gantry cranes, wall cranes, storage bridge cranes and other listed or similar types [29cfr1926.1438(a)].

If the crane is "not permanently installed in a facility," a different mix applies. The covered types include bridge cranes, launching gantry cranes and similar equipment. It does not matter whether they travel on tracks, wheels or other means [29cfr1926.1438(b)(1)]. These cranes must follow many listed sections of Part 1926 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(i)] and selected parts of § 1910.179 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(A)].

The manufacture date also matters for these cranes. If a crane was made before September 19, 2001, § 1910.179(b)(2) applies [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(C)]. If it was made on or after that date, listed sections of a standard called ASME B30.2-2005 apply [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(iii)].

For overhead and gantry cranes used in construction, permanent installation in a facility decides the rule set. Permanently installed equipment follows § 1910.179, except paragraph (b)(1), and not subpart CC. This includes semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall, storage bridge and similar cranes [29cfr1926.1438(a)].

Equipment not permanently installed also includes overhead/bridge and launching gantry cranes, however it travels [29cfr1926.1438(b)(1)]. It must meet these:

First, §§ 1926.1400 through 1926.1414, 1926.1417 through 1926.1425, 1926.1426(d), 1926.1427 through 1926.1434, 1926.1437, 1926.1439 and 1926.1441 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(i)].

Second, selected provisions within paragraphs (b), (e), (f) and (h) of § 1910.179, plus paragraphs (g), (k) and (n) [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(A)].

Third, the definitions in § 1910.179(a). For "hoist" and "load," however, use § 1926.1401 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(B)].

Manufacture date adds another layer. Section 1910.179(b)(2) applies only to this equipment if manufactured before September 19, 2001 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(C)]. For equipment manufactured on or after that date, specified sections of ASME B30.2-2005 apply, including 2-3.5. In 2-3.5.1(b), 29 CFR 1910.147 replaces ANSI Z244.1 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(iii)].

For permanently installed equipment used in construction, apply § 1910.179, except (b)(1), and not subpart CC. Coverage includes overhead, gantry, semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall, storage bridge and others "having the same fundamental characteristics" [29cfr1926.1438(a)].

For equipment not permanently installed, coverage adds overhead/bridge cranes, launching gantry cranes and similar equipment, whatever its means of travel [29cfr1926.1438(b)(1)]. Verify against:

§§ 1926.1400-.1414, .1417-.1425, .1426(d), .1427-.1434, .1437, .1439 and .1441 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(i)].

§ 1910.179(b)(5),(6),(7); (e)(1),(3),(5),(6); (f)(1),(4); (g); (h)(1),(3); (k); and (n) [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(A)].

§ 1910.179(a) definitions, except "hoist" and "load," which take § 1926.1401 definitions [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(B)].

§ 1910.179(b)(2), only if manufactured before September 19, 2001 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(C)].

If manufactured on or after September 19, 2001, check ASME B30.2-2005, incorporated by reference (see § 1926.6): 2-1.3.1, 2-1.3.2, 2-1.4.1, 2-1.6, 2-1.7.2, 2-1.8.2, 2-1.9.1, 2-1.9.2, 2-1.11, 2-1.12.2, 2-1.13.7, 2-1.14.2, 2-1.14.3, 2-1.14.5, 2-1.15, 2-2.2.2, 2-3.2.1.1 and 2-3.5. In 2-3.5.1(b), substitute 29 CFR 1910.147 for ANSI Z244.1 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(iii)].

This section is about dedicated pile drivers. The starting point is simple: the rules in subpart CC apply to these machines "except as specified in this section" [29cfr1926.1439(a)]. This matters because you should not assume that a dedicated pile driver is outside subpart CC. You also should not assume that every part of it applies in the usual way. This section tells you where the differences are.

There are three specific differences. First, the provision labeled "Anti two-blocking device," which is Section 1926.1416(d)(3), "does not apply" [29cfr1926.1439(b)]. Second, Section 1926.1416(e)(4), covering "Load weighing and similar devices," has a date limit. It applies only to dedicated pile drivers made after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1439(c)]. To use this rule, you need to know when the machine was manufactured. Third, there is a limit within § 1926.1433. Out of that section, only paragraphs (d) and (e) apply to dedicated pile drivers [29cfr1926.1439(d)].

The text here names these other provisions but does not spell out what they require. To learn their requirements, you need to read those provisions themselves.

For work with dedicated pile drivers, subpart CC is the baseline. Its provisions apply "except as specified in this section" [29cfr1926.1439(a)]. The changes described here concern two paragraphs of § 1926.1416 and the application of § 1926.1433.

On anti two-blocking devices, Section 1926.1416(d)(3) "does not apply" [29cfr1926.1439(b)]. The statement is specific to that cited paragraph. This section does not use it to remove the rest of § 1926.1416.

On load weighing and similar devices, your deciding fact is the date of manufacture. Section 1926.1416(e)(4) "applies only to dedicated pile drivers manufactured after November 8, 2011" [29cfr1926.1439(c)]. When deciding whether that paragraph covers a particular machine, the test stated is when it was manufactured.

For § 1926.1433, the application is narrowed: "only §§ 1926.1433(d) and (e) apply to dedicated pile drivers" [29cfr1926.1439(d)]. The other parts of § 1926.1433 therefore do not apply to these machines.

This section identifies which provisions apply, do not apply, or apply conditionally. It does not state the content of the referenced requirements, so the cited provisions are where those details are found.

When verifying compliance for a dedicated pile driver, begin with the general rule: subpart CC provisions apply "except as specified in this section" [29cfr1926.1439(a)]. Any departure from subpart CC based on this section should therefore be matched to one of its specified exceptions or limits.

First, Section 1926.1416(d)(3), identified as "Anti two-blocking device," "does not apply" [29cfr1926.1439(b)]. This paragraph states no date condition for that exclusion.

Second, Section 1926.1416(e)(4), "Load weighing and similar devices," applies "only to dedicated pile drivers manufactured after November 8, 2011" [29cfr1926.1439(c)]. The applicability fact to check is the manufacture date. The stated condition is manufacture after that date.

Third, within § 1926.1433, "only §§ 1926.1433(d) and (e) apply to dedicated pile drivers" [29cfr1926.1439(d)]. A finding under another part of § 1926.1433 would fall outside what this paragraph makes applicable.

The cross-references are subpart CC generally, § 1926.1416(d)(3), § 1926.1416(e)(4), and § 1926.1433(d) and (e). This section does not define "dedicated pile drivers" or state the substance of the referenced requirements.

This section tells you which rules cover sideboom cranes. In general, "The provisions of this standard apply," but four sections are left out: § 1926.1402 on ground conditions, § 1926.1415 on safety devices, § 1926.1416 on operational aids, and § 1926.1427 on operator qualification and certification [29cfr1926.1440(a)].

Section 1926.1426, on free fall and controlled load lowering, also applies, except for § 1926.1426(a)(2)(i). Some sideboom cranes have a boom designed to free fall, called a "live boom". These are allowed only if they were "manufactured prior to November 8, 2010" [29cfr1926.1440(b)].

More requirements cover sideboom cranes mounted on wheel or crawler tractors. They must meet all the listed requirements from a consensus standard, ASME B30.14-2004 [29cfr1926.1440(c)]. The listed parts include load ratings [29cfr1926.1440(c)(1)], tractor travel [29cfr1926.1440(c)(2)], ropes and reeving accessories [29cfr1926.1440(c)(3)], booms [29cfr1926.1440(c)(4)], and several general requirements, such as exhaust gases and clutch and brake protection [29cfr1926.1440(c)(5)] [29cfr1926.1440(c)(8)]. The list also reaches rated load testing, operator qualifications, operating practices and moving the load. Some of these include only certain paragraphs or have limits [29cfr1926.1440(c)(9)] [29cfr1926.1440(c)(12)].

For sideboom cranes, this standard applies except §§ 1926.1402 (ground conditions), 1926.1415 (safety devices), 1926.1416 (operational aids) and 1926.1427 (operator qualification and certification) [29cfr1926.1440(a)]. Section 1926.1426 on free fall and controlled load lowering applies, except § 1926.1426(a)(2)(i). A sideboom crane whose boom is designed to free fall (live boom) is permitted only if manufactured before November 8, 2010 [29cfr1926.1440(b)].

If the crane is mounted on a wheel or crawler tractor, it must meet all the listed ASME B30.14-2004 requirements [29cfr1926.1440(c)]. These are Sections 14-1.1 (load ratings), 14-1.3 (travel), 14-1.5 (ropes and reeving accessories) and 14-1.7.1 (booms) [29cfr1926.1440(c)(1)] [29cfr1926.1440(c)(4)]. They also include 14-1.7.2 (exhaust gases), 14-1.7.3 (stabilizers, wheel-type tractors), 14-1.7.4 (welded construction) and 14-1.7.6 (clutch and brake protection) [29cfr1926.1440(c)(5)] [29cfr1926.1440(c)(8)].

The rated load test in 14-2.2.2 applies "only to equipment that has been altered or modified" [29cfr1926.1440(c)(9)]. From 14-3.1.2, paragraph (a) is included, without the phrase "When required by law." [29cfr1926.1440(c)(10)]. From 14-3.1.3, the included paragraphs are (e), (f)(1)-(f)(4), (f)(6), (f)(7), (h) and (i) [29cfr1926.1440(c)(11)]. From 14-3.2.3, they are (j), (l) and (m) [29cfr1926.1440(c)(12)].

Apply this standard to sideboom cranes, excluding §§ 1926.1402, 1926.1415, 1926.1416 and 1926.1427 [29cfr1926.1440(a)]. Section 1926.1426 applies "except § 1926.1426(a)(2)(i)". For a boom designed to free fall (live boom), check the manufacture date: it is permitted only if manufactured prior to November 8, 2010 [29cfr1926.1440(b)].

For sideboom cranes mounted on wheel or crawler tractors, verify all listed requirements of ASME B30.14-2004, incorporated by reference (see § 1926.6) [29cfr1926.1440(c)]. The cross-references are Sections 14-1.1, 14-1.3 and 14-1.5 [29cfr1926.1440(c)(1)] [29cfr1926.1440(c)(3)]; 14-1.7.1 through 14-1.7.4, as individually listed, and 14-1.7.6 [29cfr1926.1440(c)(4)] [29cfr1926.1440(c)(8)]. Section 14-1.7.3 is titled for stabilizers on "Wheel-Type Side Boom Tractors" [29cfr1926.1440(c)(6)].

Section 14-2.2.2 (rated load test) applies only to altered or modified equipment [29cfr1926.1440(c)(9)]. In 14-3.1.2 (operator qualifications), use paragraph (a), "except the phrase “When required by law.”" [29cfr1926.1440(c)(10)]. In 14-3.1.3 (operating practices), the listed paragraphs are (e), (f)(1)-(f)(4), (f)(6), (f)(7), (h) and (i); (f)(5) is not listed [29cfr1926.1440(c)(11)]. In 14-3.2.3 (moving the load), the listed paragraphs are (j), (l) and (m); (k) is not listed [29cfr1926.1440(c)(12)].

This section covers employers using equipment with a maximum rated lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less [29cfr1926.1441]. Your employer must also follow listed rules in this subpart, including rules on power lines, signals, fall protection and keeping clear of the load [29cfr1926.1441(a)].

Before you operate the equipment, your employer must train you to safely operate that type [29cfr1926.1441(e)]. Signal persons must be trained to properly use the signals that apply [29cfr1926.1441(f)]. The employer must ensure the equipment is not used "to hoist personnel" [29cfr1926.1441(j)].

The load chart must be available to the operator at the control station [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)(i)]. Operating information, including the operator's manual and hazard warnings, must be readily available [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)(ii)]. Sometimes capacities appear at the control station only electronically. If a failure then makes them inaccessible, the operator immediately stops or follows safe shut-down procedures until they are available [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)(iii)].

The employer also has duties for assembly [29cfr1926.1441(b)], operating procedures [29cfr1926.1441(c)], safety devices [29cfr1926.1441(d)], inspections [29cfr1926.1441(h)] and design by a qualified engineer [29cfr1926.1441(k)]. Certain newer equipment needs protection for a "two-block situation": a qualifying device, or a design that prevents damage or load failure [29cfr1926.1441(d)(2)]. "Newer" here means manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010.

For equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less, the employer must comply with listed subpart provisions, including ground conditions, assembly/disassembly, power lines, wire rope, signals, stop authority and fall protection [29cfr1926.1441(a)].

Assembly must also meet component, configuration and manufacturer-prohibition rules [29cfr1926.1441(b)(1)]. Choices affecting capacity or safe operation must follow manufacturer documents or meet approved-modification requirements. If manufacturer information is unavailable under the first route, a familiar registered professional engineer must give written approval [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(i)]. The equipment is inspected after assembly [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(ii)]. Applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1441(b)(3)] and operating procedures, including attachment use, must be followed [29cfr1926.1441(c)(1)]. Missing procedures trigger development duties [29cfr1926.1441(c)(2)].

Keep in mind that the load chart must be at the control station, and procedures and manuals readily available. If electronic-only capacities become inaccessible through failure, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until capacities are available [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)].

Original safety devices and aids are maintained, and equipment inspected, according to manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1441(d)(1)] [29cfr1926.1441(h)]. Equipment manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 needs compliant anti two-block protection or a protective design [29cfr1926.1441(d)(2)]. Operators need pre-operation training [29cfr1926.1441(e)], and signal persons need signal training [29cfr1926.1441(f)]. Hoisting personnel is prohibited [29cfr1926.1441(j)]. A qualified engineer must design the equipment [29cfr1926.1441(k)].

Applicability: maximum rated capacity of 2,000 pounds or less [29cfr1926.1441]. Check the provisions listed in [29cfr1926.1441(a)], spanning §§ 1926.1400 through 1926.1438 selectively; § 1926.1425(c)(3) (qualified rigger) is excepted.

Assembly: verify §§ 1926.1403 and 1926.1406 plus [29cfr1926.1441(b)(1)]. Capacity or safety-related components and configuration follow manufacturer documents or approved § 1926.1434 modifications; if those documents and information are unavailable, the manufacturer route requires written approval by a familiar registered professional engineer [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(i)]. Check post-assembly inspection (see § 1926.1412(c)) [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(ii)] and applicable prohibitions [29cfr1926.1441(b)(3)].

Operations: check manufacturer procedures, including attachments [29cfr1926.1441(c)(1)]. Under "Unavailable operation procedures," verify developed, enforced safe procedures; a qualified person develops operational-control procedures, and a familiar registered professional engineer develops and signs capacity procedures [29cfr1926.1441(c)(2)]. Check load-chart availability, readily available operating materials, and the electronic-capacity failure response [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)].

Verify original-device maintenance [29cfr1926.1441(d)(1)]. For manufacture more than one year after November 8, 2010, require a § 1926.1416(d)(3) anti two-block device or design preventing damage or load failure [29cfr1926.1441(d)(2)]. Also verify operator pre-operation training [29cfr1926.1441(e)], signal training [29cfr1926.1441(f)], manufacturer-based inspections [29cfr1926.1441(h)], no personnel hoisting [29cfr1926.1441(j)], and qualified-engineer design [29cfr1926.1441(k)].

This section covers railroad machines. It applies to equipment covered by this subpart that also fits the meaning of "roadway maintenance machine" in 49 CFR 214.7. The basic rule is that employers using it must follow this subpart.
