There are seven exceptions, (b)(1) through (7), tied to being "subject to the authority of the Federal Railroad Administration" [29cfr1926.1442(a)].

The subpart's operator qualification, certification and training sections do not apply. Some other qualification and training rules also drop out, including those for equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less [29cfr1926.1442(b)(1)]. Certain rules on rail clamps, rail stops and work-area controls do not apply [29cfr1926.1442(b)(2)]. The same is true for limits on out-of-level work, rules on crane-level indicators and their inspection [29cfr1926.1442(b)(3)], and the cited ban on dragging a load sideways [29cfr1926.1442(b)(4)].

A boom-hoist limiting device is one named requirement. It does not apply to these machines when the cranes raise their booms with hydraulic cylinders [29cfr1926.1442(b)(5)]. Finally, certain requirements to follow the manufacturer's guidance, including for modifications, do not apply if the employer is subject to 49 CFR part 214 [29cfr1926.1442(b)(6)] [29cfr1926.1442(b)(7)]. These two exceptions reach only the provisions they cite.

For subpart equipment meeting the 49 CFR 214.7 definition of "roadway maintenance machine," employers must comply with this subpart, except as paragraphs (b)(1) through (7) provide when subject to Federal Railroad Administration authority [29cfr1926.1442(a)].

Sections 1926.1427 and 1926.1430 do not apply. Nor do the qualification and training requirements for derricks, sideboom cranes, and equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less in the cited provisions [29cfr1926.1442(b)(1)].

Also removed are the rail clamp and rail stop requirements in § 1926.1415(a)(6) and the work-area controls in § 1926.1424(a)(2) [29cfr1926.1442(b)(2)]. Out-of-level work restrictions and requirements for crane-level indicators and their inspections do not apply [29cfr1926.1442(b)(3)]. Neither does the § 1926.1417(q) prohibition on dragging a load sideways [29cfr1926.1442(b)(4)].

The § 1926.1416(d)(1) boom-hoist limiting device requirement is lifted for roadway maintenance machines "when the cranes use hydraulic cylinders to raise the booms" [29cfr1926.1442(b)(5)].

If the employer is subject to 49 CFR part 214, the manufacturer-guidance requirements set forth in § 1926.1434 for modifications do not apply [29cfr1926.1442(b)(6)]. Under the same condition, specified manufacturer guidance, instructions, procedures, prohibitions, limitations or specifications in listed provisions of §§ 1926.1404, 1926.1415, 1926.1417, 1926.1433 and 1926.1441 also do not apply [29cfr1926.1442(b)(7)].

Check coverage: subpart equipment meeting the 49 CFR 214.7 "roadway maintenance machine" definition. The subpart applies, except as (b)(1) through (7) provide "when subject to the authority of the Federal Railroad Administration" [29cfr1926.1442(a)].

Excluded: §§ 1926.1427 and 1926.1430, plus qualification and training requirements in §§ 1926.1436(q), 1926.1440(a), and 1926.1441(a) (2,000 pounds or less) [29cfr1926.1442(b)(1)]; § 1926.1415(a)(6) rail clamps [29cfr1926.1442(b)(2)(i)] and rail stops [29cfr1926.1442(b)(2)(ii)]; § 1926.1424(a)(2) work-area controls [29cfr1926.1442(b)(2)(iii)]; out-of-level restrictions and crane-level indicator and indicator-inspection requirements, including §§ 1926.1402(b), 1926.1412(d)(1)(xi), and 1926.1415(a)(1) [29cfr1926.1442(b)(3)]; and § 1926.1417(q) side-dragging [29cfr1926.1442(b)(4)].

For § 1926.1416(d)(1), verify that cranes raise booms with hydraulic cylinders [29cfr1926.1442(b)(5)].

For manufacturer-based relief, check whether the employer is subject to 49 CFR part 214. This condition governs § 1926.1434 modification guidance [29cfr1926.1442(b)(6)]. It also governs requirements to follow manufacturer guidance, instructions, procedures, prohibitions, limitations, or specifications in § 1926.1404(j), (m), or (q); § 1926.1415(a)(6); § 1926.1417(a), (r), (u), or (aa); § 1926.1433(d)(1)(i); or § 1926.1441 [29cfr1926.1442(b)(7)].

Rigging is checked before use on each shift, and as needed during use; defective gear comes out of service [29cfr1926.251(a)(1)]. Each day before use, a competent person chosen by the employer checks slings, fastenings and attachments. Damaged or defective slings are removed immediately [29cfr1926.251(a)(6)]. Rigging needs legible maker's load markings and must stay within them [29cfr1926.251(a)(2)]. Idle gear leaves the immediate work area [29cfr1926.251(a)(3)]. Special custom lifting accessories are marked and first proof-tested to 125 percent of rated load [29cfr1926.251(a)(4)].

For chain, attachments must be at least as strong as the chain [29cfr1926.251(b)(2)]; makeshift ones are banned [29cfr1926.251(b)(3)]. Chain worn beyond Table H-1 is removed [29cfr1926.251(b)(5)]. Thorough chain checks occur at least every 12 months [29cfr1926.251(b)(6)(i)].

For wire rope, eye splices generally need three full tucks, and rope is removed if broken wires exceed 10 percent within eight diameters, or for other wear, corrosion or defects [29cfr1926.251(c)(4)]. Table H-2 sets clip number and spacing [29cfr1926.251(c)(5)]. Never shorten slings with knots, bolts or makeshift devices [29cfr1926.251(c)(6)]. Keep fingers and hands from between a tightening sling and load [29cfr1926.251(c)(10)]. "Shock loading is prohibited." [29cfr1926.251(c)(11)] Minimum lengths are 10, 40 or 96 times diameter, by sling type [29cfr1926.251(c)(13)]. Heat above 200 °F retires fiber-core slings; for other cores above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F, follow the maker [29cfr1926.251(c)(14)]. Welded end attachments need proof testing at twice capacity [29cfr1926.251(c)(15)(ii)].

Fiber splices need three (eye) or six (short) tucks in manila, four or eight in synthetic. Tails extend six diameters under 1 inch, otherwise 6 inches; tapered tails need two extra tucks. Eye angles cannot exceed 60 degrees, and clear length between eye splices is 10 diameters [29cfr1926.251(d)(4)]. The usual range is minus 20 °F to plus 180 °F [29cfr1926.251(d)(3)]. Web limits are 180 °F for polyester and nylon, 200 °F for polypropylene [29cfr1926.251(e)(7)]. Damage such as cuts means immediate removal [29cfr1926.251(d)(6)] [29cfr1926.251(e)(8)]. Hooks without applicable maker guidance are tested at twice intended load first [29cfr1926.251(f)(2)].

Inspect rigging before use each shift and as necessary during use [29cfr1926.251(a)(1)]. A designated competent person checks slings and attachments daily before use, and during use where conditions warrant [29cfr1926.251(a)(6)]. Remove defective gear. Stay within marked capacities, never use unmarked rigging [29cfr1926.251(a)(2)], and clear idle gear from the immediate work area [29cfr1926.251(a)(3)]. Proof-test special custom accessories to 125 percent before use and mark safe loads [29cfr1926.251(a)(4)].

Chain attachments must match chain capacity [29cfr1926.251(b)(2)]; no makeshift fasteners [29cfr1926.251(b)(3)]. Apply Table H-1 wear limits [29cfr1926.251(b)(5)]. Thorough inspection intervals depend on use and experience, never exceeding 12 months [29cfr1926.251(b)(6)(i)].

Wire eye splices need three full tucks or a qualifying equally efficient alternative. Remove rope showing excessive wear, corrosion or defect, or visible broken wires above 10 percent in eight diameters. Clips or knots cannot form eyes in bridles, slings or bull wires [29cfr1926.251(c)(4)]. U-bolt clips follow Table H-2, with the U on the dead end for eye splices [29cfr1926.251(c)(5)]. Pad sharp edges [29cfr1926.251(c)(9)]; shock loading is banned [29cfr1926.251(c)(11)]. Minimum lengths: cable laid, 6 × 19 and 6 × 37, 10 diameters; braided, 40; grommets and endless, 96 [29cfr1926.251(c)(13)]. Fiber-core slings exposed above 200 °F are permanently retired; nonfiber-core use above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F follows maker advice [29cfr1926.251(c)(14)]. Welded end attachments require twice-capacity proof testing [29cfr1926.251(c)(15)(ii)].

Fiber splices need three eye or six short tucks in manila, four or eight in synthetic. Tails project six diameters below 1 inch, or 6 inches otherwise; tapering takes two additional tucks. Eye angle maximum is 60 degrees; minimum clear length is 10 diameters [29cfr1926.251(d)(4)]. Minus 20 °F to plus 180 °F permits full working load; outside it, or wet frozen, follow the maker [29cfr1926.251(d)(3)]. Web limits: polyester/nylon 180 °F, polypropylene 200 °F [29cfr1926.251(e)(7)]. Observe chemical restrictions [29cfr1926.251(e)(6)] and removal triggers [29cfr1926.251(d)(6)] [29cfr1926.251(e)(8)]. Keep shackles within ratings [29cfr1926.251(f)(1)]; test hooks lacking applicable recommendations to twice intended load [29cfr1926.251(f)(2)].

Verify shift and in-use rigging inspections [29cfr1926.251(a)(1)], daily competent-person sling checks [29cfr1926.251(a)(6)], markings and loading [29cfr1926.251(a)(2)], idle storage [29cfr1926.251(a)(3)], and 125 percent proof tests with load marking for special custom accessories [29cfr1926.251(a)(4)]. Check sling scope [29cfr1926.251(a)(5)] and material-specific identification and capacity provisions [29cfr1926.251(b)(1)] [29cfr1926.251(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.251(c)(1)] [29cfr1926.251(c)(16)] [29cfr1926.251(d)(1)] [29cfr1926.251(d)(7)] [29cfr1926.251(e)(1)] [29cfr1926.251(e)(2)] [29cfr1926.251(f)(1)].

For chain, check attachments [29cfr1926.251(b)(2)] [29cfr1926.251(b)(3)], Table H-1 wear [29cfr1926.251(b)(5)], periodic inspections at most 12 months apart, and the available record of each sling's latest inspection month [29cfr1926.251(b)(6)].

For wire, check three-tuck eye splices or the qualifying alternative; continuity exceptions for end eye splices and endless slings; prohibited eyes; and removal for defects or over 10 percent visible broken wires within eight diameters [29cfr1926.251(c)(4)]. Knots are barred except on scraper haul back lines [29cfr1926.251(c)(3)]. Check Table H-2 [29cfr1926.251(c)(5)], handling rules [29cfr1926.251(c)(6)] through [29cfr1926.251(c)(12)], protected strand ends [29cfr1926.251(c)(2)], and 10, 40 and 96 diameter minimums [29cfr1926.251(c)(13)]. Temperature thresholds are 200 °F for fiber core, and above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F for nonfiber core [29cfr1926.251(c)(14)]. Except thimble covers, weld before assembly; require twice-capacity proof tests and retained, available certificates [29cfr1926.251(c)(15)].

Check fiber splices under both [29cfr1926.251(d)(2)] and [29cfr1926.251(d)(4)]: manila three eye/six short tucks; synthetic four/eight; tails six diameters below 1 inch, otherwise 6 inches; two extra tucks when tapered; maximum 60-degree eye angle. Also verify 10-diameter clear length, clamps and recommendations [29cfr1926.251(d)(4)], end edges [29cfr1926.251(d)(5)], removal [29cfr1926.251(d)(6)], and the minus 20 °F to plus 180 °F range and wet-frozen exception [29cfr1926.251(d)(3)].

For web slings, check construction, fittings and stitching [29cfr1926.251(e)(3)] [29cfr1926.251(e)(4)] [29cfr1926.251(e)(5)], chemicals [29cfr1926.251(e)(6)], 180 °F polyester/nylon and 200 °F polypropylene limits [29cfr1926.251(e)(7)], and removal [29cfr1926.251(e)(8)]. Hooks lacking applicable recommendations require twice-intended-load tests before initial use, with dates and results recorded [29cfr1926.251(f)(2)].

This appendix gives sample ways to lower the risk of a boom moving dangerously by accident during assembly or disassembly [29cfr1926.cc.appB]. The basic rule it describes is that when pins or similar devices are being removed, "employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components" unless an exception is met. The exception applies when the employer shows that site limits require someone to be there. The A/D director must then use procedures that reduce both the risk of unintended dangerous movement and how long and how much workers are exposed under the boom [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In one example, piping forces workers to take a boom apart in the air from an aerial lift. An assist crane supports the section being detached. Workers remove the far side pins first, move to the near side as soon as possible so they are no longer under the boom, then remove the near side pins [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

The center of gravity of a load must be identified if the method for keeping it stable requires this. If there is not enough information to find it accurately, measures must be used to prevent dangerous movement caused by getting it wrong. In an example, everyone stays clear while a section is raised a few inches to see whether it tips [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

For pin removal, the appendix cites § 1926.1404(f)(1): employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components unless § 1926.1404(f)(2) is met. That exception applies when the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be there. The A/D director must then implement procedures that "minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom" [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In the sample, aboveground piping prevents lowering the boom, and the aerial lift, based on the near side, cannot be repositioned, so its basket must go under the boom. A rigged assist crane supports the detaching section, with particular care that the end near the pin removers is well supported. Far side pins come out first, the basket returns to the near side as soon as possible, then near side pins come out [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

During assembly/disassembly, the load's center of gravity must be identified if the stability method requires it. With insufficient information, measures must prevent unintended dangerous movement from misidentifying it. In the sample, the director cannot determine the pick point above a non-symmetrical top section's center of gravity. With personnel clear, it is raised a few inches to check for tipping. If it tips, the hoist line is repositioned and the test repeated until the director determines it can be moved without dangerous movement [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

Check pin removal against § 1926.1404(f)(1), as summarized here: employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components while pins or similar devices are removed, except where § 1926.1404(f)(2) requirements are met. For the exception, the employer must demonstrate that "site constraints require one or more employees to be under the boom, jib, or other components" during removal. The A/D director must then implement procedures minimizing both the risk of unintended dangerous movement and the duration and extent of exposure [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

The sample involves aboveground piping preventing ground disassembly and lack of room preventing repositioning the aerial lift. Its measures are a rigged assist crane supporting the detaching section, particular care supporting the end near employees, and removing far side pins first, moving the basket near side as soon as possible, then removing near side pins [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

Under § 1926.1404(h)(6)(i), center of gravity identification during assembly/disassembly is required if necessary for the stability method. Under (h)(6)(ii), insufficient information for accurate identification requires measures designed to prevent unintended dangerous movement from inaccurate identification. The sample for (h)(6)(ii) keeps all personnel clear before and while raising the section a few inches. Tipping indicates it is not rigged over the center of gravity; repositioning and retesting continue until the director determines it is, and that it can be moved safely into place [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

This appendix is about what a crane operator's written exam on technical knowledge can be built around. It has information for employers, accredited testing organizations, auditors and government entities that are "developing criteria for a written examination" [29cfr1926.cc.appC]. For you, it is a map of knowledge topics. It sets out no numeric limits.

The first group is general technical knowledge. It starts with what the crane and its attachments can and cannot do [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(1)]. It also covers wire rope [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(2)] and rigging gear such as slings and lifting beams [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(3)]. Another topic is the limits of protections against electrical hazards, such as grounding [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(4)]. You will also see basic crane terms [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(6)], gauge readings [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(8)], and forces on the equipment from things like wind or impact [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(16)].

The site group includes judging whether the ground or surface can support the expected loads. Weak spots may be below the surface, such as voids, or on it, such as slopes [29cfr1926.cc.appC(b)(1)]. It also covers spotting hazards like power lines and traffic [29cfr1926.cc.appC(b)(3)], and reviewing plans with supervisors and other workers, such as the signal person [29cfr1926.cc.appC(b)(4)].

The operations group includes handling loads smoothly and safely [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(1)] and communicating on site [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(2)]. It includes checking load and rigging weight before the lift starts [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(8)]. It also includes securing equipment you leave unattended [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(5)] and responding to emergencies such as fires or power line contact [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(15)].

The last group is load charts. This means knowing the words used with them [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)(1)], making sure a chart fits the equipment's setup and use [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)(2)], and knowing how to use it [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)(3)].

Appendix C gives information to those developing criteria for a written test of an operator's technical knowledge of crane operation [29cfr1926.cc.appC]. It states no numeric limits. Its topics relate to daily work as follows.

Technical topics include crane and attachment limitations [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(1)], wire rope capacity, line pull and selection [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(2)], rigging devices [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(3)], limits of electrical protective measures and proximity to power lines, radii and microwave structures [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(4)], and multi-crane load share and transfer [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(5)]. Others include power flow systems [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(7)], instruments [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(8)], safety devices and operational aids [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(11)], net capacity for every possible configuration [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(13)], load dimensions, weight and center of gravity [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(15)], dynamic and side loading, and backward stability [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)].

Site topics cover ground support, mats, cribbing and supports, hazards, plan reviews (including working height, boom length, load radius and travel clearance), and room to extend crawlers, outriggers or stabilizers, and counterweights [29cfr1926.cc.appC(b)].

Operating topics include load handling, communication, reeving, changing conditions, shutdown, weather, leveling, verifying weights and radii, basic rigging and shift inspection [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)]. Operations such as personnel hoisting, pile driving or work on water are identified as requiring "specific procedures and skill levels" [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(12)]. Safe procedures are listed for conditions including traveling with suspended loads, power lines, reduced outrigger, crawler or stabilizer extension, and blind lifts [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(13)]. Load control, tag lines, emergencies such as overload or control malfunction, and outrigger use also appear [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)].

Load chart topics include choosing the appropriate chart, footnote limitations, configuration, structural versus stability limits, range diagrams, work area charts, "parts-of-line" information, and use with load indicators and/or load moment devices [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)].

Scope: this appendix "contains information" for employers, accredited testing organizations, auditors and government entities developing written examination criteria on technical knowledge of crane operation [29cfr1926.cc.appC]. Its text states no numeric limits, passing score or exceptions. When comparing criteria with it, the topic groups are these.

Paragraph (a) covers crane functions, wire rope, rigging, electrical protection limits, multi-crane effects, terms, power systems, instruments, hydraulic thermal effects, inspection background, devices, duty-cycle versus lifting work, capacity, attachments, load properties, dynamic and side loading, and backward stability [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)]. Wire rope background relates to inspection and removal criteria in § 1926.1413 and § 1926.1414 [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(2)(i)]. Safety devices and operational aids are those required under § 1926.1415 and § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(11)]. Net capacity covers "every possible configuration" using the manufacturer's load chart [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(13)].

Paragraph (b) covers surface and subsurface support weaknesses, supporting gear, site hazards, plan review and extension room [29cfr1926.cc.appC(b)].

Paragraph (c) covers handling, communication, reeving and block or ball selection, changing conditions, unattended shutdown, weather, leveling, weight and radius verification, rigging and tag lines [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)]. Handling on rubber tires, outriggers/stabilizers or crawlers is qualified "where applicable" [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(1)]. Shift inspection is that required in Subpart CC [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(11)]. Also check specialized operations, such as demolition or magnet work [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(12)]; special conditions, such as two-block approach or underwater lifts [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(13)]; emergency responses, from fires to carrier or travel malfunction [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(15)]; and outrigger/stabilizer use per manufacturer specifications [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(16)].

Paragraph (d) covers chart terminology, appropriateness, use and pairing with load indicators and/or load moment devices [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)]. Chart use includes limitations, footnotes, configuration, capacity basis and ratings, diagrams, work area charts and parts-of-line data [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)(3)].
